teile.einleitung: The Pugwash Conferences are meetings of scientists from all over the world who work for peace and against nuclear weapons. They began in 1957 in the small village of Pugwash in Canada. For their work they received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1995, together with Joseph Rotblat.
wichtigste: The first Pugwash Conference took place in 1957 in Pugwash in Canada.
22 scientists took part in it.
It was prompted by the Russell-Einstein Manifesto of 1955.
The businessman Cyrus Eaton invited the researchers to his home village.
The main aim is to reduce the danger of armed conflicts.
During the Cold War the conferences made unofficial talks between East and West possible.
In 1995 Joseph Rotblat and the Pugwash Conferences received the Nobel Peace Prize.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War the USA and the Soviet Union built more and more **nuclear weapons**. Many scientists were afraid that a nuclear war could wipe out all of humanity. In 1955 the British philosopher Bertrand Russell and other well-known researchers published the **Russell-Einstein Manifesto**. In it they called on researchers and governments to avoid wars peacefully. Albert Einstein signed it shortly before his death.

In 1957 the businessman **Cyrus Eaton** invited the scientists to his home village of Pugwash in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia. 22 scientists took part in the first conference. They came from countries on both sides of the **Cold War**, including the USA, the Soviet Union and Japan. They talked about the dangers of nuclear weapons and of radioactive radiation. The conferences are still named after this village today.

During the Cold War the governments of East and West often hardly talked to each other. The Pugwash Conferences made **unofficial talks** possible, in which researchers could discuss things openly. They passed the results on to their governments. In this way the conferences helped to prepare important **disarmament treaties**, such as treaties banning nuclear tests. The main aim was and is to reduce the danger of armed conflicts.

abschnitte.titel: Joseph Rotblat and the Nobel Prize
abschnitte.text: **Joseph Rotblat** was a physicist born in Poland who later lived in Great Britain. In the Second World War he first worked on the **Manhattan Project**, in which the USA developed the atomic bomb. But he was the only scientist to leave the project early for reasons of conscience. Later he was for a long time one of the most important figures in the Pugwash movement. In 1995, exactly 50 years after the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, he and the Pugwash Conferences received the **Nobel Peace Prize**.

The Pugwash Conferences still exist and take place in different countries. Today, as well as nuclear weapons, they deal with chemical and biological weapons, conflicts in various regions of the world and new technologies. In many countries there are national Pugwash groups and groups for young researchers. Geneva, where many international **disarmament talks** take place, is also an important place for such topics. The idea remains the same: science bears responsibility for peace.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bomb that gets its huge destructive power from splitting or fusing atomic nuclei.
The long tension between the USA and the Soviet Union after 1945 without a direct war between them.
Reducing the number of weapons.
A public declaration with important demands.

gewusst: The Russell-Einstein Manifesto was signed by eleven famous scientists, many of them Nobel Prize winners.
The village of Pugwash has only a few hundred inhabitants but has become world-famous through the conferences.
Joseph Rotblat lived to almost 97 and campaigned for a world without nuclear weapons until his death in 2005.

teile.einleitung: The Pyramids of Giza in Egypt are among the most famous buildings in the world. They were built about 4,500 years ago as huge tombs for three pharaohs. The largest of them, the Pyramid of Khufu, is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that is still standing today.
wichtigste: At Giza there are three large pyramids: the pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure.
The largest is the Pyramid of Khufu, which was originally about 146 metres high.
The pyramids lie on the west bank of the Nile on the edge of today's capital, Cairo.
They were built around 2600 to 2500 BC as tombs for pharaohs.
They consist mainly of huge stone blocks.
In front of the pyramids lies the Sphinx, a figure with a lion's body and a human head.
The Pyramid of Khufu is the only surviving one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

abschnitte.text: The pyramids stand on a plateau near the city of **Giza** on the west bank of the **Nile**. Today the huge city of Cairo borders directly on the site. The ancient Egyptians usually buried their dead in the west, where the Sun sets. That is why many large burial sites are on this side of the river.

The oldest and largest pyramid was built for Pharaoh **Khufu** (Cheops) around 2560 BC. Next to it stands the somewhat smaller pyramid of his son **Khafre** (Chephren), which looks almost the same size because it stands on higher ground. The third and smallest belongs to Pharaoh **Menkaure** (Mycerinus). Around the large pyramids there are also smaller pyramids for queens, as well as temples and tombs of officials.

The Pyramid of Khufu consists of about 2.3 million **stone blocks**, most of them limestone. Many blocks weigh more than two tonnes, and some granite blocks inside weigh many times that. The stones were quarried with copper tools and probably pulled up on sledges over **ramps**. They were not built by slaves, as was long believed, but by well-organised teams of workers who lived in their own settlement. Originally the pyramids were covered with smooth, light limestone slabs, which are missing almost everywhere today.

In front of the pyramids lies the **Sphinx** of Giza, a huge figure with the body of a lion and the head of a human. It was carved directly out of the rock and is about 73 metres long. Most researchers think that its face shows Pharaoh Khafre. The lion's body stood for strength, the human head for wisdom.

abschnitte.titel: Wonder of the world and importance
abschnitte.text: For almost 4,000 years the Pyramid of Khufu was the tallest building in the world. It is the only one of the **Seven Wonders** of the Ancient World that has survived. Since 1979 the pyramids have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Every year very many people from all over the world visit the site, and researchers with modern instruments are still discovering new hollow spaces inside.

begriffe.erklaerung: The title of the kings in ancient Egypt.
A building with a square base and triangular sides that meet in a point at the top.
A mythical figure with a lion's body and a human head.
One of seven especially admired buildings of ancient times.
A room inside a tomb in which the dead person was buried.

gewusst: The four sides of the Pyramid of Khufu are amazingly precisely aligned to north, south, east and west.
The Pyramid of Khufu is a few metres lower today than it used to be, because its tip and its casing are missing.
Even for the ancient Greeks and Romans the pyramids were ancient sights that they visited as tourists.

teile.einleitung: A perovskite solar cell is a new kind of solar cell that turns sunlight into electricity. It is made of materials with a special crystal structure called the perovskite structure. Researchers all over the world, including in Switzerland, are working to make these cells cheaper and longer-lasting.
wichtigste: The crystal structure of perovskites is described with the general formula ABX3.
The structure is named after the mineral perovskite, chemically calcium titanate.
Most of today's perovskite solar cells contain the toxic heavy metal lead.
Their biggest problem is their poor long-term stability.
They can be made from solutions at low temperatures.
In tandem solar cells with silicon, both layers use different parts of the solar spectrum.
The band gap can be changed deliberately by swapping the halide.

abschnitte.text: Originally, **perovskite** is a mineral made of calcium titanate. It was discovered in 1839 in the Urals and named after the Russian politician Lev Perovski. Today all substances with the same crystal structure are called perovskites. Their structure follows the formula **ABX3**, where A, B and X stand for different atoms or groups of atoms. In solar cells, compounds of lead, organic molecules and halides such as iodine or bromine are usually used.

When sunlight hits the thin perovskite layer, electrons in it are excited. They can then move freely and flow away as an electric **current**. How much light is used depends on the **band gap**, a property of the material. In perovskites the band gap can be changed deliberately, for example by replacing iodine with bromine. In this way the material can be adapted to particular colours of light.

The first perovskite solar cell was presented in 2009 in Japan and turned only a few per cent of the light into electricity. Within just over ten years its **efficiency** in the laboratory rose to over 25 per cent. That is about as good as the usual silicon cells on house roofs. Hardly any other solar technology has improved so quickly. A big advantage is that the layers can be made from solutions at low temperatures, almost like printing.

**Tandem solar cells** are especially promising. Here a perovskite layer lies on top of a silicon cell. The perovskite uses mainly the blue and green light, the silicon more the red and infrared. Together such cells reach efficiencies of over 30 per cent in the laboratory (as of about 2024). In Switzerland, for example, EPFL and CSEM in Neuchâtel are researching this technology.

The biggest problem is the poor **long-term stability**. Moisture, oxygen, heat and UV light can break the material down after a short time. But solar cells on roofs should last 20 years or more. In addition, most perovskite cells contain toxic **lead**, which must not get into the environment. So researchers are looking for better protective layers and lead-free materials.

At **EPFL in Lausanne**, Michael Grätzel developed the dye-sensitised solar cell named after him, also called the Grätzel cell, around 1991. His research team later also contributed a great deal to the development of perovskite solar cells. Grätzel is one of the most cited chemists in the world. His work made Lausanne an important centre of solar research.

begriffe.erklaerung: The regular arrangement of atoms in a solid substance.
What percentage of sunlight a solar cell turns into electricity.
A property of a material that decides which light a solar cell can use.
A solar cell made of two layers on top of each other that use different light.
A compound with elements such as iodine, bromine or chlorine.

gewusst: The perovskite layer in a solar cell is much thinner than a human hair.
The mineral perovskite was discovered as early as 1839, but its structure has only been used for solar cells since 2009.
Perovskite solar cells might one day be flexible and printed on films.

teile.einleitung: Rayleigh scattering explains why the sky is blue on a clear day. Tiny particles in the air deflect sunlight in all directions, and blue light much more strongly than red. It is named after the British physicist Lord Rayleigh.
wichtigste: Rayleigh scattering is the deflection of light by particles that are much smaller than the wavelength of light.
Blue light is scattered by the air much more strongly than red light.
That is why the sky looks blue on clear days.
At sunrise and sunset the sky looks red and orange, because the light takes a long path through the air.
There is no air on the Moon, so the sky there is black even during the day.
High in the mountains the sky is a darker blue, because there is less air above us.
The explanation comes from the British physicist Lord Rayleigh in the 19th century.

abschnitte.text: The light of the Sun looks white but contains all the colours of the **rainbow**. Each colour has a different **wavelength**: red light has long waves, blue and violet light short waves. In a rainbow, raindrops split sunlight into these colours. In the air something else happens: the light is scattered by tiny particles, that is, deflected in all directions.

The air consists mainly of nitrogen and oxygen particles, which are much smaller than a wave of light. With such particles, short-wavelength light is scattered much more strongly than long-wavelength light; this is called **Rayleigh scattering**. Blue light is scattered about five times more strongly than red. That is why it comes to our eyes from everywhere in the sky. Violet light is scattered even more strongly, but the Sun sends out less of it and our **eyes** see blue better, which is why we see a blue sky and not a violet one.

When the Sun is low on the horizon, its light has to travel a much longer path through the **atmosphere**. On the way almost all the blue light is scattered to the side. What is left is mainly yellow, orange and red colours. This is how the **red evening sky** and the red morning sky arise. After volcanic eruptions with a lot of dust in the air, sunsets are often especially colourful.

High in the Alps the sky is a deeper blue, because there is less air above us to scatter light. Mountains far away look bluish, because between us and them there is a lot of air that scatters blue light into our eyes. Over cities the sky sometimes looks whitish, because larger particles of **haze** and dust scatter all colours almost equally. For the same reason clouds are white; their water droplets are much larger than the air particles. Thick thunderclouds let hardly any light through and therefore look dark grey.

The explanation was given by the British physicist **John William Strutt**, known as Lord Rayleigh, around 1871. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1904, but for discovering the noble gas argon. On the **Moon** there is no air that could scatter light, so the sky there is black even in sunshine. At night our sky is dark because the Sun is then shining on the other side of the Earth. On a clear day the blue is usually strongest high up in the sky.

begriffe.erklaerung: When light is deflected in many directions by small particles.
The distance between two wave crests; it determines the colour of the light.
The layer of air that surrounds the Earth.
Fine particles and droplets in the air that make it harder to see.

gewusst: On Mars the sky during the day is rather yellowish to reddish, but the sunset there is bluish.
From space, astronauts see the Earth's atmosphere as a thin blue layer.
Photographers like the time shortly after sunset because the sky then glows deep blue; it is called the blue hour.

teile.einleitung: Penguins are birds that cannot fly but are excellent swimmers and divers. They live almost only in the Southern Hemisphere, from the icy Southern Ocean to the Galápagos Islands on the equator. With their black and white plumage and their waddling walk they are among the most popular animals in the world.
wichtigste: Penguins cannot fly but are excellent swimmers.
The largest penguin is the emperor penguin, the smallest the little penguin.
Penguins eat mainly fish, krill and squid.
In emperor penguins the father keeps the egg warm on his feet.
In icy storms emperor penguins stand close together.
The white belly camouflages penguins in the water against enemies from below.
The Galápagos penguin lives almost on the equator.

abschnitte.text: Penguins have a streamlined body, short legs and wings that have become stiff **flippers**. Their back is dark and their belly light. This colouring is called **countershading**: from above they blend in with the dark sea, from below with the bright sky. Dense, short feathers and a thick layer of fat protect them from the cold.

There are about 18 species of penguin, and almost all of them live in the **Southern Hemisphere**. They are found in Antarctica, South America, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand. The Galápagos penguin even lives close to the equator, because cold ocean currents bring a lot of food there. At the North Pole, on the other hand, there are no wild penguins.

Penguins eat fish, squid and **krill**, which are small crustaceans. Under water they are fast and agile, because they really fly through the water with their flippers. Emperor penguins can dive several hundred metres deep and stay under water for many minutes. Their tongue and palate have backward-pointing spines so that slippery prey cannot escape.

Emperor penguins breed in the middle of the Antarctic winter at temperatures far below minus 30 degrees. In storms thousands of animals huddle closely together and keep changing places, so that each one gets a turn in the warm middle. This is called a **huddle**. On the ice penguins often slide on their bellies and push themselves along with their feet, which saves energy.

The female emperor penguin lays a single egg and hands it over to the male. The father balances the egg on his feet for about two months under a warm fold of skin, the **brood pouch**. During this time he eats nothing. When the chick hatches, the mother returns from the sea and feeds it with food from her stomach.

Many penguin species are endangered, for example by **climate change**, overfishing and oil pollution. When the sea ice melts, emperor penguins lose their breeding grounds. In Switzerland you can see king penguins at Zurich Zoo and Basel Zoo. In winter they are even allowed to waddle through the zoo on a walk.

begriffe.erklaerung: Camouflage colouring with a dark back and a light belly.
Small, shrimp-like crustaceans in the sea.
A fold of skin under which penguins keep an egg or chick warm.
A large group of animals that breed together.

gewusst: Penguins can drink salt water, because a gland above their eyes gets rid of the extra salt.
An emperor penguin is about as tall as a child at nursery school.
Penguins have no fur but very many small, densely packed feathers.

teile.einleitung: Radioactivity is the spontaneous decay of unstable atomic nuclei, in which radiation is given off. This radiation can be neither seen nor smelled, but it can be detected with measuring instruments. It is dangerous, but it is also used in medicine and research.
wichtigste: Radioactivity is the spontaneous decay of unstable atomic nuclei, giving off radiation.
It was discovered in 1896 by the Frenchman Henri Becquerel.
In 1898 Marie and Pierre Curie found the radioactive elements polonium and radium.
There are three main kinds of radiation: alpha, beta and gamma.
The half-life tells you when half of the nuclei have decayed.
Radioactivity is measured, for example, with a Geiger counter.
There is also radioactivity in nature, for example from the gas radon.

abschnitte.text: Some atomic nuclei are not stable because they have too many or too few neutrons. At some point they change by themselves and give off energy as **radiation**. Exactly when a single nucleus decays is pure chance. But with many nuclei you can say exactly how fast the amount decreases.

In 1896 the physicist **Henri Becquerel** put uranium salt on a wrapped photographic plate and found that it turned black. So the uranium was sending out invisible rays by itself. The Polish-French researcher **Marie Curie** studied this further and coined the word “radioactive”. With her husband Pierre she discovered polonium and radium in 1898. In 1903 Becquerel and the Curies jointly received the Nobel Prize in Physics.

**Alpha radiation** consists of small helium nuclei and is stopped even by a sheet of paper. Beta radiation consists of fast electrons and is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Gamma radiation is high-energy light that you cannot see. To shield against it you need thick plates of lead or concrete.

The **half-life** is the time after which half of the radioactive nuclei have decayed. For iodine-131 it is about eight days, for carbon-14 about 5,700 years. Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years, which is roughly the age of the Earth. With carbon-14 researchers can work out the age of wood, bones or cloth.

In medicine radiation is used to fight cancer and to examine organs. In **nuclear power stations** such as Beznau, Gösgen and Leibstadt, nuclear fission produces heat for electricity. But too much radiation damages cells and can cause cancer. In the accidents at Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011 a lot of radioactive material was released.

Radioactivity is also naturally everywhere: from rock, from space and even from our food. In Switzerland most of the natural radiation exposure comes from the gas **radon**, which seeps from the ground into cellars and houses. Areas in the Alps and the Jura are especially affected. Airing rooms regularly and sealing cellars help to reduce the exposure.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
The time after which half of a radioactive substance has decayed.
A measuring instrument that shows radioactive radiation with audible clicking sounds.
A natural radioactive gas that comes out of the ground.
The unit for the number of atomic nuclei that decay per second.

gewusst: Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive today and are kept in lead boxes.
Even bananas are very slightly radioactive, because they contain a lot of potassium.
To this day Marie Curie is the only person who has received Nobel Prizes in two different natural sciences.

teile.einleitung: In biology a population is a group of living things of the same species that live in the same area at the same time. For example, all the ibexes in a mountain valley form a population. Biologists study how such groups grow, shrink and change.
wichtigste: A population includes all individuals of a species in a particular area.
The population density tells you how many individuals live in a particular area.
Births, deaths, immigration and emigration change the size of a population.
Food, space, enemies and diseases limit growth.
The largest number that a habitat can feed in the long term is called the carrying capacity.
With predators and prey, the numbers often rise and fall with a time lag.
In Switzerland the first ibexes were reintroduced in 1911.

abschnitte.text: A **population** consists of living things of the same species that live together in an area and can breed with each other. They might be the trout in a lake, the beeches in a forest or the chamois in a valley. The **population density** tells you how many animals or plants live in an area, for example 5 roe deer per square kilometre. Several populations of different species together form a community.

The size of a population depends on four things: births, deaths, **immigration** and emigration. If the animals have unlimited food and space at first, the population grows **exponentially**, that is, faster and faster. At some point food and space become scarce, and growth slows down. The curve then looks like an S lying on its side.

No habitat can feed an endless number of living things. The highest number that can find space and food in the long term is called the **carrying capacity**. Lack of food, enemies, diseases and a lack of hiding places keep a population within limits. If the carrying capacity is exceeded, more animals die or move away.

Predators and prey animals affect each other. If there are many hares, lynxes find a lot of food and multiply, after which the number of hares falls. Then the lynxes find less food, and their number falls too, a little later. Famous are the figures for snowshoe hares and **Canada lynxes**, which a fur-trading company in Canada recorded over many decades.

In the 19th century the **Alpine ibex** had been wiped out in Switzerland. A few animals from the Gran Paradiso area in Italy came to a wildlife park in St Gallen, and in 1911 the first were released in the Weisstannen valley. Today many thousands of ibexes live in Switzerland again. Because they all descend from a few animals, their **genetic diversity** is low, which can make them more vulnerable to diseases.

The people on Earth or in a country also form a population. In 2025 the world population was about 8.2 billion people. In 2025 about 9 million people lived in Switzerland. Population experts study similar questions to biologists, for example about births, lifespan and **migration**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single living thing.
The number of living things of a species per area.
The highest number of living things that a habitat can feed in the long term.
Growth that gets faster and faster.
Differences in the genetic material within a population.

gewusst: Very small, isolated populations easily lose their genetic diversity.
The ibex kids for the first reintroductions in Switzerland were smuggled from Italy, because the king there would not give any animals away.
Some insect populations can multiply a thousandfold in a single summer.

teile.einleitung: A Petri dish is a flat, round dish with a lid that is used in laboratories all over the world. Bacteria and fungi are grown in it so that they can be studied. Without this simple piece of equipment, many important discoveries in medicine would hardly have been possible.
wichtigste: A Petri dish is flat and round and has a lid.
It is named after the German doctor Julius Petri.
Bacteria and fungi are often grown in Petri dishes.
So that bacteria can grow, a culture medium is put inside.
The visible dots made of many bacteria are called colonies.
The lid stops germs from the air falling in.
The dishes are often placed upside down so that no water drips from the lid onto the culture medium.

abschnitte.text: A **Petri dish** consists of two parts, a flat bottom dish and a slightly larger lid. In the past all Petri dishes were made of glass, which could be cleaned after use and sterilised by heating. Today many are made of clear **plastic** and are used only once. They often have a diameter of about 9 to 10 centimetres. Because they are transparent, you can watch the growth well from outside.

The dish is named after the German doctor and bacteriologist **Julius Richard Petri**, who lived from 1852 to 1921. He worked as an assistant to the famous researcher Robert Koch in Berlin. In 1887 Petri described the practical dish with a lid. Before that, bacteria had been grown, for example, on glass plates under a glass bell. Petri's idea was so simple and useful that it is still used almost unchanged today.

So that bacteria or fungi can grow, a **culture medium** is poured into the dish. It is usually a mixture of nutrients and **agar**, a gelling agent made from algae. The agar is poured in hot and sets as it cools into a firm, clear mass, a bit like jelly. Then a sample is spread on it, for example from a cotton bud. After one or two days in an incubator you can see what has grown.

Through division, a single bacterial cell becomes millions of cells in a short time. They form a visible dot, a **colony**. Each kind of bacterium has colonies with a typical colour, shape and size. In this way experts can tell which germs are in a sample. In hospitals and in food control, for example, this is how people check whether dangerous germs are present.

The best-known discovery in a Petri dish was made in 1928 by the Scotsman **Alexander Fleming**. A mould had grown by chance on one of his dishes of bacteria. Around the mould, no more bacteria grew. In this way he discovered **penicillin**, the first antibiotic, which later saved millions of lives. At school, cress is often grown on damp cotton wool in similar dishes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance with nutrients on which bacteria or fungi can grow.
A gelling agent made from algae that makes the culture medium firm.
A visible heap of millions of identical bacteria.
A researcher who studies bacteria.
A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing.

gewusst: The idea of using agar from algae as a culture medium came from Fanny Hesse, who worked in Robert Koch's circle.
A fingerprint on a culture medium grows many visible colonies after a few days.
Some artists paint pictures with coloured bacteria in Petri dishes.

teile.einleitung: r- and K-selection describes two ways in which living things keep their species going. r-strategists have very many offspring that they hardly look after. K-strategists have few offspring but raise them carefully.
wichtigste: r-strategists have many offspring and give little parental care.
The letter r stands for the growth rate of a population.
The letter K stands for the capacity, that is, the maximum number a habitat can feed.
The African elephant is a typical K-strategist, the aphid a typical r-strategist.
r-strategists have an advantage in unstable, often disturbed habitats.
Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson introduced the terms in 1967.
Today the classification is seen as a continuum with many forms in between.

abschnitte.titel: What do r and K mean?
abschnitte.text: The letters come from a mathematical formula for the **growth** of populations. The r stands for the growth rate, that is, how fast a group can multiply. The K stands for the **carrying capacity**, the largest number of animals that a habitat can feed in the long term. r-strategists rely on fast growth, K-strategists on a life close to this limit.

r-strategists are usually small, grow up quickly and have a short lifespan. Examples are **aphids**, mice, many insects, fish and oysters. An oyster releases millions of eggs into the water, and almost all the young die early. But because there are so many, enough still survive.

K-strategists are usually large, live long and have only a few young. A typical example is the **African elephant**. An elephant calf is looked after by its mother and the herd for years. Whales, great apes and eagles also tend to be K-strategists.

In **unstable habitats**, which are often disturbed by floods, fires or storms, r-strategists have the advantage. They can quickly settle an area that has become free, just as dandelions do on a new building site. In stable habitats with strong competition, on the other hand, K-strategists have better chances. There quality counts more than quantity.

Researchers record how many animals born in the same year are still alive at each age. With r-strategists such as oysters, this gives a type III **survival curve** with very high death rates among the young. K-strategists tend to have a type I curve, in which most only die in old age. The terms were introduced in 1967 by Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson; today they are understood as the ends of a continuum with many forms in between.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the living things of one species that live together in an area.
The care and protection of offspring by the parents.
The maximum number of living things that a habitat can feed in the long term.
A graph that shows how many animals born in the same year are still alive at each age.

gewusst: In summer aphids can multiply so fast that a single aphid becomes a huge colony within a few weeks.
A single oyster can release millions of eggs in one season.
Many living things fit into no box: sea turtles, for example, live very long but lay many eggs and do not look after their young.

teile.einleitung: The phenotype is the appearance of a living thing with all its characteristics. These include, for example, eye colour, height, flower colour or behaviour. It results from the interplay of genes and the environment.
wichtigste: The phenotype means the appearance with all its characteristics.
Besides the genes, the environment also affects the phenotype.
Eye colour is an example of a characteristic of the phenotype.
Hydrangeas flower blue or pink depending on the soil.
A person's height also depends on diet and environment.
If red is dominant, plants with RR and Rr both flower red.
A change in the phenotype caused by the environment that is not inherited is called a modification.

abschnitte.text: The **phenotype** includes everything that can be observed or measured in a living thing. This includes appearance, size and colour, but also blood group or behaviour. Its counterpart is the **genotype**, that is, the whole set of genes. The word phenotype comes from Greek and means roughly “form of appearance”. The Danish researcher Wilhelm Johannsen introduced the terms genotype and phenotype at the beginning of the 20th century.

The genes set a framework, and the environment helps decide what comes of it. A person may have the genes to grow tall but also needs a good **diet** for this. Plants of the same variety grow differently in the shade than in the sun. Identical twins have almost the same genes and look very alike. Even so, they often differ a little because they do not experience exactly the same things.

**Hydrangeas** flower blue on acidic soil with a lot of aluminium and pink on chalky soil. Their genes are the same; only the soil is different. In **Siamese cats** an enzyme only makes pigment in cooler parts of the body, which is why the ears, paws and tip of the tail are dark. Flamingos are pink because they take in red pigments with their food. Without this food their feathers become pale.

For many characteristics, one gene variant wins over the other. It is called **dominant**, the other **recessive**. If in a plant red flower colour (R) is dominant over white (r), plants with RR and with Rr both flower red. So they have the same phenotype but a different genotype. Only plants with rr flower white. The monk Gregor Mendel discovered these rules with peas in the 19th century.

Changes in the phenotype caused by the environment are called **modification**. An example is a suntan or the muscles that grow through training. Such changes are not passed on to the offspring, because the genes stay the same. So a child of sporty parents does not automatically have strong muscles. Only changes in the genetic material, mutations, can be passed on.

begriffe.erklaerung: The visible and measurable appearance of a living thing.
The whole set of genes of a living thing.
A gene variant that wins over another one.
A gene variant that only shows when no dominant variant is present.
A change caused by the environment that is not inherited.

gewusst: Gardeners can turn pink hydrangeas blue by making the soil more acidic.
Siamese cats are born almost white and only gradually get their dark markings.
Flamingos are not naturally pink; their colour comes from their food.

teile.einleitung: Phineas Gage was an American railway worker who survived an incredible accident in 1848. An iron bar flew through his head, and yet shortly afterwards he could talk and walk again. His case became famous because it showed that certain parts of the brain have to do with our personality.
wichtigste: Phineas Gage was a foreman on railway construction in the USA.
His accident happened in 1848.
In an explosion, an iron tamping bar pierced his skull.
Above all the left frontal lobe of his brain was injured.
After the accident it was reported that his personality had changed.
The doctor John Martyn Harlow treated him and described his case.
After the accident Gage lived for about twelve more years and worked for some years in Chile as a stagecoach driver.

abschnitte.text: Phineas Gage was born in 1823 in the US state of New Hampshire. He worked as a **foreman** on the building of a railway line in the state of Vermont. His job was to blast rocks to make room for the tracks. For this, holes were drilled in the stone, filled with gunpowder and sand, and everything was pressed down with an iron bar. His bosses thought he was capable and reliable.

On 13 September 1848 the accident happened near Cavendish in Vermont. While it was being tamped down, the powder caught fire, and the explosion shot the **tamping iron** out of the hole. The bar was about a metre long and weighed around six kilograms. It entered under his left cheekbone, pierced the front part of his brain and came out again at the top of his skull. Amazingly, Gage was conscious again shortly afterwards and could talk.

The doctor **John Martyn Harlow** treated the wound and cared for Gage for weeks. A severe infection developed, but Gage survived. Harlow later described the case in medical reports. He wrote that after the accident Gage had become impatient, moody and unpredictable. His friends had said he was “no longer Gage”.

Above all the left **frontal lobe**, the very front part of the brain, was injured. Gage's case gave researchers an early sign that this area is important for planning, self-control and personality. It became one of the best-known cases in **neuroscience**. Today it appears in many textbooks of psychology and medicine. However, modern researchers believe that some reports about him were exaggerated.

After the accident Gage could no longer work as a foreman. He travelled around and for a while showed himself with his iron bar. From about 1852 to 1859 he lived in **Chile** and drove stagecoaches there between Valparaíso and Santiago. That was demanding work, which shows that he had probably recovered well. He died in 1860 in San Francisco, about twelve years after the accident.

begriffe.erklaerung: The very front part of the cerebrum, important for planning and self-control.
The science that studies the brain and the nerves.
The typical way a person thinks, feels and behaves.
An iron bar used to press blasting powder firmly into a drill hole.

gewusst: Gage's skull and the iron bar are still kept today in a museum at Harvard University.
Gage kept the iron bar that had injured him and took it everywhere with him.
Only in 2009 was a photo discovered that shows Phineas Gage with his bar.

teile.einleitung: Plants are living things that make their own food with the help of sunlight. They include tiny mosses as well as huge trees, colourful flowers and our vegetables. Without plants there would be no oxygen to breathe and hardly anything to eat.
wichtigste: Plants make their own food through photosynthesis.
To grow, most plants need light, water and soil.
They also take in carbon dioxide from the air.
In doing so they give off oxygen, which people and animals need to breathe.
Typical parts of a flowering plant are the root, stem, leaves and flowers.
Several hundred thousand plant species are known worldwide.
About 3,000 different ferns and flowering plants grow in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Plants are living things that usually grow fixed in one place and cannot walk around. Their cells have a firm cell wall and often contain green **chloroplasts**. These contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**, which captures light. Plants include mosses, ferns, conifers and the flowering plants, which form the largest group.

To grow, most plants need **light**, water and soil. With their roots they take water and nutrient salts such as nitrogen from the soil. With their leaves they take in carbon dioxide from the air. In **photosynthesis** they use the Sun's energy to build sugar from these and give off oxygen. Some plants, such as many orchids in the rainforest, even grow on trees without soil.

The **root** holds the plant firmly in the ground and takes in water. The stem or trunk carries the water upwards and holds the leaves. Photosynthesis takes place in the leaves. The flowers attract bees and other insects, which carry the pollen on. From this, fruits and seeds develop, from which new plants grow.

The tallest known tree is a coast redwood in California over 115 metres high. Some pines in the USA are almost 5,000 years old and are among the oldest living things on Earth. The giant rafflesia on Sumatra has flowers up to one metre across. The smallest flowering plant is the watermeal, which is smaller than a pinhead.

In Switzerland there are plants from warm Ticino right up to the glacier region. About a third of the country is covered by **forest**; the most common trees are spruce and beech. Protected flowers such as edelweiss and gentian grow in the Alps. On the summit of the Dom in Valais, flowering plants have been found at over 4,000 metres.

Plants give us food such as cereals, potatoes, fruit and vegetables. From them we also get wood, cotton, paper and many medicines. They give off oxygen and store carbon dioxide, which is important for the climate. In addition, roots hold the soil together and in the mountains protect against landslides and avalanches.

begriffe.erklaerung: The process in which plants use light to make sugar and oxygen from water and carbon dioxide.
The green pigment in plants that captures sunlight.
The part of the plant in the ground that takes in water and gives support.
Carrying pollen to another flower, often by insects.

gewusst: Carnivorous plants such as the sundew, which also grows in Swiss moors, catch small insects.
Bamboo is one of the fastest-growing plants and can grow almost a metre in a day.
Almost all the oxygen in the air comes from plants, algae and cyanobacteria.

teile.einleitung: Rationalism is a school of philosophy that says we gain certain knowledge mainly through our thinking, through reason. Its most famous representatives lived in the 17th century, among them René Descartes, Baruch de Spinoza and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Their model was mathematics.
wichtigste: According to rationalism, reason is the most important source of certain knowledge.
With methodical doubt, Descartes searched for a secure foundation of knowledge.
Rationalists believe in innate ideas such as God, number and infinity.
Spinoza wrote his “Ethics” using the geometric method with definitions and propositions.
Leibniz distinguished between truths of reason and truths of fact.
The opponent of rationalism is empiricism, which relies on experience.
Immanuel Kant tried to unite both schools in the “Critique of Pure Reason”.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin **ratio**, which means reason. Rationalists think that our senses can deceive us. According to them, only what the mind recognises clearly and distinctly is really certain. An example is mathematics: you know that 2 plus 2 equals 4 by thinking, not by measuring.

**René Descartes** first doubted everything that can be doubted, even his senses. This approach is called **methodical doubt**. In doing so he found a sentence he could not doubt: “I think, therefore I am”. In his “Meditations on First Philosophy” of 1641 he developed these thoughts in six meditations.

The Dutch philosopher **Baruch de Spinoza** wrote his “Ethics” like a geometry book, with definitions, propositions and proofs. The German scholar **Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz** thought that the world consists of simple, indivisible substances, which he called monads. Leibniz distinguished necessary truths of reason, for example from logic, from truths of fact about the world. He was also an important mathematician.

According to the rationalist view, people have some ideas from birth. These include ideas such as God, number and **infinity**. These cannot be gained from experience, because nobody has ever seen anything infinite. The Greek philosopher Plato had already had similar thoughts.

**Empiricism** says the opposite: all knowledge comes from experience through the senses. Well-known empiricists were John Locke and David Hume in Great Britain. In 1781, in the “Critique of Pure Reason”, Immanuel Kant tried to combine both schools. He thought that knowledge needs both experience and the order given by the mind.

begriffe.erklaerung: The human ability to think logically and to judge.
The teaching that all knowledge comes from experience.
The part of philosophy that asks how we can know something for certain.
According to Leibniz, a simple, indivisible basic unit of reality.

gewusst: Leibniz developed calculus at about the same time as Isaac Newton, which led to a long dispute.
Spinoza earned part of his living by grinding lenses for spectacles and telescopes.
The sentence “I think, therefore I am” is “Cogito, ergo sum” in Latin.

teile.einleitung: An atomic force microscope is a microscope that scans surfaces not with light but with a fine tip. In this way it can even make individual atoms and molecules visible. It was invented in 1986, partly by researchers from the IBM laboratory in Rüschlikon near Zurich.
wichtigste: An atomic force microscope measures the forces between a measuring tip and the sample.
The tip sits on a flexible leaf spring, the cantilever.
The bending of the spring is often measured with a laser beam and a photodiode.
Unlike the scanning tunnelling microscope, it can also examine samples that do not conduct electricity.
It can also measure in liquids and is therefore suitable for biology.
In tapping mode the spring vibrates and only touches the sample briefly.
With force spectroscopy the unfolding of individual proteins can be studied.

abschnitte.titel: What is an atomic force microscope?
abschnitte.text: An atomic force microscope, **AFM** for short, is one of the scanning probe microscopes. It moves a tiny tip over a surface line by line, rather like a finger reading Braille. As it does so, it measures the tiny forces between the tip and the sample. A computer puts the measurements together into a three-dimensional image.

The tip sits on a flexible leaf spring, the **cantilever**. This is usually less than half a millimetre long. If the tip is attracted to or pushed away from the surface, the spring bends. A laser beam is reflected off its back and directed onto a **photodiode**, which notices even the smallest bending.

The force can be calculated with Hooke's law: force equals **spring constant** times deflection. If a spring has a spring constant of 0.1 newtons per metre and is deflected by 2 nanometres, the force is 0.2 nanonewtons. That is unimaginably small. Even so, it is enough to feel the shape of individual atoms.

In contact mode the tip drags directly over the sample. In **intermittent mode**, also called tapping mode, the spring vibrates and only touches the surface very briefly. This is gentle on soft samples such as cells or proteins. In **force spectroscopy** the tip pulls on a single molecule and measures how it unfolds.

abschnitte.titel: An invention with a Swiss connection
abschnitte.text: The atomic force microscope was invented in 1986 by **Gerd Binnig**, Calvin Quate and Christoph Gerber. Before that, Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer had developed the scanning tunnelling microscope at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon and received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1986. But the scanning tunnelling microscope only works with samples that conduct electricity. The atomic force microscope, on the other hand, can also examine glass, plastic or living cells.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, flexible leaf spring on which the measuring tip sits.
A component that turns light into an electrical signal.
Tells you how stiff a spring is.
Going over a surface line by line, like reading a book.

gewusst: The measuring tip of an atomic force microscope can be so fine at the end that only a few atoms sit there.
With the atomic force microscope you can observe living cells in liquid.
IBM researchers in Rüschlikon have even used such methods to image the chemical bonds inside a single molecule.

teile.einleitung: A rainbow is a coloured arc in the sky that forms when sunlight meets raindrops. The drops split the white light into its colours, from red to violet. Because sunshine and rain are needed at the same time, rainbows are often seen after a thunderstorm.
wichtigste: A rainbow forms through sunlight and raindrops.
The Sun must be behind us and the rain falling in front of us.
The drops refract the light and split it into its colours.
On the outside the rainbow is red, on the inside violet.
Sometimes you can see a fainter secondary rainbow above it with the colours reversed.
A rainbow is really a circle, of which we usually see only part.
Rainbows can also form at waterfalls and lawn sprinklers.

abschnitte.text: A rainbow is a **light effect** in the air and not an object. That is why you cannot touch it and can never reach its end. Every person sees their own rainbow, because the light falling into their eyes comes from different drops. If you move, the rainbow moves with you.

Sunlight looks white but contains all colours. When it enters a raindrop, it is bent; this is called **refraction**. Each colour is bent by a slightly different amount, and so the colours fan out. At the back of the drop the light is reflected and then comes out again at the front. We see this coloured light as an arc at an angle of about 42 degrees.

From the outside in you see red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet. In reality the colours blend smoothly into one another. The Englishman **Isaac Newton** counted seven colours because the number seven was special for him, and so he added indigo. Inside the arc the sky is often a little brighter than outside.

If the light is reflected twice inside the drop, a second arc forms further out. This **secondary rainbow** is fainter and has its colours in reverse order. Between the two arcs lies a darker band. It is called Alexander's dark band, after the Greek scholar Alexander of Aphrodisias, who described it about 1,800 years ago.

As early as the Middle Ages the German monk Theodoric of Freiberg studied the rainbow with glass balls full of water. In 1637 the Frenchman **René Descartes** explained exactly how light travels inside the drop. A few decades later Newton showed with a glass prism that white light consists of all colours. That also made it clear where the colours of the rainbow come from.

Rainbows are best seen in the morning or late afternoon, when the Sun is low. At the **Rhine Falls** near Schaffhausen and at the Staubbach Falls in Lauterbrunnen, rainbows often appear in the spray on sunny days. From an aeroplane or a mountain top you can sometimes even see a complete circle. On bright nights with a full moon there are rare, pale moonbows.

begriffe.erklaerung: The bending of light when it passes from air into water or glass.
The range of all the colours that white light consists of.
A glass object that splits light into its colours.
A second, fainter rainbow with the colours in reverse order.

gewusst: At midday in summer you hardly ever see rainbows, because the Sun is too high.
In fog an almost white fogbow can form, because the droplets are very small.
With a garden hose you can make a rainbow yourself on a sunny day.

teile.einleitung: A ranking list shows the order in which people or teams finished in a competition. Right at the top, in 1st place, is the best. There are ranking lists in sport, in games and even for cities or schools.
wichtigste: The best is in 1st place.
In running, whoever takes the shortest time wins.
In the long jump, whoever jumps the furthest wins.
At a prize-giving ceremony there are usually three people on the podium.
1st place usually gets gold, 2nd place silver and 3rd place bronze.
With five participants, the slowest child is in 5th place.
If two people have exactly the same result, they often share the same place.

abschnitte.text: A **ranking list** puts participants in order of their performance. Each position is called a **rank** or place. 1st place is the best place, followed by 2nd place, 3rd place and so on. So if five children have a race, the slowest child is in 5th place.

How a ranking list is ordered depends on the sport. With times, **less is better**: if Ana runs 9 seconds, Ben 8 and Cem 10 seconds, Ben wins. With distances and heights, **more is better**: if Mia jumps 3 metres, Noah 2 metres 50 and Lina 3 metres 20, Lina is in 1st place. With points, for example in gymnastics, the highest score usually wins.

At a **prize-giving ceremony** the three best stand on the podium, with 1st place in the middle and highest. 1st place usually gets a gold medal, 2nd place silver and 3rd place **bronze**. At the Olympic Games this order has been usual for over a hundred years. The national anthem is often played for the winner too.

You can calculate with places. If Lia is in 2nd place and Max in 4th place, there is exactly one child between them, the one in 3rd place. If two people have exactly the same result, they share the same place **ex aequo**. The next place is then usually skipped.

In Switzerland people know ranking lists from **ski races**, from wrestling festivals or from school sports days. In the Ski World Cup, skiers collect points, and at the end of the season there is an overall ranking. Football league tables are ranking lists too; there the points from all the matches count. There are also ranking lists outside sport, for example for hits in the charts.

begriffe.erklaerung: The position in an order, for example 1st place for the best position.
A small stand with three steps on which the three best are honoured.
Latin for “equally”, when two share the same place.
The celebration at which the best receive medals or prizes.

gewusst: Olympic gold medals today are mostly made of silver and are only coated with gold.
In some ski races, hundredths of a second decide the place.
In golf, whoever needs the fewest strokes wins, that is, the smallest number.

teile.einleitung: Pliny the Elder was a Roman scholar, officer and writer who lived in the 1st century AD. He wrote the “Naturalis historia”, a huge work about almost everything that was known about nature at the time. He is also famous because of his death during the eruption of Vesuvius in the year 79.
wichtigste: Pliny the Elder was born in Como, near today's Swiss border.
His great work is called “Naturalis historia” and consists of 37 books.
The “Naturalis historia” is often seen as an early encyclopaedia.
Pliny wrote in Latin.
At the time of the eruption of Vesuvius he was commander of the Roman fleet.
He died in AD 79 in the eruption of Vesuvius.
His nephew Pliny the Younger described his death in letters to Tacitus.

abschnitte.text: His full name was **Gaius Plinius Secundus**. He was born around AD 23 in Novum Comum, today's **Como** on Lake Como. As a young man he served as an officer in the Roman army, among other places in Germania. Later he held important posts in the service of the emperors Vespasian and Titus.

Translated, **Naturalis historia** means “Natural History”. In 37 books Pliny deals with the sky and the Earth, countries and peoples, animals, plants, remedies, metals and stones. According to his own account, he used the works of about a hundred authors for it. Because it is so comprehensive, it is now seen as one of the first **encyclopaedias**.

Pliny was famous for how hard he worked. He even had books read aloud to him while eating and travelling and was constantly making notes. His nephew reported that Pliny had said no book was so bad that you could not learn something from it. Besides the Natural History he also wrote works about wars and history, but these are lost.

In AD 79 Pliny was **fleet commander** at Misenum on the Bay of Naples. When **Vesuvius** erupted, he set off with ships to rescue the people on the coast and to observe the eruption. He died at Stabiae, probably from poisonous gases or from heart failure. In the same eruption the towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum were buried.

His nephew **Pliny the Younger** described the eruption and his uncle's death in two letters to the historian Tacitus. These letters are the oldest detailed description of a volcanic eruption. That is why particularly violent, explosive eruptions are called **Plinian eruptions** today. The Natural History was widely read in the Middle Ages and is still an important source on the knowledge of the Romans.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large reference work covering many areas of knowledge.
A very violent, explosive volcanic eruption with a high column of ash.
A group of warships under one command.
The language of the ancient Romans.

gewusst: Pliny the Younger was not only the nephew but also the adopted son of Pliny the Elder.
Some stories in the Natural History are wrong, for example about fabulous creatures with only one foot.
In Como, statues on the front of the cathedral commemorate the two Plinys.

teile.einleitung: Programming means giving a computer exact instructions in a language it understands. This is how apps, games, websites and the controls of robots are made. Today even children learn at school how to write simple programs.
wichtigste: When programming, you write instructions for a computer.
A person who writes programs is called a programmer.
Scratch is a well-known programming language for children with coloured blocks.
When you start a new project in Scratch, you see a cat.
A loop repeats instructions.
Niklaus Wirth invented the programming language Pascal at ETH Zurich.
A program on a smartphone or tablet is called an app.

abschnitte.text: A computer can only do what you tell it exactly. So when **programming** you write a series of instructions, a **program**. For this you use a **programming language** such as Python, JavaScript or Java. A program on a smartphone or tablet is called an app.

Every program is made of simple building blocks. A **loop** repeats instructions, for example taking a step forward ten times. With a condition, the program decides what happens, for example: if it is raining, show an umbrella. In variables a program stores values such as the score in a game.

For children there is **Scratch**, a programming language with coloured blocks that you fit together like puzzle pieces. It was developed at MIT in the USA and is free. When you start a new project, an orange cat appears that you can move with instructions. In Switzerland, under Lehrplan 21, computing is part of the subject Media and Computer Science.

Around 1843 the Englishwoman **Ada Lovelace** wrote instructions for a calculating machine by Charles Babbage, which are considered one of the first programs. In Germany Konrad Zuse built the Z3 computer in 1941. Around 1970 the Swiss **Niklaus Wirth** invented the programming language **Pascal** at ETH Zurich, with which many people around the world learned to program. For this he received the Turing Award in 1984, one of the highest honours in computer science.

Almost no program works completely correctly the first time. A mistake in a program is called a **bug**, an English word for a small insect such as a beetle. Looking for and fixing mistakes is called debugging. That is why programmers test their programs again and again.

Today programs are almost everywhere: in cars, washing machines, traffic lights and hospitals. Without programming there would be no internet and no video games. If you can program, you understand better how digital devices work. Many companies in Switzerland are looking for computer experts.

begriffe.erklaerung: A series of instructions that a computer carries out.
A language with fixed rules in which programs are written.
A part of a program that repeats instructions several times.
A mistake in a program.
An exact step-by-step set of instructions for solving a task.

gewusst: The programming language Pascal is named after the French mathematician Blaise Pascal.
A recipe is basically an algorithm too, that is, a step-by-step set of instructions.
A well-known story says that a real moth once disrupted a computer and made the word bug famous.

teile.einleitung: A scanning tunnelling microscope is a device with which individual atoms can be made visible. It was invented in 1981 at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon near Zurich. For it Gerd Binnig and the Swiss Heinrich Rohrer received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
wichtigste: With the scanning tunnelling microscope individual atoms on a surface can be imaged.
An extremely fine tip, often made of tungsten, scans the surface line by line.
There is a gap of only about one nanometre between the tip and the sample.
A tiny tunnelling current flows, which depends strongly on the distance.
The sample must conduct electricity.
It was invented by Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer, who received the Nobel Prize in 1986.
The device has greatly advanced nanotechnology.

abschnitte.text: A scanning tunnelling microscope is not a microscope with lenses but a device that **scans** a surface. A very fine metal tip moves over the sample, rather like a finger over Braille. Ideally the tip ends in a **single atom**. This produces images in which individual atoms can be seen as small bumps.

There is a small electrical voltage between the tip and the sample, but they do not touch. Even so, electrons jump across the tiny gap of about one nanometre. This process is called the **tunnel effect** and comes from quantum physics. The current is very small, in the range of **picoamperes to nanoamperes**. Because it depends exponentially on the distance, the device detects differences in height of fractions of the diameter of an atom.

When **scanning**, the tip goes over the area line by line, as when reading a book. It is moved by **piezo crystals**, which stretch by tiny distances when a voltage is applied. In constant current mode the tip is adjusted so that the current stays the same. In constant height mode the tip stays at a fixed height, and the change in the tunnelling current is recorded. A computer puts the measurements together into an image.

Even tiny vibrations, for example from footsteps or cars, would change the distance. That is why a scanning tunnelling microscope stands on an elaborate **vibration damping** system. For especially precise experiments it is cooled to a few **kelvin**, that is, almost to absolute zero. Then the atoms do not wander around by themselves through their heat motion.

Gerd Binnig from Germany and **Heinrich Rohrer** from Buchs in the canton of St Gallen developed the device in 1981 at IBM in **Rüschlikon**. As early as 1986 they received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it. In 1989 IBM researchers in the USA wrote the letters “IBM” with 35 individual xenon atoms. In this way they showed that the tip can be used not only to see atoms but also to move them.

The scanning tunnelling microscope is regarded as the starting signal for **nanotechnology**, technology with the tiniest components. With **scanning tunnelling spectroscopy** the electronic states at individual points on a surface are also studied. The idea also led to the atomic force microscope, which can even scan samples that do not conduct electricity. Today such devices help in the development of computer chips and new materials.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny basic building block of all substances.
A billionth of a metre, about as wide as a few atoms side by side.
Electrons can jump across a small gap even though, according to everyday physics, they could not.
A crystal that moves a tiny distance when a voltage is applied.

gewusst: A nanometre compares to a metre roughly as a hazelnut compares to the whole Earth.
IBM even made a tiny cartoon with moved atoms called “A Boy and His Atom”.
There were only five years between the invention of the scanning tunnelling microscope and the Nobel Prize, which is very rare.

teile.einleitung: In a redox reaction one substance gives off electrons and another takes them up. These two processes are called oxidation and reduction and always happen at the same time. Redox reactions are behind fire, rust, batteries and even our breathing.
wichtigste: In a redox reaction one substance gives off electrons and another takes them up.
Giving off electrons is called oxidation.
Taking up electrons is called reduction.
Oxidation and reduction always happen together.
The word redox is made up of reduction and oxidation.
Burning, rusting and breathing are redox reactions.
Redox reactions also take place in batteries and supply electricity.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of atoms, which are surrounded by tiny, negatively charged **electrons**. In a redox reaction electrons move from one substance to another. The substance that gives off electrons is **oxidised**. The substance that takes them up is **reduced**. One never happens without the other, just as giving always needs someone who takes.

The substance that gives off electrons is called the **reducing agent**, because it reduces the other one. The substance that takes up electrons is called the oxidising agent. A particularly strong oxidising agent is oxygen. That is why oxidation used to mean simply “combining with oxygen”, as the Frenchman Antoine Lavoisier described it in the 18th century.

When wood burns, carbon and hydrogen from the wood react quickly with the oxygen in the air, and heat and light are released. **Rust** forms much more slowly when iron reacts with oxygen and water. A cut apple also turns brown because substances in it react with oxygen. In thermite welding, railway rails are joined using a very hot redox reaction between aluminium and iron oxide.

In a **battery** the two parts of the redox reaction are separated. So the electrons have to flow through a wire, and that is electric current. Around 1800 the Italian Alessandro Volta built the first battery, the voltaic pile. The other way round, electricity can be used to drive redox reactions; this is called electrolysis.

In a blast furnace, iron ore is reduced with carbon, producing iron for steel. Aluminium is produced by **electrolysis**, that is, with a great deal of electricity. From 1888 Neuhausen am Rheinfall was one of the first places in Europe where aluminium was made in this way, using electricity from the water power of the Rhine. Copper and many other metals are also obtained from their ores by reduction.

Our body gets energy by slowly oxidising sugar from food with oxygen. This **cellular respiration** takes place in tiny power stations in the cells, the mitochondria. In photosynthesis plants do the opposite and build sugar again from carbon dioxide and water. In this way respiration and photosynthesis are linked like a cycle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, negatively charged particle in the outer part of an atom.
The giving off of electrons by a substance.
The taking up of electrons by a substance.
A chemical reaction driven by electric current.

gewusst: The Statue of Liberty in New York is green because its copper has oxidised in the air.
Glow sticks and glow-worms glow thanks to a redox reaction that releases light instead of heat.
At school people often remember: oxidation is losing electrons, reduction is gaining electrons.

teile.einleitung: Radiocarbon dating is a method for finding out the age of things that were once alive. It measures how much radioactive carbon, C-14 for short, is still in wood, bones or cloth. In this way finds up to about 50,000 years old can be dated.
wichtigste: Radiocarbon dating determines the age of the remains of living things.
It is based on the radioactive carbon isotope C-14, which slowly decays.
The half-life of C-14 is about 5,730 years.
It was invented by the chemist Willard Libby, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1960.
Finds up to about 50,000 years old can be dated, for example charcoal, bones or seeds.
Radiocarbon ages are given in years before 1950, abbreviated BP.
Calibration curves such as IntCal20 are used to convert the measurements into calendar years.

abschnitte.text: Carbon is a building block of all living things. Most carbon atoms are of the type C-12, but a tiny part is **carbon-14**. A C-14 atom has two more neutrons in its nucleus than a C-12 atom and is **radioactive**. C-14 is constantly being made in the upper atmosphere when cosmic radiation hits nitrogen atoms. After that it gets into plants as part of carbon dioxide, and through food into animals and people.

As long as a living thing is alive, it constantly takes in new carbon, and the proportion of C-14 stays the same. When it dies, no new C-14 is added, and the “C-14 clock” starts to run. After about 5,730 years half of the C-14 has decayed; this is the **half-life**. After two half-lives a quarter is left, which corresponds to an age of about 11,460 years. After about 50,000 years so little is left that it can hardly be measured.

The American chemist **Willard Libby** developed the method at the end of the 1940s. He tested it on wood from Egyptian tombs whose age was already known from history. For his invention he received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** in 1960. The method changed archaeology greatly, because finds from the Stone Age could now be placed more accurately. Today C-14 is usually measured with accelerator mass spectrometry, for which tiny samples are enough, for example at ETH Zurich.

The C-14 content of the air was not the same at all times. That is why the measurements are compared with **calibration curves**, which are obtained from tree rings, among other things. For land samples from the Northern Hemisphere the curve **IntCal20** has been used since 2020. Radiocarbon ages are given in “BP”, which means “before present” and refers to the year 1950. Shells and other samples from the sea seem too old because of the **reservoir effect**, since the sea contains old carbon.

Since industrialisation, people have burned a lot of coal, oil and natural gas. These **fossil fuels** no longer contain any C-14 and have diluted the proportion of C-14 in the air. That is why wood from the early 20th century seems too old when measured. Around 1963, on the other hand, the C-14 content rose sharply, because nuclear weapons tests above ground had produced a lot of new C-14. Today this **bomb peak** even helps to date samples from the last few decades precisely.

Radiocarbon dating was also used to study the glacier mummy **Ötzi**, which was found in the Ötztal Alps in 1991. It is about 5,300 years old and dates from the Neolithic. Wooden posts from pile dwellings on Swiss lakes, charcoal from fireplaces and old bones are also dated in this way. But the method is not suitable for rock or dinosaur bones. These are far too old and usually no longer contain any original carbon.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of atom of an element with a different number of neutrons in the nucleus.
When atomic nuclei decay by themselves and give off radiation.
The time after which half of a radioactive substance has decayed.
Finding out the age of a find.
Comparing a measurement with known reference values.

gewusst: Willard Libby originally calculated with a half-life of 5,568 years, which was later corrected.
For a modern C-14 measurement a sample lighter than a grain of rice is often enough.
Thanks to the bomb peak, it is even possible to find out from which decade ivory or wine comes.

teile.einleitung: A rocket is a vehicle that moves forward through the thrust of gases streaming out of it. Because it carries its own fuel and the oxygen to burn it, it also works in the airless emptiness of space. People fly into space with rockets, and rockets carry satellites into their orbits.
wichtigste: People fly into space with rockets.
Rockets work on the principle of thrust (recoil).
They carry fuel and an oxidiser with them and need no air.
Large rockets consist of several stages that are dropped one after another.
The first simple rockets existed many hundreds of years ago in China.
From 1969 the Saturn V took astronauts to the Moon.
Today some rocket stages can land and be reused.

abschnitte.text: A rocket is a flying vehicle with a **rocket engine**. In it fuel burns, and the hot gases shoot out backwards at enormous speed. This pushes the rocket forwards. Unlike an aeroplane, it needs no air from outside, which is why it can fly in space.

You can try out the **principle of thrust** with a balloon: if you let go of it, the air escapes backwards and the balloon whizzes forwards. The English physicist Isaac Newton described this law back in the 17th century. Every force produces an equal and opposite force. To orbit the Earth, a rocket has to reach a speed of about 28,000 kilometres per hour.

As early as the 13th century the Chinese used rockets with **gunpowder**, similar to today's fireworks. Around 1903 the Russian Konstantin Tsiolkovsky calculated how rockets could get into space. In 1926 the American Robert Goddard launched the first rocket with liquid fuel. In 1957 a Soviet rocket carried Sputnik, the first satellite, into space, and in 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first person to fly into space.

NASA's **Saturn V** was over 110 metres tall, higher than most church towers. The Apollo astronauts flew to the Moon on it. Large rockets are built in **stages**: when one stage's fuel is used up, it is dropped and the next one ignites. In this way the rocket does not have to carry any unnecessary weight.

In the past rockets were used only once and then crashed into the sea. In 2015 the first stage of a Falcon 9 rocket from the company SpaceX landed upright back on Earth for the first time. Today rockets are launched from many countries, for example the USA, China, Russia, India and Europe. The European rocket **Ariane 6** is launched from the Kourou spaceport in French Guiana.

Switzerland does not build large rockets itself, but since 1975 it has been a founding member of the European Space Agency, **ESA**. Swiss companies make important parts, for example the payload fairing that protects the satellites at the tip of the rocket. These fairings are built in Emmen in the canton of Lucerne. The Swiss astronaut Claude Nicollier flew into space four times on the Space Shuttle.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force that arises when something is pushed out backwards with great force.
A part of a rocket with its own engine and fuel that is dropped.
A device that orbits the Earth, for example for weather pictures, navigation or television.
The path along which an object circles a planet or star.

gewusst: In its first few minutes a large rocket such as the Saturn V used more fuel than a car uses in its whole life.
The word rocket comes from the Italian “rocchetta”, which means a small spindle.
Rockets are often launched near the equator, because there they get extra momentum from the Earth's rotation.

teile.einleitung: The chanterelle is an egg-yolk yellow edible mushroom that grows in woods and is very popular with mushroom pickers. In Switzerland it is called “Eierschwämmli”. It has a delicate flavour and smells a little of apricot.
wichtigste: The chanterelle is egg-yolk yellow and is called “Eierschwämmli” in Switzerland.
Under its cap it has ridges that run down the stem.
Older chanterelles are often shaped like a funnel.
It smells slightly of apricot.
Chanterelles that you can buy are gathered in the woods.
The false chanterelle looks similar and is often confused with it.
In Switzerland chanterelles are often eaten in a cream sauce.

abschnitte.text: The **chanterelle** is egg-yolk yellow to orange-yellow. In young mushrooms its cap is domed, and later it becomes like a **funnel** with a wavy edge. Under the cap it has no real gills, but thick, forked **ridges** that run down the stem. The flesh is firm and whitish to pale yellow. The mushroom smells pleasantly fruity, a little of apricot.

Chanterelles grow in coniferous and deciduous woods, often under spruces, beeches or oaks. They live in a partnership with the roots of the trees called **mycorrhiza**. The fungus supplies the tree with water and minerals, and the tree gives the fungus sugar. That is why chanterelles can hardly be cultivated; all chanterelles you buy have been gathered in the woods. Many come from Eastern Europe.

In Switzerland chanterelles are usually found from June to October, especially after warm rain. They often grow in mossy places and keep appearing in the same spots. Many cantons have rules on **mushroom picking**, for example a maximum amount per person per day or days when picking is not allowed. If you are unsure, you can have your mushrooms checked free of charge at an official **mushroom inspection**. This is very important, because some mushrooms are poisonous.

The **false chanterelle** looks similar to the real one. But it is more orange and has real, thin gills instead of thick ridges. It is not very poisonous, but it does not taste good and is hard to digest. Confusing it with poisonous species such as the jack-o'-lantern mushroom, which grows in clumps on wood, is more dangerous. So the rule is: only eat mushrooms that you are completely sure of.

Chanterelles are one of the most popular edible mushrooms in Switzerland. They are fried in butter or cooked in a **cream sauce**, for example with pasta, rösti or meat. Before cooking they are cleaned with a brush, because they soak up water. You should never eat chanterelles raw. They are quite expensive because they have to be gathered by hand in the woods.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mushroom that you can eat.
Thick, forked folds under the cap, typical of the chanterelle.
Thin plates under the cap of many mushrooms.
A partnership between fungi and tree roots from which both benefit.
A place where experts check gathered mushrooms for poisonous ones.

gewusst: Chanterelles are hardly ever attacked by maggots, so they are often especially clean.
The mushroom you see is only the fruiting body; the actual fungus lives as a fine network in the soil.
Almost all chanterelles in the shops come from woods, because they can hardly be cultivated.

teile.einleitung: Every year on 10 December, one of the most solemn award ceremonies in the world takes place in Stockholm. There outstanding researchers and writers receive the Nobel Prizes from the hands of the King of Sweden. This is followed by a famous banquet with over a thousand guests.
wichtigste: The Nobel Prizes are presented in Stockholm on 10 December.
10 December is the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death.
The King of Sweden presents the prizes.
The ceremony takes place in the Stockholm Concert Hall.
In the evening there is a large banquet in Stockholm City Hall.
The Nobel Peace Prize is presented not in Stockholm but in Oslo.
The men at the ceremony usually wear tailcoats.

abschnitte.text: The Swedish chemist and inventor **Alfred Nobel** became rich through dynamite. In his will he decided that his fortune should be used to award prizes for the greatest achievements of humanity. He died on 10 December 1896, which is why the ceremony takes place on this day. The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in 1901. In Stockholm there are prizes for physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and economics.

abschnitte.titel: The ceremony in the Concert Hall
abschnitte.text: The award ceremony takes place in the **Concert Hall** in Stockholm, the capital of Sweden. An orchestra plays, and the guests wear formal clothes, the men usually a **tailcoat**. For each prize a member of the academy responsible gives a short speech about the achievement. Then the **King of Sweden** presents each prizewinner with a gold medal and a diploma. The ceremony is shown on television.

In the evening a large banquet, the Nobel Banquet, takes place in Stockholm **City Hall**. About 1,300 guests sit at long tables in the splendid Blue Hall. The menu is kept secret until the evening. Hundreds of waiters and waitresses carry in the food in a carefully planned order. Later the prizewinners give short speeches of thanks.

The ceremony is the highlight of **Nobel Week** in December. In the days before it the prizewinners give a **lecture** about their work, the Nobel Lecture. There are press conferences, visits to schools and receptions. The prize also includes prize money, which the winners in a category share if there are several. The prize in economics was only established in 1968 by the Swedish central bank.
