The **Nobel Peace Prize** is presented not in Stockholm but on the same day in Oslo in Norway. Alfred Nobel decided this himself. Exactly why is not known, but at that time Sweden and Norway were joined in a union. Researchers from Switzerland have also stood on the stage in Stockholm. For example, the Lausanne researcher Jacques Dubochet received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017. In 2019 the Geneva astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering a planet orbiting another star.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the most famous prizes in the world for great achievements in science, literature and peace.
A very formal black suit with long tails at the back.
A large, formal feast.
Another word for prizewinner.

gewusst: The flowers for the Nobel ceremony traditionally come from Sanremo in Italy, where Alfred Nobel died.
Anyone who wins in physics or chemistry receives a gold medal showing Alfred Nobel's face.
When the ceremony is over, the guests go on dancing after the banquet until late at night.

teile.einleitung: The prefrontal cortex is the very front part of the brain, directly behind the forehead. It helps us to plan, to concentrate, to control our feelings and to resist temptations. Amazingly, it is only fully mature at about the mid-twenties.
wichtigste: The prefrontal cortex lies in the very front part of the frontal lobe.
It is important for executive functions such as planning, controlling actions and thinking flexibly.
According to what we know today, it matures until about the mid-twenties.
The orbitofrontal cortex lies above the eye sockets and helps with decisions and with judging feelings.
The marshmallow test studies delay of gratification in children.
In the Stroop test you have to name the ink colour of colour words.
The leucotomy, an operation on the frontal brain that is rejected today, was honoured with a Nobel Prize in 1949.

abschnitte.text: The outer layer of the cerebrum is called the **cortex** or cerebral cortex. The **prefrontal cortex** lies in the very front part of the frontal lobe, just behind the forehead. In humans it is especially large compared with other animals. Directly above the eye sockets lies a part of it, the **orbitofrontal cortex**, which is involved in decisions and in judging feelings.

The prefrontal cortex is often compared with a conductor who leads many musicians at the same time. It controls the so-called **executive functions**. These include planning, controlling actions, thinking flexibly and working memory, which you use to remember things for a short time. It also helps to put the brakes on feelings such as anger and to think about the consequences of what you do.

In the famous **marshmallow test**, children are given a sweet and the promise of a second one if they wait for a while. It studies **delay of gratification**, the ability to wait for something better. In the **Stroop test**, for example, the word “blue” is written in red, and you have to name the ink colour. This is hard because you have to stop yourself reading, and that is exactly when the prefrontal cortex is active.

The prefrontal cortex is one of the last parts of the brain to mature, according to what we know today until about the mid-twenties. That is why children and teenagers sometimes find it harder to judge risks or to resist sudden ideas. This is completely normal and part of development. Sleep, exercise and learning help the brain to develop well.

In 1848, in an accident in the USA, an iron bar went through the head of the railway worker **Phineas Gage**. He survived, but afterwards his behaviour had changed a great deal, which showed how important the frontal brain is for personality. In the 20th century the **leucotomy** was developed, in which nerve connections of the frontal brain were cut. It was honoured with a Nobel Prize in 1949 but is rejected today because of the serious damage it caused.

begriffe.erklaerung: The outer, folded layer of the cerebrum, also called the cerebral cortex.
Abilities for planning, steering and controlling your own behaviour.
A short-term store in your head, for example to remember a phone number for a moment.
The ability to wait for a bigger reward later.

gewusst: In humans the frontal lobe makes up about a third of the cerebral cortex.
You can easily try the Stroop test yourself by writing colour words in the wrong colours.
When you are tired it is harder to control yourself, because the prefrontal cortex also needs rest.

teile.einleitung: Jellyfish are transparent, jelly-like sea animals that drift through the water like living umbrellas. They are made mostly of water and have no brain, no heart and no bones. With their tentacles some species can give a painful sting.
wichtigste: Jellyfish belong to the animal group of cnidarians.
They are about 98 per cent water.
They swim by contracting their bell.
On their tentacles there are stinging cells with which they catch prey.
Sea turtles like to eat jellyfish.
Even dead jellyfish on the beach can still sting.
A small freshwater jellyfish that is harmless to people lives in Swiss lakes.

abschnitte.text: A jellyfish consists of a bell-shaped **umbrella** with catching arms, the **tentacles**, hanging from it. Its body is usually transparent and soft like jelly. Jellyfish have no brain, no heart and no bones, but a simple network of nerves. Some are only a few millimetres in size, while the lion's mane jellyfish can have a bell up to two metres across.

Jellyfish contract their bell and so push water out, rather like the thrust of a rocket. Then the bell opens again. But they can hardly move against strong currents and so often drift with the water. They live in all oceans, from warm waters to the polar seas and the deep sea.

On the tentacles there are thousands of **stinging cells**. If something touches the cell, a tiny thread with venom shoots out at lightning speed. In this way jellyfish paralyse small fish and crustaceans and pull them to their mouth. In people some species, such as the fire jellyfish, cause burning red skin, and the box jellyfish in Australia can even be life-threatening.

Jellyfish are food for **sea turtles**, sunfish and some birds. Sadly, turtles often mistake plastic bags for jellyfish and swallow them. Many jellyfish grow from a **polyp** fixed to the seabed, which buds off small jellyfish. Jellyfish have existed for over 500 million years and are among the oldest animals on Earth.

Do not touch jellyfish on the beach, even if they look dead, because the stinging cells can still release venom. If you have been stung, rinse the spot with seawater and do not rub it. Fresh water can set off even more stinging cells. With severe pain, difficulty breathing or large red areas, you need medical help.

In warm summers the **freshwater jellyfish** sometimes appears in Swiss lakes and ponds. It is only about two centimetres in size and almost transparent. It is completely harmless to people, because its stinging cells cannot get through our skin. It probably originally comes from China and was brought to Europe by people.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal group with stinging cells that includes jellyfish, corals and sea anemones.
A long, flexible catching arm.
A tiny cell that fires a venomous thread when touched.
The fixed form of many cnidarians, which looks like a small tube.

gewusst: A small kind of jellyfish from the Mediterranean can change back into a younger stage and is therefore sometimes called the immortal jellyfish.
Some jellyfish glow in the dark because they produce light themselves.
In some countries in Asia jellyfish are eaten.

teile.einleitung: Poliomyelitis, polio for short and also known as infantile paralysis, is an infectious disease caused by the poliovirus. It can damage nerves in the spinal cord and so cause permanent paralysis. Thanks to vaccinations, polio has disappeared almost everywhere in the world today.
wichtigste: Infantile paralysis is caused by the poliovirus.
The virus is usually spread through dirty water and dirty hands.
A serious consequence is paralysis, especially of the legs.
Jonas Salk developed the first effective vaccine, which was introduced in 1955.
Albert Sabin developed the oral vaccine.
In Switzerland today people are vaccinated with an injection of inactivated viruses.
The WHO declared the European Region polio-free in 2002.
According to the WHO, wild polio now only occurs in Afghanistan and Pakistan (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: Polio is caused by the **poliovirus**, a very small virus that multiplies in the gut. Most people who are infected notice nothing or have only mild complaints such as fever and a sore throat. But in a small proportion the virus attacks the nerve cells in the **spinal cord** that control the muscles. Then muscles can be permanently paralysed, usually in the legs.

The virus is passed out in faeces and gets into the mouth via **dirty water**, food or unwashed hands. Experts call this smear infection. Children under five are especially at risk, which is why it was also called infantile paralysis. There is no cure for polio; you can only protect yourself by being vaccinated.

If polio paralyses the breathing muscles, a person can no longer breathe on their own. From 1928 the **iron lung** was used for this, a large metal container in which the patient lay with only their head sticking out. The machine changed the air pressure in the container and so helped with breathing. In the middle of the 20th century many hospitals had whole wards full of such machines.

The American **Jonas Salk** developed a vaccine made of killed viruses, which was introduced in 1955 and is injected. Shortly afterwards **Albert Sabin** developed an oral vaccine with weakened viruses, which was often taken on a sugar lump. In Switzerland an injection with inactivated viruses is used today. It is usually given in the first year of life as a combination vaccine and boosted later.

In 1988 the World Health Organization, **WHO**, and its partners started a worldwide initiative to eradicate polio. At that time hundreds of thousands of children fell ill every year; since then the number has fallen by more than 99 per cent. The European Region, which includes Switzerland, has been considered polio-free since 2002. According to the WHO, wild poliovirus now only occurs in **Afghanistan and Pakistan** (as of 2026).

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny germ that can only multiply in cells.
When muscles can no longer be moved, or hardly at all.
A substance that prepares the body for a germ and protects it.
The bundle of nerves in the back that connects the brain and the body.
The World Health Organization of the United Nations, based in Geneva.

gewusst: Jonas Salk did not patent his vaccine so that it could help as many people as possible.
After smallpox, polio could be the second disease that humans eradicate completely worldwide.
The WHO, which leads the fight against polio, has its headquarters in Geneva.

teile.einleitung: A rubber, also called an eraser, is a small, soft block that you use to remove pencil lines from paper. It belongs in almost every school pencil case. Its story begins with breadcrumbs and a substance from South America.
wichtigste: A rubber removes pencil lines from paper.
The first rubbers were made from natural rubber.
Before that, people rubbed out with breadcrumbs.
Most rubbers today are made of plastic.
After rubbing out, crumbs of rubber are left on the page.
Ballpoint pen can hardly be rubbed out, because the ink soaks into the paper.
The German word for rubbing out, “radieren”, comes from the Latin word for scratching.

abschnitte.text: A pencil line consists of tiny particles of **graphite** that lie loosely on the paper fibres. If you rub over them with a rubber, these particles stick to the rubber. At the same time a little of the rubber wears away. This produces the **rubber crumbs**, in which the graphite is trapped.

In the past, pencil lines were removed with squeezed **breadcrumbs**. Around 1770 people in England discovered that **natural rubber** was much better for this. Natural rubber is the dried milky sap of the rubber tree from South America. Because you could rub with it, it is still called a “rubber” in British English today, and also an “eraser”.

abschnitte.titel: What rubbers are made of today
abschnitte.text: Over time natural rubber became sticky and brittle. Only when people had learned around 1840 to make rubber durable by heating it with sulphur did rubbers last longer. Today most rubbers are made of **plastic**. Many manufacturers now make sure they no longer use worrying plasticisers.

The ink of ballpoint pens and fountain pens **soaks into the paper** and colours the fibres. That is why a normal rubber can hardly remove it. So-called ink erasers are rather hard and take off a thin layer of paper as well. With ink eradicators, on the other hand, the blue ink is made colourless chemically.

Some pencils have a small rubber at the **top end**, an idea that was patented in the USA in 1858. Artists like to use a soft **putty rubber**, which can be shaped like modelling clay. With it you can lighten lines without making crumbs. There are also electric erasers for very fine corrections in technical drawings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A soft, grey form of carbon from which the lead of a pencil is made.
A stretchy substance made from the milky sap of the rubber tree.
Small bits of rubber that form when rubbing out and pick up the graphite.
A soft rubber that can be shaped and is used mainly by people who draw.

gewusst: The German word “radieren” comes from the Latin “radere”, which means to scratch or scrape.
Before there were rubbers, people rubbed out with breadcrumbs.
A pencil line is so loose that it can sometimes even be smudged with a finger.

teile.einleitung: Recycling means making new raw materials and products out of used materials. Old PET bottles become new bottles, and waste paper becomes recycled paper. In this way raw materials, energy and space in landfill sites are saved.
wichtigste: In recycling, waste is turned into new raw materials.
Collected PET bottles can become new PET bottles again.
Waste paper becomes recycled paper, which saves wood from trees.
Used glass is melted down and made into new glass bottles.
Recycling aluminium cans saves a particularly large amount of energy.
The well-known recycling symbol consists of three arrows in a circle.
Even better than recycling is making less rubbish.

abschnitte.text: The word **recycling** means something like reusing. Used things are collected, sorted and turned into new **raw materials**. The well-known recycling symbol consists of three arrows in a circle and shows this cycle. It was designed in the USA around 1970.

Collected **PET bottles** are washed, shredded and made into new PET bottles or into fibres for clothes. **Used glass** is separated by colour, melted down and shaped into new bottles and jars. Waste paper becomes recycled paper, for example for newspapers, exercise books or cardboard. Because less fresh wood is needed for this, paper recycling protects the forests.

Making aluminium needs a great deal of electricity. Recycling aluminium cans, on the other hand, needs only a small part of this energy. That is why collecting aluminium is especially worthwhile. Aluminium can also be melted down almost any number of times without getting worse.

In Switzerland glass, PET, aluminium, paper, cardboard, batteries and electrical appliances are usually collected separately. Glass is sorted by colour into white, brown and green containers. PET bottles and batteries can be returned to many shops, and electrical appliances to the shops where you buy them. What is not recycled is burned in **waste incineration plants**, which use it to produce electricity and heat.

Recycling is good, but even better for the environment is making less rubbish. You can, for example, refill a water bottle, use bags several times and repair things instead of throwing them away. Experts speak of the order **avoid, reuse, recycle**. Compost made from vegetable peelings is also a form of recycling.

begriffe.erklaerung: Material from which new things are made, for example wood, ore or crude oil.
A plastic from which many drinks bottles are made.
A plant in which rubbish is burned and used to produce electricity and heat.
A process in which material is used again and again.

gewusst: Glass can be melted down again and again without losing quality.
Fleece jumpers can even be made from recycled PET bottles.
Old mobile phones contain small amounts of gold and other valuable metals that can be recovered.

teile.einleitung: Punctuated equilibrium is an idea from evolutionary research. It says that many species hardly change for a very long time and then change rapidly in a short time. The idea sparked a big debate about how evolution actually works.
wichtigste: Punctuated equilibrium was published in 1972 by Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould.
In German it is called “Punktualismus”; the English name means roughly “interrupted balance”.
Long periods in which species hardly change alternate with short periods of rapid change.
The long quiet periods are called stasis.
The opposite model is gradualism, in which species change slowly and evenly.
Punctuated equilibrium aims to explain why transitional forms are often rare in the fossil record.
According to this idea, new species often arise in small, separated populations at the edge.

abschnitte.text: Punctuated equilibrium is a model of the speed at which **evolution** happens. According to this model, a species often stays almost the same for millions of years. Then a new species arises in a time that is short in the history of the Earth. However, “short” here still means thousands of years, which is only a moment in the Earth's history.

The two American researchers **Niles Eldredge** and **Stephen Jay Gould** presented their idea in a scientific article in 1972. Eldredge had studied changes in trilobites, extinct sea animals with armour. Gould had worked on snails. Both found that the fossils hardly changed over long sequences of rock layers.

Charles Darwin himself wondered why fine transitions between two species are rarely found in the **fossil record**. Darwin assumed that the fossil record is simply very incomplete. Eldredge and Gould interpreted the gaps differently. They thought that the missing transitions are real, because the change happened quickly and in a small place.

To explain this, the two used **peripatric speciation**. Here a small group of animals at the edge of the range is separated from the rest, for example by a river or a mountain range. In such a small group, changes can spread quickly. Because the group is small and exists only for a short time, it leaves hardly any fossils.

**Gradualism** assumes that species change step by step and evenly. For decades there were heated debates between the supporters of the two ideas. Today many researchers see both models as parts of the truth. Depending on the animal group and the time period, sometimes one model fits better and sometimes the other.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change of living things over many generations.
A long period in which a species hardly changes.
The petrified remains or traces of living things from earlier times.
The idea that species change slowly and evenly.
Extinct sea animals with armour made of three lengthwise parts.

gewusst: Critics mockingly called punctuated equilibrium “evolution by jerks”, after which Gould called gradualism “evolution by creeps”.
Stephen Jay Gould also became known through many popular books about natural history.
Trilobites existed for over 250 million years before they died out.

teile.einleitung: Plankton are tiny living things that float in the water and are carried around by the current. They include plant plankton such as algae and animal plankton such as copepods. Plankton is the basis of the food chain in seas and lakes.
wichtigste: The word plankton means “that which drifts”.
Plant plankton is called phytoplankton, animal plankton zooplankton.
Phytoplankton lives near the top of the water, where light reaches.
Larger animals such as jellyfish also count as plankton, because they drift in the water.
Almost all sea animals depend directly or indirectly on plankton.
The whale shark is the largest fish in the world and eats mainly plankton.
Much zooplankton rises to the surface at night and dives down during the day.

abschnitte.text: The word **plankton** comes from Greek and means “that which drifts”. It refers to living things that can swim but can hardly move against the current. Most are tiny, and some can only be seen under a microscope. Larger animals such as **jellyfish** also count as plankton, because they drift in the water.

Tiny algae that float in the water are called **phytoplankton** or plant plankton. Like land plants they need light and make sugar and oxygen through **photosynthesis**. That is why most phytoplankton lives near the top of the water, where light reaches. Experts estimate that phytoplankton produces about half of the oxygen on Earth. It grows especially well when it is warm and bright.

Animal plankton is called **zooplankton**. In a pond, for example, the **copepod**, the water flea and the **rotifer** belong to it; the rotifer has a crown of tiny hairs on its head that looks like a turning wheel. In the sea small crustaceans such as **krill** and the larvae of many fish count as zooplankton. Much zooplankton rises to the surface at night to feed and hides in the dark from predators during the day.

abschnitte.titel: The basis of the food chain
abschnitte.text: Phytoplankton is eaten by zooplankton, and this by small fish. Small fish are eaten by larger fish, birds and seals. So almost all sea animals depend directly or indirectly on plankton. Even the largest animals, such as the **blue whale** and the **whale shark**, feed on plankton, which they filter out of the water.

On some coasts the sea glows bluish at night when waves break or when you move your hand through the water. This **sea sparkle** comes from tiny plankton that can produce light itself. The glow comes from a chemical reaction in the cells. This ability is called **bioluminescence**.

A lot of plankton also lives in Swiss lakes and ponds. Researchers catch it with a very **fine net** that they pull through the water. In Lake Murten a blue-green alga used to turn the water reddish at times; it was called **Burgundy blood alga**. The name recalls the Battle of Murten in 1476, in which the Swiss Confederates defeated Charles the Bold of Burgundy. In lakes, young fish such as whitefish like to eat zooplankton.

begriffe.erklaerung: Plant plankton, mainly tiny algae.
Animal plankton, such as small crustaceans and larvae.
The order of who eats whom, from plants to the big predators.
The ability of living things to produce light themselves.

gewusst: The daily up-and-down migration of zooplankton is thought to be the largest animal migration on Earth.
The whale shark can grow over 12 metres long and still eats mainly tiny plankton.
Some plankton blooms are so big that they can be seen on satellite images from space.

teile.einleitung: A doctorate is the path to a doctor's degree, the highest academic degree at a university. For it you do research on a topic for several years and write a large piece of work about it, the dissertation. In Switzerland it is usually called the “Doktorat”.
wichtigste: For a doctor's degree you write a research paper called a dissertation.
In Switzerland you normally need a master's degree for a doctorate.
A doctorate in Switzerland typically takes about three to five years.
At many universities you defend your work in an oral exam, the disputation.
The highest grade is “summa cum laude”.
The abbreviation PhD stands for Philosophiae Doctor.
“Dr. h.c.” means honorary doctor.

abschnitte.text: The German word **“Promotion”** for a doctorate comes from the Latin “promovere”, which means “to promote”. Someone who does a doctorate shows that they can do scientific research independently. At the end you receive the **title of doctor**, which you write in front of your name, for example “Dr Anna Muster”. There are different forms, such as Dr. med. for medicine, Dr. phil. for the humanities or Dr. sc. nat. for the natural sciences.

In Switzerland the universities as well as ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne award doctorates. As a rule the requirement is a **master's degree** with good marks. Many doctoral students are employed by the university, for example as assistants, and receive a salary. A doctorate usually takes about three to five years.

The heart of it is the **dissertation**, an extensive piece of research that must contain new knowledge. A supervisor, in German often called “Doktorvater” or “Doktormutter”, guides the work. In **structured doctoral programmes** there are also courses and several supervisors. Today some dissertations also consist of several articles that have been published in journals.

At the end there is often an oral exam, the **disputation** or defence. In it you present the work and answer critical questions from experts. The grades are traditionally in Latin: **summa cum laude** is the highest, followed by magna cum laude, cum laude and rite. At many universities you may only use the title after the work has been published.

Doctor's degrees have existed since the Middle Ages; the first were awarded at universities such as Bologna and Paris. Internationally the title **PhD** is widespread; it stands for Philosophiae Doctor and is awarded in almost all subjects. An **honorary doctorate**, abbreviated Dr. h.c., is awarded without a dissertation for special achievements. Universities use it to honour, for example, researchers, artists or public figures.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large research paper for a doctor's degree.
A person who is working on their doctoral thesis.
The oral defence of the doctoral thesis in front of experts.
Latin for “with highest praise”, the best grade.
Latin for “for the sake of honour”.

gewusst: In Switzerland the title “Dr.” is not part of your official name and so does not appear in your passport.
Some people have several honorary doctorates from different universities.
Anyone who copies in their doctoral thesis without giving the sources can lose the title again.

teile.einleitung: Quorum sensing is a kind of language of bacteria. Using signal substances, they notice how many other bacteria are nearby. Only when enough of them are together do they start certain actions together, for example glowing.
wichtigste: Quorum sensing is a form of communication with which bacteria measure their cell density.
The signal molecules are generally called autoinducers.
Quorum sensing was first described in the glowing bacterium Vibrio fischeri.
Vibrio fischeri lives in symbiosis in the light organ of a squid.
Many gram-negative bacteria use acyl-homoserine lactones as signal substances.
Quorum sensing often controls the formation of biofilms.
Bonnie Bassler researched communication between different kinds of bacteria.
Quorum quenching is meant to disrupt the quorum sensing of germs.

abschnitte.text: The word **quorum** comes from Latin and means the minimum number of members who must be present for a vote. “Sensing” means “noticing”. Bacteria constantly give off small amounts of a signal substance. If many bacteria are together, the amount of this substance rises, and above a certain threshold they all switch on certain genes at the same time.

Quorum sensing was discovered around 1970 in the sea bacterium **Vibrio fischeri**. On their own these bacteria do not glow, but in large numbers they do. They live in the **light organ** of the Hawaiian bobtail squid. The squid uses the light at night as camouflage, so that seen from below it does not cast a shadow in the moonlight.

The signal molecules are generally called **autoinducers**. Many gram-negative bacteria use acyl-homoserine lactones for this. Gram-positive bacteria, on the other hand, usually use small pieces of protein called peptides. The researcher **Bonnie Bassler** showed that there are also signal substances with which different kinds of bacteria communicate with each other.

Many bacteria form a shared layer of slime on surfaces, a **biofilm**. Examples are plaque on teeth or the coating in water pipes. Germs such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa also often wait until there are enough of them before they release their harmful substances. That gives the immune system less time to fight them early.

A new idea against infections is called **quorum quenching**. Here the signal substances are broken down or blocked, so that the bacteria can no longer act together. The bacteria are not killed, only made “deaf”. Researchers hope that in this way less resistance will develop than with classic antibiotics.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny single-celled living things without a nucleus.
A signal substance that bacteria give off to measure their numbers.
A slimy layer of many bacteria on a surface.
Living together in a way that benefits both partners.

gewusst: The term “quorum sensing” was only coined in 1994, although the phenomenon had been known for decades.
Every morning the Hawaiian bobtail squid pushes out a large part of its glowing bacteria and lets the rest grow back during the day.
Plaque on teeth is also a biofilm in which bacteria communicate with each other.

teile.einleitung: In ecology, producers are living things that can make their own food. They include above all green plants, algae and some bacteria. They are at the start of every food chain, because without them animals and people would have nothing to eat.
wichtigste: Producers are living things that make their own food.
The technical term for them is autotrophic.
Green plants make their food through photosynthesis.
For this they take in carbon dioxide from the air.
Chlorophyll makes plants green and makes photosynthesis possible.
The phytoplankton in the sea supplies a large part of the Earth's oxygen.
In the lightless deep sea there are bacteria that get energy from chemical substances.

abschnitte.text: **Producers** are called this because they “produce”, that is, make, food. From simple substances such as water and carbon dioxide they build energy-rich substances such as sugar. Living things that can do this are called **autotrophic**, which means “feeding themselves”. Producers include trees, grasses, flowers, mosses and algae. Some bacteria are producers too.

Green plants make their food through **photosynthesis**. In this process they take in carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil. With the energy of sunlight they build glucose from these and give off **oxygen**. The green pigment **chlorophyll** in the leaves captures the light. Without photosynthesis there would be hardly any oxygen to breathe.

abschnitte.titel: At the start of the food chain
abschnitte.text: In every **food chain** the producers are right at the start. Plant-eaters such as hares or cows eat plants; they are primary consumers. Meat-eaters such as the fox in turn eat the plant-eaters. At the end, fungi and bacteria break down dead living things; they are called **decomposers**. This creates a cycle in which substances are used again and again.

In the sea the most important producers are tiny algae, the **phytoplankton**. These living things float in the water and can usually only be seen under a microscope. They supply a large part of the Earth's oxygen; estimates say about half. In a Swiss lake too, floating algae form the basis of food in the open water. Tiny crustaceans feed on them, and these in turn are eaten by fish such as whitefish.

In the deep sea there are hot springs where no sunlight reaches. Even so, mussels, crabs and tube worms live there. The producers here are **bacteria** that get energy from chemical substances such as sulphur compounds. This process is called **chemosynthesis**. It shows that life is possible even entirely without the Sun.

begriffe.erklaerung: Able to make your own food from simple substances.
The process in which plants use sunlight to make sugar and oxygen.
A living thing that eats other living things.
A living thing that breaks down dead material, for example fungi and bacteria.
Tiny algae and bacteria floating in water that carry out photosynthesis.

gewusst: A single large broadleaved tree can produce several kilograms of oxygen on a summer's day.
In Lake Murten the so-called Burgundy blood alga used to turn the water reddish at times.
Carnivorous plants such as the sundew are still producers, because they carry out photosynthesis.

teile.einleitung: The Permian-Triassic mass extinction was the largest extinction of species in the history of the Earth. About 252 million years ago the vast majority of all living things in the sea and many species on land disappeared. After that a new geological age began, in which the dinosaurs later appeared.
wichtigste: The Permian-Triassic mass extinction happened about 252 million years ago.
It was the largest of the five great mass extinctions in the Earth's history.
The main cause is thought to be the enormous volcanic activity of the Siberian Traps.
The trilobites disappeared for good.
It is the only known mass extinction of insects.
The plant-eater Lystrosaurus survived and became extremely common in the early Triassic.
It took several million years for ecosystems to largely recover.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the **Permian** period most animal and plant species died out within a short time. Researchers estimate that about nine out of ten species in the sea disappeared. On land, too, many vertebrates, plants and insects died. At that time all the continents together formed the supercontinent **Pangaea**. Because of its huge scale, the event is also called “The Great Dying”.

Today the main cause is thought to be the volcanic activity of the **Siberian Traps** in present-day Russia. There, over a long period, huge amounts of lava poured out of the Earth and covered an enormous area. Vast amounts of carbon dioxide and other gases entered the air. The climate warmed sharply, the seas became more acidic and they increasingly lacked oxygen. Many living things could not adapt quickly enough.

Researchers recognise the disaster in the rock layers of the **Permian-Triassic boundary**. Below this boundary you find many different fossils, above it only a few. The rocks also show a clear drop in the isotope ratio of **carbon-13**. This is a sign that the Earth's carbon cycle was severely disturbed. With precise measurements the age was determined as about 252 million years.

The **trilobites**, primitive arthropods that had existed for over 250 million years, disappeared for good. Many corals, sea lilies and brachiopods also died out. For insects it is the only known mass extinction in their history. Among the survivors was **Lystrosaurus**, a plant-eating relative of mammals about the size of a pig. In the early Triassic it was so common that its bones are found on several continents.

After the extinction it took several million years for life to recover. In the **Triassic** new groups of animals then developed, including the first dinosaurs and the first mammals. In Switzerland, **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino bears witness to this time. Many well-preserved fossils of marine reptiles and fish from the middle Triassic were found there. The mountain is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

begriffe.erklaerung: When a very large number of species all over the Earth die out within a short time.
The geological period before the Triassic, which ended about 252 million years ago.
The geological period after the Permian, in which the first dinosaurs appeared.
A huge area of layers of solidified lava that looks like steps.
The remains or traces of a living thing from long ago.

gewusst: The word “trap” comes from Swedish and means “stairs”, because the lava layers look like steps.
Without the Permian-Triassic mass extinction there might never have been dinosaurs.
Trilobites lived in the seas for about 270 million years before they disappeared.

teile.einleitung: A pictogram is a simple picture sign that gives information without words. You see pictograms at railway stations, on road signs, at emergency exits and on smartphones. In maths similar little pictures are also used in pictograms or picture charts to show amounts clearly.
wichtigste: A pictogram is a simplified picture that you can understand without language.
There are many pictograms at railway stations and airports so that everyone can find their way.
The emergency exit sign with the running figure is green.
A pictogram with a knife and fork means that you can get something to eat here.
In a picture chart one picture stands for a particular number.
A picture chart must always say what one picture stands for.

abschnitte.text: A **pictogram** is a greatly simplified picture that gives a message without words. The word is made up of the Latin pictum for painted and the Greek gramma for something written. Good pictograms are drawn so clearly that you understand them at a glance. A knife and fork, for example, means restaurant, a cup of coffee and a bed mean a place to stay overnight.

At railway stations and airports people from many countries who speak different languages meet. That is why there are particularly many pictograms there for toilets, luggage, platforms or exits. With SBB you find such signs on almost every board. Road signs on the street also work on this principle.

Some pictograms save lives, such as the green sign with the running figure that shows the **emergency exit**. Green signs mean rescue, red ones warn of fire or forbid something, yellow ones point out dangers. Blue signs say that you must do something, for example wear a helmet. These colours are internationally standardised so that they mean the same everywhere.

In maths a **picture chart** shows amounts with small pictures. If one apple picture stands for 2 apples, then 4 apple pictures show 8 apples. If a whole picture stands for 10 bikes, half a picture shows 5 bikes. So that the chart can be read, there must always be a **key** that says what one picture stands for.

Even the oldest scripts, such as the **hieroglyphs** in ancient Egypt, began with picture signs. In the 1920s Otto Neurath in Vienna developed a picture language to make statistics understandable with small figures. For the 1972 Olympic Games in Munich the graphic designer **Otl Aicher** created famous sports pictograms. Today the emojis on your phone are also a modern form of pictograms.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simple picture sign that shows information without words.
A chart in which small pictures stand for a particular number.
An explanation next to a chart or map of what the signs mean.
The picture writing of the ancient Egyptians.

gewusst: Otl Aicher's sports pictograms are still used today as a model for the Olympic Games.
The figure on the emergency exit sign always runs towards a door.
The symbols on washing machines and clothing labels are pictograms too.

teile.einleitung: Plant fossils are remains or impressions of plants that lived millions of years ago. They are found as leaf impressions in stone, as petrified wood or as coal. They reveal what the plant world used to look like and how the climate has changed.
wichtigste: A leaf impression forms when a leaf is covered with mud and leaves its shape behind.
Fern impressions in stone are often dark or black.
Fern impressions are found especially often in the rock next to coal.
In good impressions you can even see the fine leaflets.
The counterpart that shows the shape the other way round is called the counterpart impression.
Huge fern forests existed long before flowering plants, which only appeared later.
Leaves of broadleaved trees can also form impressions and become fossils.

abschnitte.text: If a leaf falls into a swamp or lake, it is sometimes quickly covered with **mud**. Then hardly any oxygen gets to it, and the leaf does not rot straight away. Over a long time the layers are pressed together and turn into stone. Often all that is left of the leaf is a thin, dark film of carbon and its shape in the rock. If you split the stone, you see the **impression** on one side and the counterpart on the other.

As well as impressions there is also **petrified wood**. Here the cells of the wood were gradually replaced by minerals such as quartz, so that you can even see tree rings. Some plant parts are trapped in **amber**, the fossilised resin of trees. Tiny pollen grains also often survive for millions of years. Researchers use them to find out which plants grew in an area.

abschnitte.titel: The forests of the Coal Age
abschnitte.text: About 300 million years ago, in the **Carboniferous**, huge swamp forests grew. In them stood tree ferns, club-moss trees up to 30 metres tall such as the scale trees, and horsetails the size of trees. Dead plants sank into the swamp and over millions of years became **coal**. That is why particularly many impressions of ferns are found in the rock next to coal seams. There were no flowers yet at that time.

**Flowering plants** only appeared much later, in the Cretaceous, that is, at the time of the dinosaurs. Before that the plant world consisted of ferns, mosses, horsetails and conifers. So for a long time there were huge fern forests but no colourful flower meadows. Grasses, too, only really spread after the dinosaurs. Plant fossils show this development step by step.

Plant fossils show what plants looked like millions of years ago. But they also reveal a lot about the **climate** in the past. If, for example, impressions of palms or cinnamon trees are found in Europe, it was once much warmer there. In Switzerland, impressions of leaves are found in the **Molasse** rocks of the Central Plateau, showing that an almost subtropical climate once existed here. If you find fossils, you should show them to experts at a museum.

begriffe.erklaerung: The remains or trace of a living thing from prehistoric times, usually preserved in rock.
The counterpart of an impression, showing the shape the other way round.
A geological period about 300 million years ago in which a lot of coal formed.
Rock layers of sand and mud that are widespread in the Swiss Central Plateau.
The many small parts of a leaf that make up a fern frond.

gewusst: The coal that used to power steam locomotives is made of plants that lived about 300 million years ago.
Some prehistoric horsetails grew as big as trees; today they are usually only knee-high.
In petrified wood you can sometimes still count the tree rings after millions of years.

teile.einleitung: Pile dwellings are the remains of villages from the Neolithic and Bronze Age that stood on the shores of lakes and in moors around the Alps. Their wooden posts, tools and even food remains have survived for thousands of years under water. Since 2011 they have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and most of them are in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Pile dwellings are settlements from the period from about 5000 to 500 BC.
The first were discovered in 1854 on Lake Zurich near Meilen.
Their wood survived because it lay without air under water or in mud.
The pile dwellers lived from farming, keeping livestock and fishing.
The roofs were usually covered with reeds or straw.
Since 2011, 111 sites in six countries have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
With 56 sites, most of them are in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In the dry winter of 1853/54 the water level of **Lake Zurich** fell very low. Near Obermeilen many wooden posts, shards and tools came to light. The Zurich researcher **Ferdinand Keller** realised that these were the remains of very old villages. He imagined that the houses stood on platforms above the water and so created the image of the pile dwellers.

abschnitte.titel: What did the villages look like?
abschnitte.text: The houses were built of wood and stood on posts that were driven into the soft ground. The walls were often made of wattle smeared with clay. The roofs were covered with **reeds** or straw. Today we know that many villages stood on the shore or on land that was sometimes flooded, and not in the middle of the lake.

The pile dwellers were **farmers**: they grew cereals such as wheat and barley and kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. They also fished, hunted and gathered berries, hazelnuts and apples. They made cloth from flax. Later they learned to cast tools from copper and **bronze**.

Normally wood, cloth and food remains rot after a while. But in the lakes and moors the remains lay under water or mud, where hardly any **oxygen** gets in. That is why posts, wooden vessels, nets and even charred bread have survived. Using the tree rings in the wood, **dendrochronology**, it is often possible to say to the exact year when a tree was felled.

In 2011, 111 sites were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List as **Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps**. They are in Switzerland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy and Slovenia. With 56 sites, Switzerland has the largest share, for example on Lake Zurich, Lake Biel, Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Constance. Most sites lie invisibly under water and are explored by divers.

At the Laténium near Neuchâtel and at the Swiss National Museum in Zurich you can look at finds from pile-dwelling settlements. On Lake Constance in Germany the **Pfahlbaumuseum Unteruhldingen** shows reconstructed houses in the water. In Switzerland too there are reconstructions where you can try out the life of the pile dwellers for yourself. In this way the Stone Age comes to life for visitors.

begriffe.erklaerung: The period when people settled down, farmed and ground tools from stone.
The science that studies the past using finds from the ground.
Dating wood with the help of tree rings.
Especially valuable places that UNESCO wants to protect for all humanity.

gewusst: Because of the enthusiasm for pile dwellings in the 19th century, the pile dwellers became a kind of ancestors in Switzerland with whom the whole country felt connected.
Remains of bread baked several thousand years ago have been found in pile-dwelling settlements.
One of the oldest wooden wheels in the world was found in a moor near Ljubljana in Slovenia, which is also part of the pile-dwelling World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: The base rate fallacy is a typical error in thinking when dealing with probabilities. You pay attention only to a test result or a clue and forget how common something is in the first place. As a result you can misjudge things enormously, for example with medical tests.
wichtigste: In the base rate fallacy you ignore how common a characteristic is to begin with.
This basic frequency is also called the base rate or prevalence.
With rare diseases, many positive tests are false positives.
Bayes' theorem can be used to avoid the error correctly.
Gerd Gigerenzer recommends presenting it with natural frequencies.
The positive predictive value tells you how likely you really are to be ill if a test is positive.
Rare diseases are often only tested for in people with symptoms or risks.

abschnitte.text: **Prevalence** is how common a characteristic is in a group, for example how many people have a particular disease. In the base rate fallacy you overlook this basic frequency, which is also called the **base rate**. You rely only on a striking clue, such as a positive test result. The error was studied closely in the 1970s by the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky.

1 per cent of the population has a disease; a test detects 90 per cent of those who are ill and is **false positive** in 9 per cent of healthy people. Imagine 1,000 people: 10 are ill, and 9 of them test positive. But of the 990 healthy people, about 89 also test positive. So of 98 positive tests only 9 come from people who are ill, which is about 9 per cent.

In a city 85 per cent of the taxis are green and 15 per cent blue. A witness recognises colours correctly 80 per cent of the time and says that the taxi in the accident was blue. Many people estimate the probability at 80 per cent, but in fact it is only about 41 per cent. Because there are many more green taxis, the witness quite often thinks a green taxi is blue too.

Mathematically, such problems are solved with **Bayes' theorem**, named after the English clergyman Thomas Bayes from the 18th century. It is much easier with **natural frequencies**, as recommended by the psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer. Instead of using percentages, you take a group of, say, 1,000 people and simply count. In this way non-experts understand the result much better too.

Important figures for a test are its **sensitivity**, the proportion of ill people it detects, and its specificity, the proportion of healthy people with a negative result. But for patients what matters most is the positive predictive value. If a disease is very rare, even a good test is often false positive. That is why rare diseases are tested for mainly in people with symptoms or risks, because the base rate is higher there.

begriffe.erklaerung: How common a characteristic is in a group.
The basic frequency of an event before you know any further clues.
The test reacts even though the person is healthy.
The proportion of healthy people whom the test correctly recognises as healthy.
A rule of calculation for adjusting probabilities with new clues.

gewusst: With a disease that affects 1 in 1,000 people, even with a test that has a 99 per cent hit rate and 5 per cent false alarms, a positive result means you are really ill only about 2 per cent of the time.
In studies, many doctors have also badly misjudged such problems.
The base rate fallacy also plays a role in court verdicts and police searches.

teile.einleitung: A travel diary is a notebook or book in which you record the experiences of a journey. You write in it what you have seen, eaten and experienced, and often add drawings too. Famous explorers kept travel diaries that are now valuable sources for science.
wichtigste: In a travel diary you write down the experiences of a journey.
Explorers kept diaries to record their discoveries.
A ship's diary is called a logbook.
Many travellers draw pictures as well as writing text in their travel diary.
The date and place are often written above each entry.
250 years ago explorers wrote with quill and ink.
Charles Darwin's travel diary later became a well-known book.

abschnitte.text: A **travel diary** is a special kind of diary. A single text in it is called an **entry**, and the date and place are usually written above each entry. You describe landscapes, people, food and special experiences. In this way you can still remember the journey exactly even after many years.

Explorers and researchers kept diaries on their journeys to record their **discoveries**. 250 years ago they wrote with quill and ink, often by candlelight on rolling ships. They noted down plants, animals, the weather and their meetings with people. Today their records are important sources for history and natural science.

On ships the diary is called a **logbook**. In it the course, speed, weather and special events are recorded. The name comes from the “log”, a device that was used in the past to measure the speed of a ship. Christopher Columbus also kept a ship's journal on his first voyage to America in 1492.

From 1831 to 1836 the young naturalist **Charles Darwin** travelled around the world on the ship Beagle. On the way he wrote a detailed diary and many notebooks. From these a well-known book was later made, often called “The Voyage of the Beagle”. His observations, for example on the Galápagos Islands, later helped him with his theory of evolution.

abschnitte.titel: Tips for your own travel diary
abschnitte.text: Write down briefly every day what you have experienced, ideally with the **date and place**. You can make drawings and stick in tickets, postcards or pressed leaves. Smells, sounds and funny mishaps belong in it too. It does not have to be a long journey; even a trip to the mountains or a school camp is worth an entry.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single text in a diary.
The official diary of a ship.
A quick, simple drawing.
A text or object from which you learn something about the past.

gewusst: Today the word “logbook” is also used for space stations and even for computer programs.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe turned his travel notes into the famous book “Italian Journey”.
When the Beagle set sail, Darwin was only 22 years old.

teile.einleitung: Permafrost is ground or rock that stays frozen without a break for at least two years. It is found in the cold polar regions, but also high up in the Swiss Alps. Because the Earth is warming, permafrost is thawing in many places, which brings new dangers.
wichtigste: Permafrost is ground that has been frozen without a break for at least two years.
Permafrost is especially widespread in Siberia, Alaska and Canada.
In Switzerland it is found mainly in the high mountains, often above about 2,500 metres.
If permafrost thaws in steep rock faces, rockfalls and landslides threaten.
The Swiss monitoring network PERMOS observes the permafrost.
Rock glaciers are masses of debris and ice that slowly creep down the valley.
The greenhouse gas methane can escape from thawing permafrost.

abschnitte.text: The word **permafrost** means permanent frost. It refers to ground or rock whose temperature stays at or below 0 °C without a break for at least two years. It often contains ice, which holds stones and soil together like cement. In summer only a thin top layer thaws, the **active layer**.

Worldwide, permafrost is widespread above all in **Siberia**, Alaska, Canada and on the Tibetan Plateau. In Siberia the frozen ground reaches several hundred metres deep in places. In the permafrost of Siberia people have even found remains of mammoths that stayed well preserved for thousands of years. There is also permafrost under some seabeds of the Arctic.

In Switzerland permafrost lies mainly in the high mountains, often above about 2,500 metres. It occurs especially on shady north-facing slopes and in scree slopes. Since about the year 2000 the monitoring network **PERMOS** has been observing the temperature of the ground in boreholes and the movement of rock glaciers. The measurements show that the permafrost in the Alps is clearly warming.

A **rock glacier** is a tongue-shaped mass of rock debris and ice. It creeps slowly down the valley, usually only a few centimetres to metres a year. From the outside it looks like a pile of stones, but inside there is frozen ice. In recent years many rock glaciers in the Alps have become faster because the ground is getting warmer.

When permafrost thaws in steep rock faces, the rock loses its hold. Then **rockfalls** and landslides threaten, which can endanger hiking paths, roads and villages. Mountain railway stations and mountain huts need special foundations because the ground can sink or move as it thaws. That is why experts monitor endangered slopes with measuring instruments.

Huge amounts of old plant remains are stored in the permafrost of the polar regions. If the ground thaws, bacteria break these remains down. This produces carbon dioxide and **methane**, both greenhouse gases that make the warming even stronger. In addition, houses, roads and pipelines in the north sink when the ground becomes soft.

begriffe.erklaerung: Ground that stays permanently frozen for at least two years.
The top layer of ground that thaws in summer and freezes again in winter.
A slowly creeping mass of stones and ice in the mountains.
A gas that strongly warms the Earth when it gets into the air.

gewusst: You usually cannot see permafrost from the outside at all, because it lies below the surface.
Mammoths with preserved skin and hair have been found in the Siberian permafrost.
Even under some peaks of the Swiss Alps the rock is frozen inside.

teile.einleitung: Popcorn is a snack made from maize kernels that burst open with a loud pop in great heat. In the process the small, hard kernels turn into big, white, fluffy flakes. Behind the pop there is an exciting physical process involving steam.
wichtigste: For popcorn you need a special kind of maize, popcorn maize.
In the hot pan the water in the kernel turns to steam.
The steam bursts the hard shell, and the kernel pops open.
Popcorn is much bigger than the original maize kernel.
The burst inside is white and fluffy.
Kernels with too little water do not pop.
Popcorn originally comes from America.

abschnitte.text: Popcorn is made from **popcorn maize**, a special kind of maize. Its kernels have a very hard, tight shell and inside they have starch and a little water. Ordinary maize, like the kind you eat as corn on the cob, is not suitable for it. Popcorn is eaten sweet with sugar or caramel, or salty with butter and salt.

When the kernel is heated strongly, the water inside turns into **steam**. Because the hard shell is airtight, the steam cannot escape, and the pressure keeps rising. At about 180 degrees Celsius the shell can no longer withstand the pressure and bursts with a pop. The soft, hot starch foams up and sets immediately, which is how the white, fluffy flake forms.

You put a little oil and a thin layer of kernels in a pan and heat it strongly. A **lid** is important so that the popping kernels do not fly out. Only great heat produces enough steam, so you need a hot pan. When the popping almost stops, you take the pan off the hob so that nothing burns.

Almost always a few kernels stay hard and closed. This is usually because they contain too little **water** or their shell has a crack through which the steam escapes. That is why popcorn maize is stored tightly closed, so that it does not dry out. Completely dry kernels do not pop at all any more.

Popcorn comes from **America**, where maize has been grown for thousands of years. In Peru researchers have found remains of popped maize that are several thousand years old. Maize only came to Europe after the voyages of Christopher Columbus. In the USA popcorn became the typical **cinema snack** in the 20th century, because it was cheap and easy to make.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of maize with a hard shell that is suitable for popcorn.
Water that has turned into a gas through heat.
A nutrient in maize that foams up when heated.
The force with which a gas pushes against its surroundings.

gewusst: Popped popcorn has two typical shapes: a butterfly with wings, and round like a mushroom.
A popping popcorn kernel can jump a few centimetres into the air.
In cinemas popcorn is usually made in a machine with a hot kettle.

teile.einleitung: Smallpox was one of the most dangerous infectious diseases in human history. It was caused by the variola virus and killed millions of people over centuries. Thanks to a worldwide vaccination campaign, it has been considered eradicated since 1980.
wichtigste: The cause of smallpox is the variola virus.
Typical were pus-filled blisters on the skin, which often left scars on the face.
In the severe form about a third of those who fell ill died.
Smallpox was spread mainly from person to person through droplets.
The first signs of illness usually appeared about 12 days after infection.
In 1796 Edward Jenner developed vaccination with cowpox.
The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

abschnitte.text: Smallpox was caused by the **variola virus**. It was spread mainly from person to person through **droplets** when coughing, sneezing or talking. The clothes and bedding of sick people could also be infectious. After infection it usually took about 12 days for the first signs of illness to appear. Animals played no role in spreading it; the virus only attacked people.

At first the sick had a high fever, headache and backache. After that a rash with **pus-filled blisters** formed, especially on the face, arms and legs. In the severe form about a third of those who fell ill died. Those who survived often had **scars** on their face for ever. Some also went blind because of the disease.

Smallpox already existed in ancient Egypt; traces have even been found on mummies. In Europe, in the past, almost everyone caught it at some point, including kings and emperors. When Europeans came to America from the 16th century onwards, they brought smallpox with them. The **indigenous peoples** had no defences against the virus, and very many of them died. This contributed to the fall of great empires such as that of the Aztecs.

The English doctor **Edward Jenner** noticed that milkmaids who had had the harmless cowpox did not catch smallpox. In 1796 he gave cowpox to a boy and showed that he was protected afterwards. That was the beginning of modern **vaccination**. The word “vaccine” comes from the Latin “vacca”, meaning cow. In the 19th century many countries and also Swiss cantons introduced smallpox vaccination.

From 1967 the World Health Organization, **WHO**, started a large programme to defeat smallpox worldwide. Experts looked for every case of the disease and vaccinated everyone in the surrounding area. The last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977. On 8 May 1980 the WHO officially declared smallpox **eradicated**. To this day it is the only human disease that has been completely defeated.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny germ that can only multiply in living cells.
Protection against a disease in which the body learns to fight off a germ.
The time between infection and the first signs of illness.
A disease that spreads to very many people in a short time.

gewusst: Today the smallpox virus is officially kept in only two high-security laboratories, one in the USA and one in Russia.
Because smallpox has been eradicated, children are no longer vaccinated against it today.
Even before Jenner, people in Asia tried to protect others from severe illness with a little smallpox scab.

teile.einleitung: A plaster is a small wound dressing that you stick on cuts, grazes or blisters. It protects the wound from dirt and germs so that it can heal in peace. Plasters belong in every medicine cabinet and in every rucksack for outings.
wichtigste: A plaster protects small wounds from dirt and germs.
Before sticking it on, you should clean the wound.
The soft pad in the middle lies directly on the wound.
Thin strips of film protect the sticky surface until you need the plaster.
Blister plasters help against blisters on the feet.
If a wound becomes red and hot, it could be infected.
The outer layer of many waterproof plasters is made of plastic.

abschnitte.text: A **plaster**, in technical language an adhesive dressing, consists of a sticky strip and a soft **wound pad** in the middle. The pad lies directly on the wound and soaks up blood and fluid from the wound. It is coated so that it does not stick to the wound. Thin **strips of film** protect the sticky surface until you put the plaster on.

Before you stick on a plaster, you should clean the wound. Small grazes are best rinsed with clean water. After that you can use a **disinfectant**, which kills germs. The skin around the wound should be dry so that the plaster sticks well.

Small wounds usually heal under a plaster in a few days. But if the wound becomes red, hot, swollen or hurts more and more, it could be **infected**. Then you should tell an adult and go to the doctor. A plaster is also not enough for deep cuts, bites or heavy bleeding.

There are plasters in many shapes and sizes, for fingers, knees or heels. **Blister plasters** are thick and padded and help against blisters on the feet, for example when hiking. Waterproof plasters have a plastic outer layer so that you can shower or bathe with them. For children there are plasters with colourful pictures.

In the past, wounds were bandaged with strips of cloth that you had to cut yourself. Around 1920 the American Earle Dickson invented a ready-made plaster with a gauze pad, because his wife often hurt herself while cooking. This became the well-known brand Band-Aid. Shortly afterwards the German company Beiersdorf brought the Hansaplast plaster onto the market.

begriffe.erklaerung: An injury to the skin, for example a cut or a graze.
Tiny living things such as bacteria that can cause diseases.
A defence reaction of the body in which a spot becomes red, hot and swollen.
To kill germs with a special substance.

gewusst: In English a plaster is often simply named after the brand Band-Aid.
The German word “Pflaster” also means the surface of stones on old streets and squares.
Small wounds usually heal faster under a plaster because they stay moist and no thick scab forms.

teile.einleitung: A promoter is a section of DNA where the reading of a gene begins. You can think of it as a start button in front of each gene. Whether and how hard this button is pressed decides how much of a protein a cell makes.
wichtigste: A promoter is a DNA sequence where transcription begins.
In many eukaryotic promoters the TATA box lies about 25 to 30 bases before the start.
In bacteria the sigma factor of RNA polymerase recognises the promoter.
The sequence at -10 in bacterial promoters is called the Pribnow box.
Enhancers can boost transcription even from a great distance.
François Jacob and Jacques Monod described the operon model in 1961.
Heavy methylation in the promoter region usually switches a gene off in vertebrates.

abschnitte.text: In DNA the building plans for proteins are stored in **genes**. So that a cell can use a gene, it is first copied into a messenger RNA; this is **transcription**. The **promoter** is the section of DNA directly in front of the gene where this process begins. Here the enzyme RNA polymerase, which makes the RNA, binds. So the promoter decides where reading starts and in which direction.

In bacteria a part of the RNA polymerase, the **sigma factor**, recognises the promoter. It looks for two short recognition sites. One lies about 10 bases before the start and is called the **Pribnow box**; the other lies about 35 bases before it. The better these sites match the sigma factor, the more often the gene is read. Once the polymerase has started, the sigma factor comes away again.

In plants, animals and humans, promoters are more complicated. In many of them the **TATA box**, named after its sequence of letters, lies about 25 to 30 bases before the start. Helper proteins, the **transcription factors**, bind there first, and only then the RNA polymerase. In addition there are **enhancers**, sections of DNA that boost transcription even from a great distance. The DNA forms loops so that sites far apart touch.

A famous example is the **lac operon** of the gut bacterium E. coli. It contains genes for using milk sugar, lactose. When there is no lactose, a **repressor** sits on the operator and blocks the reading. If lactose is present, the repressor comes away and the genes are read. This operon model was described in 1961 by the Frenchmen François Jacob and Jacques Monod, who received the Nobel Prize for it in 1965.

In vertebrates chemical tags, **methyl groups**, can be attached to promoters. Methylation of many cytosines in a promoter region usually switches the gene off. In this way different cells with the same DNA can use quite different genes, for example skin cells and nerve cells. In **biotechnology** strong promoters are used so that bacteria make large amounts of a desired protein. This is how insulin for people with diabetes is produced, for example.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of DNA with the building plan for a protein or an RNA.
Copying a gene from DNA into RNA.
An enzyme that makes RNA using DNA as a template.
A protein that blocks the reading of a gene.
A protein that helps to start the reading of a gene.

gewusst: Almost every cell in your body contains the same DNA, but thanks to promoters and how they are controlled, only some of the genes are used in each cell.
The Pribnow box is named after the researcher David Pribnow, who described it in 1975.
Researchers put promoters into bacteria that only switch on with certain substances and so use them as living sensors.

teile.einleitung: Basel is one of the most important centres of the pharmaceutical industry in the whole world. Large companies such as Roche and Novartis have their headquarters here, and thousands of people do research on new medicines. The history of this industry began over 150 years ago with colourful dyes.
wichtigste: Basel's chemical and pharmaceutical industry grew in the 19th century out of making dyes for the silk ribbon industry.
The Rhine, as a source of water and a transport route, was an important advantage of the location.
Because Switzerland for a long time had no patent protection for chemical processes, companies could copy foreign dyes.
Chemical and pharmaceutical products are Switzerland's largest export sector (as of 2024).
The cross-border life sciences region around Basel is called BioValley.
The Biozentrum of the University of Basel has been a centre of the molecular life sciences since 1971.
Novartis has its own campus in the St Johann district with buildings by well-known architects.

abschnitte.text: In the 18th and 19th centuries Basel was a city of the **silk ribbon industry**. A lot of dyes were needed for the colourful ribbons. In the middle of the 19th century the first artificial dyes made from coal tar were invented. Basel businessmen began to make such **coal-tar dyes** themselves. From these dye factories, companies gradually developed that also produced medicines.

The **Rhine** supplied water for the factories and was an important transport route. Basel lies right on the border with France and Germany and was well connected with Europe. Another reason was the law: for a long time Switzerland had no **patent protection** for chemical processes. So Basel companies could copy dyes from abroad without paying for licences. In addition, the city had capital from rich merchants and an old university.

Among the early companies were **Geigy**, **Ciba** and **Sandoz**. In 1896 Fritz Hoffmann-La Roche founded the company **Roche**, which concentrated on medicines from the start. In 1970 Ciba and Geigy joined to form Ciba-Geigy. In 1996 Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz merged to form **Novartis**, at the time one of the largest company mergers in the world. Today Roche and Novartis are among the largest pharmaceutical companies worldwide.

The **University of Basel** was founded in 1460 and is the oldest university in Switzerland. Its **Biozentrum** opened in 1971 and is a well-known centre for molecular biology. The region around Basel, with parts of France and Germany, is called **BioValley** and brings together many companies, hospitals and research institutes. People from all over the world work here. The association of research-based pharmaceutical companies, **Interpharma**, also has its headquarters in Basel.

Chemical and pharmaceutical products are Switzerland's largest export sector (as of 2024). A large part of them comes from the Basel region. The two **Roche Towers** on the Rhine are the tallest buildings in Switzerland and shape the city. On the **Novartis Campus** in the St Johann district there are buildings by famous architects. The industry brings jobs and taxes, but it also makes the region dependent on a few large companies.

Chemistry also brought problems. On 1 November 1986 a Sandoz warehouse burned down in **Schweizerhalle** near Basel. With the water used to fight the fire, toxic chemicals got into the Rhine, and countless fish died far downstream. After the disaster the safety regulations were made much stricter. Today the Rhine is much cleaner again, and salmon are expected to be able to return in the future.

begriffe.erklaerung: The industry that researches and produces medicines.
Artificial dyes that used to be made from coal tar.
When two or more companies join together to form a single one.
The sciences of life, that is, biology, medicine and related subjects.
Selling goods abroad.

gewusst: The name Novartis comes from the Latin “novae artes” and means roughly “new arts”.
Basel's pharmaceutical industry grew out of dyes for silk ribbons.
The University of Basel is older than Columbus's discovery of America.

teile.einleitung: A randomised controlled trial is a scientific experiment used to find out whether a treatment really works. The participants are divided into groups by chance, and for comparison one group receives no treatment or a different one. In medicine it is regarded as a particularly reliable kind of study.
wichtigste: The participants are divided among the groups by chance.
Because of chance, known and unknown confounding factors are spread evenly.
A control group receives a dummy medicine or the existing treatment.
The allocation list is kept secret so that nobody can influence the groups.
As early as 1747 James Lind tested remedies for scurvy in an early controlled experiment.
In 1948 streptomycin was tested against tuberculosis in one of the first modern randomised trials.
The CONSORT guideline sets out how to report fully on such trials.

abschnitte.text: **Randomised** means that chance decides who gets which treatment, rather like throwing a dice. **Controlled** means that there is a comparison group. At the end you compare how the people in the groups are doing. Because the groups differ only in the treatment, cause and effect can be shown better than in an observational study.

First researchers decide exactly what they want to measure and who may take part. The allocation stays secret until a person has definitely been accepted, so that nobody can choose who goes into which group. The control group often gets a **placebo**, a dummy medicine without an active substance. In a **double-blind trial** neither the participants nor the doctors know who is getting which remedy.

In **stratified randomisation** people are first divided into subgroups, for example by age, and then chance decides within each subgroup. In a **crossover trial** each person receives both treatments one after the other. The results are often analysed according to the intention-to-treat principle: everyone counts in the group they were allocated to, even if they drop out. In this way the advantage of random allocation is kept.

In 1747 the Scottish ship's doctor **James Lind** divided twelve sailors suffering from scurvy into groups and gave them different remedies. Only the sailors who were given oranges and lemons recovered quickly. In 1948 the antibiotic **streptomycin** was tested against tuberculosis in Great Britain in one of the first modern randomised trials. The statistician Austin Bradford Hill played a decisive role in shaping this approach.

Before a new medicine is approved in Switzerland, the authority **Swissmedic** examines the results of such trials. Studies involving people must first be approved by a cantonal ethics committee. All participants are informed and may drop out at any time. The international guideline **CONSORT** makes sure that trials are published completely and in a way that can be followed.

begriffe.erklaerung: Random allocation to the groups of a trial.
A comparison group that does not receive the new treatment.
A dummy medicine without an active substance.
Neither participants nor those giving treatment know who is getting what.
An influence that can distort the result, such as age or lifestyle.

gewusst: Even a placebo can ease complaints, because people expect it to work.
The coronavirus vaccines were tested in randomised trials with tens of thousands of participants before they were approved.
The term scurvy refers to a disease caused by a lack of vitamin C, from which many sailors used to die.

teile.einleitung: Proton therapy is a special form of radiotherapy against cancer. Instead of X-rays, tiny, very fast particles, protons, are fired at the tumour. With the Paul Scherrer Institute in Aargau, Switzerland is a world pioneer of this method.
wichtigste: Protons give off most of their energy at the end of their path.
This dose maximum is called the Bragg peak.
As a result, healthy tissue behind the tumour is protected better than with X-rays.
The depth of penetration is changed through the energy of the protons.
At PSI eye tumours have been treated with the OPTIS facility since 1984.
Spot scanning, developed at PSI, was first used on patients in 1996.
Proton therapy is especially important for children.

abschnitte.text: In **radiotherapy**, high-energy rays destroy the cells of a tumour. Usually X-rays are used for this, which pass through the whole body. In **proton therapy**, protons are used instead; these are positively charged particles from the atomic nucleus. They are brought to a very high speed in a particle accelerator. A proton is about 1,836 times heavier than an electron.

Protons only give off most of their energy at the end of their path, shortly before they stop. This dose maximum is called the **Bragg peak**, after the British physicist William Henry Bragg. X-rays, on the other hand, give off a lot of energy on the way and fly on behind the tumour. So with protons you can hit the tumour precisely and protect the **healthy tissue** behind it. The depth of penetration is changed by adjusting the energy of the protons.

The **Paul Scherrer Institute** (PSI) in Villigen in the canton of Aargau is a large federal research institute. Since 1984 eye tumours have been treated there with protons using the **OPTIS** facility. Researchers at PSI developed **spot scanning**, in which a fine beam scans the tumour point by point. This technique was first used on patients in 1996 and is used worldwide today. Since 2007 the superconducting cyclotron COMET has supplied the protons for the therapy.

A **gantry** is a huge rotating machine that directs the proton beam onto the patient from different directions. It is as big as a house with several floors and weighs many tonnes. Even so, it has to aim the beam to within fractions of a millimetre. The patient lies still on a movable couch. A treatment usually consists of several sessions over a few weeks.

Proton therapy is especially important for **children**. Their bodies are still growing, and healthy tissue is sensitive to radiation. Because protons hit less healthy tissue, there are fewer **late effects**, such as growth problems. That is why many children with tumours in the brain or on the spine are treated at PSI. Because the facilities are very expensive, there is only a limited number of such centres worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
A growth of cells that divide uncontrollably.
The point where protons give off the most energy shortly before they stop.
A circular particle accelerator.
A rotating machine that directs the beam from different directions.

gewusst: The idea of using protons against cancer comes from the American physicist Robert Wilson in 1946.
The COMET cyclotron is superconducting and has to be cooled to extremely low temperatures for this.
Small children are sometimes put into a light sleep for the treatment so that they lie completely still.

teile.einleitung: A quantum dot is a tiny crystal of semiconductor material, only a few nanometres in size. In it the electrons are so tightly trapped that it behaves like an artificial atom. The special thing is that it glows in a different colour depending on its size.
wichtigste: A quantum dot is a semiconductor nanocrystal in which electrons are confined in all directions.
