Smaller quantum dots glow bluer, larger ones redder.
They are called “artificial atoms” because, like atoms, they have separate energy levels.
In 2023 Moungi Bawendi, Louis Brus and Alexei Ekimov received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for them.
Quantum dots are used in screens for especially pure colours.
In biology they serve as glowing markers for cell structures.
Many classic quantum dots are made of cadmium selenide, which raises health concerns.

abschnitte.text: A quantum dot is a crystal of a **semiconductor** that is usually only 2 to 10 nanometres in size. A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. Such a crystal consists of only a few hundred to a few thousand atoms. Its electrons cannot move freely in it but are trapped as if in a tiny box.

Because the electrons are trapped, they can only take on very particular **energy levels**. According to the “particle in a box” model, the energy is inversely proportional to the square of the length of the box. If you halve the length, the energy becomes four times as large. That is why smaller quantum dots give off higher-energy, bluer light, and larger ones more red light.

At the beginning of the 1980s **Alexei Ekimov** in the Soviet Union discovered coloured nanocrystals in glass. Shortly afterwards **Louis Brus** in the USA found such particles in a liquid. In 1993 **Moungi Bawendi** developed a method for making quantum dots of even size. For this work the three jointly received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2023.

In some televisions and screens quantum dots provide especially strong and pure colours. Such devices are often called **QLED**. Researchers are also working on solar cells, lamps and sensors with quantum dots. In medicine and biology they are used to mark parts of cells so that they glow under the microscope.

Many classic quantum dots are made of **cadmium selenide**. Cadmium is a toxic heavy metal, which is why its use is strictly limited in many countries. So people are looking for alternatives, for example quantum dots made of indium phosphide. These contain no cadmium and are considered more environmentally friendly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material that conducts electricity poorly or well depending on conditions, for example silicon.
A millionth of a millimetre, much smaller than a cell.
A particular energy step that an electron can take on.
The glowing of a substance after it has absorbed light.

gewusst: A solution of quantum dots of the same substance can glow green, yellow or red depending on the size of the particles.
Even in the Middle Ages glassmakers coloured glass with tiny particles without knowing that they were nanocrystals.
A quantum dot is about ten thousand times thinner than a human hair.

teile.einleitung: A plasmid is a small, usually ring-shaped strand of DNA that occurs in bacteria alongside the actual genetic material. Plasmids can copy themselves independently and move from one bacterium to another. In genetic engineering they are an important tool for getting genes into cells.
wichtigste: Plasmids are small DNA rings outside the bacterial chromosome.
The copying of a plasmid begins at the origin of replication.
The term “plasmid” was coined by Joshua Lederberg in 1952.
In conjugation bacteria pass on plasmids through a connection between cells.
Plasmids spread antibiotic resistance quickly between bacteria.
In genetic engineering plasmids serve as carriers for genes, called vectors.
The Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens is used to transfer genes into plants.

abschnitte.text: Like the genetic material, a **plasmid** is made of double-stranded DNA, but it is much smaller than the bacterial chromosome. Most plasmids are closed rings. They often contain genes that the bacterium does not necessarily need but that give it advantages. Plasmids are found mainly in bacteria, sometimes also in yeasts and other single-celled organisms.

A plasmid has its own starting point for copying, the **origin of replication**. This allows it to multiply independently of the chromosome. Some plasmids exist in only one or two copies per cell, others in hundreds. When the cell divides, the plasmids are shared out among the daughter cells.

Bacteria can pass plasmids directly to each other; this is called **conjugation**. A thin connection forms between two cells, through which a copy of the plasmid travels. This even works between different kinds of bacteria. Because many plasmids carry **resistance genes**, antibiotic resistance spreads very quickly in this way, which is a big problem in hospitals.

Researchers turn plasmids into **vectors**, that is, carriers for foreign genes. A multiple cloning site is a section with many cutting sites for restriction enzymes, where a gene can be inserted. With calcium chloride and a short heat shock, bacteria are made to take up such plasmids. In this way, since the 1980s, bacteria have been producing human insulin for people with diabetes, for example.

Only a small proportion of the bacteria actually take up the plasmid. That is why many cloning plasmids carry an **antibiotic resistance gene**: on a culture medium containing an antibiotic, only bacteria with the plasmid grow. In blue-white screening, white colonies show that a foreign gene has been inserted into the lacZ gene. Blue colonies, on the other hand, contain a plasmid without a new gene.

The bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens causes growths in plants called crown galls. To do this it smuggles part of its **Ti plasmid** into the plant cells. Researchers have copied this natural trick and replaced the disease-causing genes with useful ones. In this way genes can be brought into plants in a targeted way, for example for research purposes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small DNA ring in bacteria, separate from the chromosome.
The direct passing of a plasmid from bacterium to bacterium.
A carrier used to bring a gene into a cell.
The place where the copying of DNA begins.
A bacterium's ability to withstand an antibiotic.

gewusst: A bacterium can have several different plasmids at the same time.
Some plasmids carry resistance to several antibiotics at once.
Without plasmids, the modern production of many medicines would hardly be possible.

teile.einleitung: A reflex arc is the path that a nerve signal takes in a reflex: from the sense organ via the spinal cord to the muscle. Reflexes happen at lightning speed and without thinking. They protect us, for example, from burning ourselves on a hot hob.
wichtigste: A reflex is a fast, automatic reaction of the body to a stimulus.
The reflex arc runs from the receptor via a nerve to the spinal cord and via a nerve to the muscle.
Reflexes are fast because they are often switched over in the spinal cord.
Motor nerves carry signals from the spinal cord to the muscles.
The knee-jerk reflex has only a single switching point.
Closing the eyelids when a puff of air hits the eye is an extrinsic reflex.
Newborn babies grip a finger in their hand tightly; this is the grasp reflex.

abschnitte.text: A **reflex** is a fast, involuntary reaction to a stimulus. You do not have to think about it; the body reacts by itself. If you touch a hot hob, you pull your hand away before you even feel the pain. In this way reflexes protect the body from injuries.

A **reflex arc** begins at a **receptor**, a sensor, for example in the skin. From there the signal travels via a sensory nerve into the **spinal cord**. In the spinal cord it is switched over and sent via a motor nerve to the muscle. The muscle contracts, and the movement happens.

Reflexes happen so quickly because the signal is often switched over in the spinal cord. So it does not have to go to the brain and back first. The brain only finds out shortly afterwards what has happened. That is why you sometimes only feel the pain when your hand has already been pulled away.

For the **knee-jerk reflex** the doctor taps under the kneecap with a small hammer, and the leg kicks forward. This reflex has only a single switching point and is an intrinsic reflex, because the stimulus and the reaction happen in the same muscle. In an **extrinsic reflex** the stimulus and the reaction are in different places. One example is closing the eyelids when a puff of air hits the eye.

Even newborn babies have many reflexes. If you put a finger in their hand, they grip it tightly; this is the **grasp reflex**. The sucking reflex also helps babies to drink straight after birth. Many of these early childhood reflexes disappear again in the first months of life.

In the 17th century the French philosopher René Descartes already imagined that the body reacts to stimuli automatically. The British researcher Charles Sherrington studied reflexes closely and received a Nobel Prize for it in 1932. Today doctors test reflexes to see whether the nerves and spinal cord are healthy. Missing or overly strong reflexes can be a sign of illness.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something a sense organ notices, for example heat, pressure or light.
A sensor that picks up a stimulus and turns it into a nerve signal.
A bundle of nerves inside the spine.
A nerve that carries commands to the muscles.

gewusst: Sneezing, coughing and yawning are also counted as reflexes.
You can hardly stop the knee-jerk reflex, even if you try.
Nerve signals can race through the body at over 100 metres per second.

teile.einleitung: The polar night is the time in winter when the Sun does not rise all day in the polar regions. The closer you get to a pole, the longer it lasts. At the North Pole the Sun stays below the horizon for about half a year.
wichtigste: During the polar night the Sun does not rise all day.
In the north there is polar night beyond the Arctic Circle.
In the Arctic the polar night happens in winter.
Right at the North Pole it lasts about half a year.
The reason is the tilted axis of the Earth.
Its counterpart in summer is the midnight sun.
It is often not pitch dark during the polar night, because there is twilight.

abschnitte.text: The **Earth's axis** is tilted by about 23.4 degrees. As the Earth travels round the Sun, during the northern winter the North Pole is tilted away from the Sun. Then the Sun's rays no longer reach the areas around the pole at all. Half a year later it is the other way round: the North Pole is tilted towards the Sun, and there the Sun no longer sets. This is called the **midnight sun**.

The polar night only exists beyond the **polar circles**, which lie at about 66.5 degrees north and south latitude. Right on the polar circle it lasts only about one day. The further north you go, the longer it gets. At the **North Pole** the Sun stays below the horizon from about the end of September to the middle of March. In Antarctica, on the other hand, the polar night happens during our summer, because it is winter there then.

During the polar night it is often not completely dark. Around midday the Sun is only just below the horizon, and the sky glows in a bluish **twilight**. Snow reflects the little light there is and makes the landscape brighter. Only near the poles does it get really dark for weeks. In return you can often see the **aurora**, which dances across the sky in green and violet bands.

In the Norwegian city of **Tromsø** the polar night lasts from about the end of November to the middle of January. The people there light lots of candles and lamps and still like being outdoors. Because the body makes less **vitamin D** without sunlight, many pay attention to their diet or take supplements. Some people feel tired or sad during the dark time. When the Sun returns, many places in the north hold a sun festival.

Switzerland lies far south of the Arctic Circle, so there is no polar night here. But on the shortest day in December the Sun shines in Zurich for only about eight and a half hours. In some mountain villages in narrow valleys, the mountains hide the low winter sun. There the Sun does not shine directly on the houses at all for a few weeks. But that is not a real polar night; it is a **mountain shadow**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line around the Earth beyond which there is polar night and midnight sun.
An imaginary line through the North and South Poles around which the Earth turns.
When the Sun does not set even at night in summer.
The faint light when the Sun is just below the horizon.

gewusst: In Antarctica it is darkest during the polar night in June, while in Switzerland the days are then almost at their longest.
Because light is bent in the air, the Sun can still be seen briefly on the horizon at the Arctic Circle even on the shortest day.
On Svalbard, which lies much closer to the North Pole than Tromsø, the polar night lasts several months.

teile.einleitung: In physics, reflection means that waves such as light or sound are thrown back by a surface. We can see ourselves in a mirror because light is thrown back from the mirror into our eyes. Without reflection we could not see most of the things around us at all.
wichtigste: Reflection is the throwing back of waves by a surface.
We see ourselves in a mirror because light is thrown back by the mirror.
According to the law of reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Smooth surfaces reflect in one direction; rough surfaces scatter light in all directions.
Sound is also reflected; we hear this as an echo.
Reflectors on bikes and clothes make us visible in traffic.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “reflectere”, which means “to bend back”. When light hits a surface, part of it is **thrown back**. How much is reflected depends on the material. White and shiny surfaces reflect a lot of light, black surfaces swallow most of it.

If a ray of light hits a mirror at an angle, it bounces off again at the same angle, like a ball off a wall. This is called the **law of reflection**: the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are equal. That is why you do not always see yourself in a mirror, but, depending on where you stand, other things in the room too. Curved mirrors change the direction of the rays and make things look bigger or smaller.

With a smooth mirror the order of the light rays is kept, which is why a clear **mirror image** forms. A sheet of paper, on the other hand, is rough under a microscope and throws the light back in many directions. This is called **diffuse reflection**, and it is exactly why we can see paper, trees or faces from everywhere. A mirror usually consists of glass with a very thin layer of silver or aluminium on the back.

Cars have rear-view mirrors and wing mirrors so that drivers can see behind them. **Reflectors** on bikes, school bags and high-visibility vests throw the light from headlights straight back to the light source. In this way children on the way to school are much more visible at dusk. A periscope in a submarine also works with mirrors or prisms.

**Sound** is reflected too: if you shout at a rock face in the mountains, an echo comes back. Bats and dolphins find their way with ultrasound, whose echo shows them where obstacles or prey are. Radar devices use the reflection of radio waves to detect aeroplanes or cars that are going too fast. In fibre-optic cables, light is carried over long distances by constant reflection inside.

The Moon does not shine by itself; we only see it because it reflects the light of the Sun. Fresh snow reflects a lot of sunlight, which is why you need sunglasses in the mountains. In 1969 the astronauts of Apollo 11 set up a **retroreflector** on the Moon. With laser beams that are thrown back by it, researchers still measure the distance to the Moon to within a few centimetres today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The throwing back of light, sound or other waves by a surface.
The angle at which a ray of light hits a surface.
The throwing back of light in many different directions by a rough surface.
A sound that is thrown back by a wall and comes back to us.

gewusst: In a mirror left and right seem to be swapped, but in reality front and back are swapped.
On some ambulances the writing is mirror-reversed so that it can be read correctly in a rear-view mirror.
Fresh snow throws back up to about 90 per cent of sunlight.

teile.einleitung: Population genetics is a branch of biology that studies how common certain genes are in a population and how these frequencies change. It links Gregor Mendel's theory of heredity with Charles Darwin's theory of evolution. With the help of maths it can explain how evolution works on a small scale.
wichtigste: The gene pool is the whole set of alleles in a population.
Population genetics calculates with allele frequencies, that is, with the proportions of gene variants.
Mutation is the real source of new alleles.
Selection, genetic drift, mutation and gene flow change the gene pool.
Biological fitness measures how much a genotype contributes to the next generation.
Ronald Fisher, J. B. S. Haldane and Sewall Wright are regarded as the founders of the subject.
If an allele reaches 100 per cent, this is called fixation.

abschnitte.text: Every gene can come in different variants; these are called **alleles**. For the blood group, for example, there are the alleles A, B and 0. All the alleles of all the individuals in a population together form the **gene pool**. Population genetics asks how common each allele is in the gene pool and why this changes over the generations.

The **allele frequency** tells you what proportion of all alleles belongs to a particular variant. An example: in a population there are 36 animals with AA, 48 with Aa and 16 with aa. Together they have 200 alleles, of which 72 plus 48, that is 120, are an A. So the frequency of A is 120 divided by 200, which comes to 0.6.

In 1908 the mathematician Godfrey Hardy and the doctor Wilhelm Weinberg independently showed an important rule. Without selection, mutation, immigration and chance, the allele frequencies in a large population stay the same from generation to generation. This **Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium** is like a zero point. If a real population differs from it, an evolutionary factor is at work.

**Mutation** creates new alleles when the genetic material changes by chance. **Selection** favours alleles that improve survival, for example in stabilising or directional selection. **Genetic drift** changes frequencies purely by chance, especially strongly in small populations. Through gene flow, alleles get into another population with animals that move there.

In 19th-century England tree trunks in industrial areas became dark from soot. Dark **peppered moths** were better camouflaged there and became more common, an example of directional selection. In some malaria regions of Africa the **sickle cell allele** is common, because carriers with one copy are better protected against malaria. Cheetahs have very little genetic diversity because their population once shrank greatly in the past.

In the 1920s and 1930s **Ronald Fisher**, J. B. S. Haldane and Sewall Wright developed the mathematical foundations of the subject. With them they showed that Mendel's rules of heredity and Darwin's natural selection fit together. This gave rise to the so-called **modern synthesis** of evolutionary theory. Today population genetics helps in species conservation, animal breeding and medicine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A variant of a gene.
All the alleles of all the individuals in a population together.
A change in allele frequencies by chance.
How much a living thing contributes to the next generation.
When an allele makes up 100 per cent in the population.

gewusst: Biological fitness has nothing to do with sport; it is about survival and offspring.
Wilhelm Weinberg, one of the discoverers of the equilibrium, was a doctor in Stuttgart.
When a few animals settle on an island, a rare allele can suddenly become common there; this is called the founder effect.

teile.einleitung: A pipette is a device that you can use to take up small amounts of liquid and release them exactly. It is one of the most important tools in laboratories, doctors' surgeries and schools. Pipettes range from the simple dropper to modern precision instruments.
wichtigste: With a pipette you take up a little liquid and release it again.
With a dropper you squeeze the rubber bulb to suck up liquid.
The lines on a graduated pipette show how much liquid is inside.
Small amounts in a pipette are often measured in millilitres.
In the laboratory you must never suck on a pipette with your mouth, because you could swallow dangerous substances.
Disposable pipettes are usually made of plastic.
When releasing drops you hold the pipette upright.

abschnitte.text: A **pipette** is a thin tube that you can use to suck up liquids, hold them and release them again. The word comes from French and means roughly “little pipe”. Pipettes are made of **glass** or **plastic**. Glass pipettes can be cleaned and reused. Plastic pipettes are often thrown away after being used once, so that no leftovers from earlier experiments interfere.

On a simple **dropper** there is a rubber bulb at the top. If you squeeze it and dip the tip into liquid, a partial vacuum forms when you let go. This sucks the liquid into the tube. If you gently squeeze the bulb again, it drips out. So that the drops are the same size, you hold the pipette **upright**.

A **graduated pipette** has a scale with lines on which you can read how much liquid is inside. A volumetric pipette measures exactly one particular amount, for example 10 millilitres. Modern **piston pipettes** work with a push button and a piston and use disposable tips. With them you can measure very small amounts in microlitres, which are thousandths of a millilitre. Such devices were invented in Germany in the 1950s.

In the past, liquids were often sucked into pipettes with the mouth. Today this is strictly **forbidden** in the laboratory, because you could swallow toxic, corrosive or germ-laden substances. Instead you use **pipette fillers** such as rubber bulbs or electric pumps. Safety goggles and gloves are also part of working safely. Used disposable tips go into a special waste container.

You also come across pipettes at home and at school. In an experiment you can use a pipette to put a single drop of **food colouring** into water and watch how it spreads. Many nose drops, eye drops and medicines for children are measured with small pipettes. In hospitals and in research, blood samples and solutions are measured exactly with pipettes. Pipettes are sometimes used in the kitchen too, for example for flavourings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tube for sucking up and releasing small amounts of liquid exactly.
A thousandth of a litre, about as much as 20 drops.
A thousandth of a millilitre, a tiny droplet.
When the air pressure in a space is lower than outside, so that something is sucked in.
A device for sucking liquid into a pipette without using your mouth.

gewusst: One millilitre of water is roughly 20 drops from a dropper.
With modern laboratory pipettes you can measure amounts smaller than a pinhead.
In research laboratories there are robots that work with many pipettes at the same time.

teile.einleitung: Penicillin was the first antibiotic, that is, a medicine against bacteria. The Scottish researcher Alexander Fleming discovered it in 1928 through a lucky accident in his laboratory. Since then penicillin has saved millions of lives.
wichtigste: Penicillin is an antibiotic that kills bacteria or stops them growing.
Alexander Fleming discovered it in 1928 in London.
Penicillin is produced by a mould called Penicillium.
Only around 1940 did researchers in Oxford manage to produce it as a medicine.
In 1945 Fleming, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain received the Nobel Prize for it.
Penicillin does not work against viruses, for example with a cold.
If antibiotics are used too often, bacteria can become resistant.

abschnitte.text: Alexander Fleming worked at St Mary's Hospital in London and studied bacteria. In the summer of 1928 he went on holiday and left dishes of bacteria on the laboratory bench. When he came back, a **mould** had grown on one dish. Around the mould the bacteria had disappeared. Fleming realised that the fungus gives off a substance that kills bacteria, and he called it penicillin.

Fleming did not manage to produce enough pure penicillin. Only from 1939 did **Howard Florey** and **Ernst Chain** succeed at the University of Oxford. In 1941 a patient was treated with it for the first time. During the Second World War, companies in the USA began producing penicillin in huge tanks. In this way many wounded soldiers could be saved.

Many bacteria are surrounded by a firm cell wall that protects them like armour. Penicillin disrupts the building of this wall when the bacteria multiply. Without an intact wall the bacteria burst. Human cells have no such cell wall, so penicillin does not harm them. It helps, for example, against sore throats caused by streptococci or against pneumonia.

If antibiotics are taken too often or incorrectly, a few tough bacteria sometimes survive. They multiply, and the medicine no longer works. This is called **antibiotic resistance**, which is a big problem worldwide today. In addition, some people are allergic to penicillin and need other medicines.

In Switzerland, antibiotics are only available with a **prescription** from a doctor. You should take them for exactly as long as prescribed. They do not help with a cold or flu, because these are mostly caused by viruses. Leftover medicines should be returned to the pharmacy and not thrown in the rubbish or down the toilet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A medicine that works against bacteria.
Tiny living things made of a single cell, some of which cause diseases.
A fungus that grows as a furry layer on food or other materials.
When bacteria are no longer affected by a medicine.

gewusst: As early as 1945, in his Nobel Prize speech, Fleming warned that bacteria could become resistant to penicillin.
A particularly productive penicillin mould was found in 1943 on a mouldy melon at a market in the USA.
Before antibiotics were invented, even a small wound could be fatal.

teile.einleitung: The pile dwellings on Lake Zurich are the remains of villages in which people lived on the lake shore thousands of years ago. The finds in the damp ground are so well preserved that wood, cloth and even food remains are found. Today some of these sites are part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: The pile-dwelling settlements on Lake Zurich date from the Neolithic and the Bronze Age.
In the winter of 1853/54 the lake's water level was unusually low, and posts came to light near Obermeilen.
In 1854 the Zurich antiquarian Ferdinand Keller interpreted the finds as remains of pile dwellings.
According to what we know today, many houses stood on the lake shore on ground that was sometimes flooded.
In 2010 archaeologists found a wooden door over 5,000 years old during the building of the Opéra car park in Zurich.
Six countries share the UNESCO World Heritage Site “Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps”.
The pile dwellers made threads and cloth from flax.

abschnitte.text: In the very dry winter of 1853/54 the water level of Lake Zurich fell unusually low. Near **Obermeilen**, wooden posts, shards and tools came to light in the mud of the shore. The Zurich antiquarian **Ferdinand Keller** examined the finds. In 1854 he declared that they were the remains of villages on posts. His reports set off an enthusiasm all over Europe that was called “pile-dwelling fever”.

abschnitte.titel: What did the villages look like?
abschnitte.text: Keller imagined houses on large platforms above the water. Today researchers know that many houses stood directly on the **lake shore**, on ground that was sometimes flooded. The houses stood on posts so that they stayed dry when the water was high. They were built of wood, with walls of wattle and clay and roofs of reeds or bark. A village often consisted of ten to thirty houses.

abschnitte.titel: When did the pile dwellers live?
abschnitte.text: The settlements on Lake Zurich date from the **Neolithic** and the **Bronze Age**. The oldest are about 6,000 years old, the youngest about 3,000 years. Because the wood survived in the wet ground, its age can be determined very precisely from the tree rings. This method is called **dendrochronology**. Sometimes it even tells us in which year a tree was felled for a house.

In 2010, during the building of the **Opéra car park** in Zurich, archaeologists discovered a wooden door that is over 5,000 years old. It is one of the oldest doors in Europe. Stone axes, clay pots, jewellery, nets, baskets and even charred bread were also found. The pile dwellers grew cereals, kept domestic animals, fished and gathered berries. They spun threads from **flax** and wove cloth from them.

Since 2011 the **“Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps”** have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It includes over a hundred sites in six countries, namely Switzerland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy and Slovenia. About half of them are in Switzerland, several on Lake Zurich. Most sites lie under water or in the ground and cannot be seen. The waves from boats wear away the lake bed, so some places are protected with a covering of **fleece and gravel**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A house that stands on wooden posts driven into the ground.
The period when people settled down, farmed and used tools made of stone.
The period when people made tools and jewellery from bronze.
A method of finding the age of wood from its tree rings.
The science that digs up and studies old traces of people.

gewusst: The pile-dwelling door from Zurich's Opéra car park is older than the Egyptian pyramids of Giza.
Because no oxygen reached the finds in the lake bed, even apples and bits of bread survived.
The pile-dwelling fever of the 19th century helped to create a feeling of shared Swiss history.

teile.einleitung: Personalised medicine means that a treatment is matched to the particular features of an individual person. These include above all their genes, but also age, lifestyle and the exact characteristics of their illness. In this way every patient should get the medicine that works best for them.
wichtigste: The basic idea is to match treatments to a patient's individual features, such as their genes.
By 2003 the Human Genome Project had largely decoded the human genome.
Pharmacogenetics studies how genes affect the action and breakdown of medicines.
A companion diagnostic is a test that shows before a therapy whether a medicine can work.
Imatinib (Glivec) works against the altered protein BCR-ABL in one form of leukaemia.
In CAR-T cell therapy a patient's own immune cells are changed so that they recognise cancer cells.
Since 2017 the Swiss Personalized Health Network (SPHN) has been promoting the use of health data in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In the past, everyone with the same illness usually got the same medicine. But not every medicine works equally well for everyone. **Personalised medicine** tries to look more closely. It examines a person's **genes** and the characteristics of their illness. From this, doctors choose the treatment that is most likely to succeed.

An important basis was the **Human Genome Project**. In this international research project the human genome was largely decoded between 1990 and 2003. At that time reading a genome took many years and cost billions. Today, with modern machines, it is possible in a few days and for a fraction of the price. As a result, doctors can more and more often examine the genome of patients or tumours.

**Pharmacogenetics** researches how genes affect the action of medicines. Because of their genes, some people break a medicine down very quickly, so it hardly works for them. Others break it down slowly and are more likely to get side effects. A genetic test can help to find the right dose. Before some therapies a **companion diagnostic** is done, an accompanying test that shows whether the medicine can work at all.

Personalised medicine is especially advanced in cancer. The medicine **imatinib**, known as Glivec, blocks the altered protein BCR-ABL, which causes a particular form of leukaemia. It came onto the market in 2001 and comes from the Basel company Novartis. The antibody trastuzumab, known as Herceptin, only works in breast cancer with an overexpression of HER2. That is why the tumour is tested first.

In **CAR-T cell therapy**, some of the patient's own immune cells, the T cells, are taken out. In the laboratory they are genetically modified so that they recognise cancer cells. Then the patient gets their modified cells back, and they attack the cancer. This therapy is used mainly for certain kinds of blood cancer. It is very complex and expensive, but it can help people for whom other treatments have failed.

With companies such as Roche and Novartis, Switzerland is an important location for this research. Since 2017 the **Swiss Personalized Health Network** (SPHN) has been helping health data from hospitals and research to be used better. **Data protection** is especially important here, because genetic data is very personal. Patients must give their consent before their data is used for research.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of the genome that contains a building instruction for the body.
Research into how genes affect the action of medicines.
An accompanying test that shows before a therapy whether a medicine can work.
A cancer of the blood, also called blood cancer.
Immune cells that recognise and fight diseased cells in the body.

gewusst: The human genome consists of about three billion building blocks.
Decoding the first human genome took over ten years; today it takes a few days.
Two people with the same illness can react quite differently to the same medicine because of their genes.

teile.einleitung: A zip is a fastener with which you can quickly open and close jackets, trousers, bags or tents. Two rows of small teeth interlock like fingers. Its modern form was invented around 1913.
wichtigste: With a zip you can fasten clothes quickly.
The small parts that interlock are called teeth.
The part that you pull up and down is called the slider.
Around 1913 Gideon Sundback invented the zip in its modern form.
The teeth can be made of metal or plastic.
Before that, clothes often had buttons.
If a zip sticks, it helps to rub a pencil over the teeth.

abschnitte.text: A zip has two tapes with many small **teeth** on them. Each tooth has a small bump on top and a hollow underneath. The **slider** presses the teeth of the two sides together at an angle so that they lock into each other. If you pull it the other way, a small wedge in the slider separates the teeth again.

As early as 1893 the American **Whitcomb Judson** applied for a patent for a fastener with hooks for shoes. But it often stuck and easily came open by itself. The Swedish-born engineer **Gideon Sundback** improved the idea decisively around 1913. In principle we still use his design with interlocking teeth today.

At first zips were used mainly on boots and tobacco pouches. The English name “zipper” dates from the 1920s and imitates the sound of zipping up. Only in the 1930s did zips appear in large numbers on clothes and trousers. Today billions of zips are made every year.

The teeth can be made of **metal** or plastic. On a jacket the zip comes completely apart at the bottom; it is called **open-ended**. On trousers and bags it stays joined at the bottom. There are also waterproof zips for diving suits and tents, and invisible ones whose teeth you cannot see from the outside.

If a zip sticks, you can rub a **pencil** over the teeth. The graphite acts like a lubricant, and the slider glides better again. A little soap or candle wax can also help. If the zip keeps coming open, the slider is often worn out and can be carefully squeezed together a little with pliers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The moving part with which you open and close the zip.
The small parts that interlock when you close it.
A right that protects an invention for a certain time.
Soft carbon in a pencil lead that slides easily.

gewusst: The English name “zipper” imitates the sound of zipping up.
Many zips have the letters YKK on them; this is the name of a large Japanese manufacturer.
Astronauts also wear spacesuits that are closed with special airtight zips.

teile.einleitung: Source criticism means checking a source carefully: where does it come from, who made it and can you believe it? This method comes from the study of history. Today it is more important than ever, because on the internet anyone can publish anything.
wichtigste: Source criticism means checking the origin and credibility of a source.
A diary from 1940 is a primary source because it comes from that time itself.
On websites the legal notice (imprint) states who is responsible for the content.
With Wikipedia it is best to check statements using the references given.
The labels “Advertisement” or “Sponsored” mean that a post is paid advertising.
A possible conflict of interest can influence a study.
The date of a source is important, because older information may be out of date.
The number of likes says nothing about whether a post is true.

abschnitte.text: A **source** is anything from which you gain knowledge: a book, a letter, a photo, a video or a website. In source criticism you ask questions of this source. Who created it, when, where and with what purpose? Only when you have answered these questions can you judge how reliable the information is.

Historians distinguish between **primary sources** and **secondary sources**. Primary sources come directly from the time being studied, for example a diary from 1940 or an old charter. Secondary sources were written about it later, for example a school book or an encyclopaedia article. Systematic source criticism developed in the 19th century, when history became a science.

Who is the author, and does the person know about the subject? When was the source published, and is it still up to date? Does the source want to inform, entertain or sell something? Is there **evidence**, and do other independent sources report the same thing?

On websites the **legal notice** (imprint) shows who is responsible for the content. If there is no legal notice, be careful. Posts labelled “Advertisement” or “Sponsored” are paid **advertising**. Today photos and videos can also be faked with artificial intelligence, so it is worth taking a second look.

If a drinks manufacturer pays for a study on sugary drinks, there is a possible **conflict of interest**. This does not automatically mean that the study is wrong. But you should look more closely and search for independent studies. That is why good scientific articles state who paid for the research.

begriffe.erklaerung: Anything from which you gain information about something.
A source that comes directly from the time or from the event itself.
A text written later about an event or about other sources.
Information on a website about who is responsible for its content.
When someone would themselves benefit from a particular result.

gewusst: The number of likes or views says nothing about the truth of a post; false reports often spread even faster.
In the Middle Ages some charters were forged to prove ownership or rights, and historians are still uncovering such forgeries today.
Professionals often check a photo with a reverse image search to find out where it first appeared.

teile.einleitung: A placebo is a dummy medicine that contains no active substance. Even so, many people feel better after taking it. This amazing phenomenon shows how strongly our mind can affect our body.
wichtigste: A placebo looks like a medicine but contains no active substance.
Placebo tablets are often made of sugar or starch.
The Latin word “placebo” means “I shall please”.
The placebo effect is an improvement caused only by expecting an effect.
Negative expectations can cause complaints; this is called the nocebo effect.
In clinical trials placebos are used for comparison with the real medicine.
The placebo effect is noticed especially often with pain.

abschnitte.text: A **placebo** is a tablet, capsule or injection without a medical active substance. It is usually made of sugar, starch or a salt solution. From the outside it looks exactly the same as the real medicine. The name comes from Latin and means “I shall please”. In the past doctors sometimes gave such remedies to calm sick people.

In the **placebo effect**, the expectation that a treatment will work helps. The brain can then, for example, release the body's own substances that dull pain. Trust in the doctor, a friendly conversation or expensive packaging can also strengthen the effect. Even the colour and size of the tablet play a role in experiments. But a placebo does not cure an illness such as a broken bone or an infection.

If someone expects something bad, a remedy with no effect can cause complaints. This is called the **nocebo effect**, from the Latin “I shall harm”. Someone who reads about many side effects in the package leaflet sometimes feels exactly those, even though they have only been given a dummy remedy. Typical are headaches, nausea or tiredness. That is why experts pay attention to how they talk about risks.

In **clinical trials** one group gets the real medicine and another group a placebo. Only if the first group is clearly better off does the medicine really work. In a **double-blind trial** neither the participants nor the doctors know who is getting what. In this way expectations cannot distort the result. Today this method is the standard for testing new medicines.

Using a placebo can be ethically problematic. This is especially true if sick people are denied an effective treatment as a result. For serious illnesses a new medicine is therefore often compared with the best existing treatment instead of a placebo. **Informed consent** is also important: trial participants must know that they might be given a dummy remedy. They must not be deceived without their consent.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dummy medicine without an active substance.
Complaints that arise only from negative expectations.
An experiment in which neither patients nor doctors know who is getting the real medicine.
The substance in a medicine that has the actual effect.

gewusst: In some experiments a placebo worked even when the participants knew that it was a dummy remedy.
Even sham operations, in which only a small cut in the skin is made, can have a placebo effect for some complaints.
In studies two placebo tablets often work better than a single one.

teile.einleitung: A reflex is a lightning-fast reaction of the body that happens without any thinking at all. If you touch a hot hob, your hand jerks back even before you really feel the pain. Reflexes protect us from dangers and help the body to work well.
wichtigste: A reflex is a lightning-fast movement without thinking.
If the doctor taps just below the kneecap, the leg kicks forward.
If your hand touches something hot, it jerks back immediately.
If something flies towards your eyes, they close.
Sneezing clears the nose, coughing clears the airways.
A baby grips tightly if you put a finger in its hand.
In bright light the pupils get smaller.

abschnitte.text: A **reflex** is an automatic response of the body to a stimulus. You do not have to think about it, and you can hardly stop it. Reflexes always happen in the same way and are very fast. Many of them are innate and protect the body from injuries.

The path of a reflex is called the **reflex arc**. A sensor, for example in the skin, notices the stimulus. A nerve carries the message to the **spinal cord**, and from there the command goes straight back to a muscle. Because the message saves the detour via the brain, a reflex is so fast.

For the **knee-jerk reflex** the doctor taps just below the kneecap with a small hammer. This briefly stretches the thigh muscle. The muscle contracts immediately, and the leg kicks forward. In this way doctors check whether the nerves are working properly.

If something tickles in your nose, you have to **sneeze**. If something goes down the wrong way while you are eating, you cough. If something flies towards your eyes, the lids close; this is the blink reflex. And in bright light the **pupils** narrow so that not too much light gets into the eye.

abschnitte.titel: Reflexes in babies and learned reflexes
abschnitte.text: Newborn babies have special reflexes that disappear again later. If you put a finger in a baby's hand, it grips tightly; this is the **grasp reflex**. Around 1900 the Russian researcher Ivan Pavlov showed that new reflexes can also be learned. His dogs started to produce saliva just from hearing a bell that usually announced their food.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something a sense organ notices, for example heat or light.
The path from the sensor via the nerve and the spinal cord to the muscle.
A bundle of nerves inside the spine.
The black hole in the middle of the eye through which light enters.

gewusst: Nerve signals can race through the body at over 100 metres per second, faster than a car on the motorway.
When you sneeze, the air can shoot out of your nose at great speed.
For most people it is almost impossible to sneeze with their eyes open, because the lids close by reflex.

teile.einleitung: A radiosonde is a small measuring instrument that rises into the sky on a weather balloon. On the way it measures temperature, humidity and air pressure and radios the values back to Earth. In this way meteorologists find out what the atmosphere is like up to a height of over 30 kilometres.
wichtigste: A radiosonde hangs from a weather balloon and measures the weather high up as it rises.
Today its position, and so the wind at height, is determined with GPS.
Radiosondes are launched all over the world at the same times so that all the measurements are available at once.
On its way the sonde passes through the tropopause between the troposphere and the stratosphere.
At a height of about 10 kilometres it typically measures about -50 °C.
In Payerne a special sonde regularly measures ozone.
Inversion layers can be recognised from the temperature profile.

abschnitte.text: A **radiosonde** is a light box full of sensors that hangs from a **weather balloon**. The balloon is filled with hydrogen or helium and rises a few metres per second. The sonde measures temperature, humidity and air pressure and sends the values by radio to the ground station. Today its position is determined with **GPS**, so the wind direction and wind speed at height can also be calculated.

If a balloon rises at 5 metres per second, it takes about 50 minutes to reach 15 kilometres. Because the air gets thinner and thinner higher up, the balloon expands greatly. At a height of about 30 kilometres it usually bursts, and the sonde floats back to Earth on a small parachute. Most sondes are never found again.

On the way up the sonde passes through the **tropopause**, the boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere. In our latitudes it is usually at a height of about 10 to 12 kilometres. There the sonde typically measures about -50 °C. From the temperature profile **inversions** can also be recognised, that is, layers in which it gets warmer instead of colder as you go up.

Radiosondes are launched at hundreds of stations around the world at the same times, usually at midnight and midday universal time. In this way all the measurements are available at once and give a complete picture of the atmosphere. The data goes into the computer models for **weather forecasting**. Without radiosondes, forecasts would be much less accurate.

In Switzerland **MeteoSwiss** launches radiosondes in **Payerne** in the canton of Vaud. Balloons are launched there every day. In Payerne a special sonde also regularly measures the **ozone** in the atmosphere. This series of measurements has been running for decades and is very valuable for climate research.

More than a hundred years ago people were already sending up balloons with measuring instruments, but they had to find them again to read the values. Around 1930 the first sondes were built that sent their measurements to Earth by radio. In the past the balloon was tracked with radar or direction-finding aerials to determine the wind. Today the sondes are small, light and much more accurate.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measuring instrument on a balloon that sends weather data by radio.
The boundary layer between the lower weather layer and the stratosphere.
A layer of air in which the temperature rises instead of falling as you go up.
A gas that protects the Earth from harmful UV radiation high in the atmosphere.

gewusst: At great heights a weather balloon can swell to many times its size at launch.
If you find a radiosonde, you can often send it back; some have an address on them for this.
Radiosondes can be carried over a hundred kilometres by the wind.

teile.einleitung: Tweezers are a small tool with two arms that you can use to pick up tiny things. They are needed in laboratories, in medicine, by watchmakers and at home in the bathroom. They work like two extended, very fine fingers.
wichtigste: You use tweezers to pick up small things.
Tweezers have two arms.
If you let go of tweezers that you have squeezed together, the tips spring apart.
In the laboratory samples are handled with tweezers so that they stay clean.
Many laboratory tweezers are made of stainless steel.
At home they are often needed to pull out a splinter.
The German word “Pinzette” comes from French.

abschnitte.text: **Tweezers** consist of two narrow arms that are firmly joined at one end. If you squeeze the arms together, the tips touch and hold something tight. If you let go, the arms spring apart again by themselves. This works because the metal is **elastic**. The German word “Pinzette” comes from the French “pincette”, which means “little pincers”.

abschnitte.titel: In the laboratory and in medicine
abschnitte.text: In the laboratory small samples are handled with tweezers so that they stay **clean** and are not contaminated by fingers. Many laboratory tweezers are made of **stainless steel**, because it does not rust and is easy to clean and sterilise. In medicine there are special tweezers for operations. Some have small teeth at the tip to hold tissue better. Others have smooth, grooved tips.

At home tweezers are often needed to pull a **splinter** out of the skin. They are also used for plucking eyebrows. With fine tweezers or tick pliers you can remove a **tick** by gripping it close to the skin and pulling it out slowly. That is why every first aid kit should contain tweezers. It is important to clean them before use.

There are many shapes of tweezers, depending on the job. **Stamp collectors** use tweezers with flat, wide ends so that the delicate stamps do not bend or get dirty. Electronics technicians pick up tiny components on circuit boards with pointed tweezers. There are curved tweezers, very pointed ones and ones with crossed arms that close by themselves. Some are made of plastic so that they do not conduct electricity.

Tweezers are essential for **watchmaking**. Watchmakers use them to place tiny cogs, screws and springs in a watch movement. For this they need especially fine and precise tweezers, which are often non-magnetic. In the Swiss Jura, where many watches are made, companies have long produced such **precision tweezers**. They are also used in laboratories all over the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gripping tool with two springy arms for small things.
A material that springs back into its old shape after bending.
A steel that does not rust and is easy to clean.
Very great accuracy.

gewusst: At about one year old, babies learn the “pincer grip”, in which they hold small things between thumb and index finger.
For work on watch movements there are tweezers that do not become magnetic, so that the tiny steel parts do not stick to them.
The beak of some birds such as the snipe works rather like tweezers.

teile.einleitung: Protozoa are tiny single-celled organisms with a nucleus that often move and feed like little animals. That is why they used to be called “first animals”. They are found in ponds, in the sea, in the soil, and some also as germs in the bodies of people and animals.
wichtigste: Protozoa are single-celled organisms with a nucleus.
In German they used to be called “Urtierchen”, little first animals.
The paramecium moves with cilia.
Paramecia are easy to find in ponds and hay infusions.
Amoebas flow around their food and swallow it.
Euglena can carry out photosynthesis and move with a flagellum.
Single-celled organisms cause diseases such as malaria and African sleeping sickness.

abschnitte.text: The name **protozoa** comes from Greek and means roughly “first animals”. They are **single-celled organisms** made of a single cell with a real nucleus. This makes them different from bacteria, which have no nucleus. Most are so small that they can only be seen under a microscope. Today we know that they do not form a single related group, but the term is still used as a collective name.

The **paramecium** is about 0.1 to 0.3 millimetres long and shaped like the sole of a shoe. Its surface is covered with thousands of fine **cilia**, which beat like oars. In this way it swims quickly through the water and whirls bacteria into its cell mouth. It is easy to find in ponds or in a **hay infusion**, that is, hay that has stood in water for a few days. This is a popular experiment in biology lessons.

The **amoeba** has no fixed shape. It forms bulges, the pseudopods, with which it crawls. It flows around its food and swallows it in a small bubble. **Euglena** is special: like a plant it can carry out photosynthesis and still move along with a flagellum. A red eyespot helps it swim towards the light.

Some protozoa are dangerous **parasites**. The germs that cause **malaria** are carried by mosquitoes of the genus Anopheles and attack red blood cells. Especially in Africa, malaria is one of the most common causes of death in small children. **African sleeping sickness** is caused by trypanosomes, which are carried by tsetse flies. Such diseases do not occur naturally in Switzerland, but travellers can bring them back.

Some single-celled organisms build tiny shells of lime or silica. These include the **foraminifera**, whose shells collected over millions of years on the seabed into thick layers. From these, limestone formed, which is found in many mountain ranges today. The limestone used to build the pyramids of Giza also contains shells of the coin-shaped nummulites. In lakes and streams protozoa eat a lot of bacteria and so help to keep the water clean.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that consists of only one cell.
Fine hairs on a cell that move and are used for swimming.
Bulges of an amoeba used for crawling and feeding.
A living thing that lives at the expense of another and harms it.
Hay in water in which many single-celled organisms develop after a few days.

gewusst: In the 17th century Antoni van Leeuwenhoek was one of the first to observe single-celled organisms in a drop of water.
The paramecium has a pulsating bubble that pumps extra water out of the cell so that it does not burst.
Some amoebas can be seen with the naked eye as tiny dots.

teile.einleitung: Reproducibility means that an experiment gives the same result when it is repeated by other researchers. It is one of the most important rules of science. Only what can be repeated counts as established knowledge.
wichtigste: Reproducibility means that others get the same result when they repeat something.
Repetitions reveal chance results and mistakes.
Researchers must describe their method exactly so that others can repeat the experiment.
The “cold fusion” announced in 1989 was not accepted because other laboratories could not repeat it.
In 2015, in a large project, fewer than half of about 100 psychology studies could be clearly confirmed.
The problem of studies that are not confirmed is called the replication crisis.
Many researchers today publish their raw data so that others can check the calculations.

abschnitte.text: A result is **reproducible** if another research group repeats the experiment and comes to the same result. It uses the same method but its own equipment, its own samples and its own people. If, on the other hand, the same team repeats the experiment in the same laboratory, this is more often called **repeatability**. Together, both show how reliable a measurement is.

Every measurement can be influenced by **chance**, small mistakes or false expectations. So if a surprising result happens only once, the experiment should be repeated. Only when several independent groups find the same thing can you trust the result. In this way science keeps correcting itself.

So that others can repeat an experiment, researchers must describe their **method** exactly. This includes the substances, equipment, amounts and calculations used. Today many also make their **raw data** and computer programs publicly available. In this way others can redo the analysis and find mistakes.

In 1989 the chemists Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons announced that they had produced **nuclear fusion** at room temperature. That would have meant an almost inexhaustible source of energy. Laboratories all over the world immediately tried to repeat the experiment. Because hardly anyone succeeded, “cold fusion” was not accepted by science.

A positive example is the discovery of the **Higgs particle** in 2012 at CERN near Geneva. Two independent experiments, ATLAS and CMS, found the particle with separate detectors and teams. Only that made the discovery truly convincing. In psychology, on the other hand, a project in 2015 showed that many studies could not be confirmed, which led to the **replication crisis**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planned test to check a guess.
The original measurements that have not yet been analysed.
The exact procedure in an experiment.
The problem that many published studies cannot be confirmed.

gewusst: At CERN two large experiments look for the same particles so that they can check each other.
As early as the 17th century the Royal Society in London demanded that experiments be repeated in front of witnesses.
Today some scientific journals deliberately also print repeat studies that do not confirm an earlier result.

teile.einleitung: Pharmacokinetics studies what the body does with a medicine: how it is absorbed, distributed, changed and excreted again. It helps to decide how much of a medicine to take and how often. In this way it works well without causing harm.
wichtigste: Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does with an active substance.
Pharmacodynamics, on the other hand, describes what the active substance does to the body.
The abbreviation LADME stands for liberation, absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion.
The half-life tells you when only half of an active substance is left in the body.
If an active substance is injected directly into a vein, its bioavailability is 100 per cent.
In the first-pass effect the liver breaks down part of a swallowed substance on its first passage.
Many medicines are broken down in the liver by enzymes of the cytochrome P450 family.

abschnitte.text: The word is made up of the Greek pharmakon for medicine and kinesis for movement. **Pharmacokinetics** follows the path of a medicine through the body. **Pharmacodynamics**, on the other hand, studies how the active substance works in the body. In short: kinetics is what the body does with the substance, dynamics is what the substance does to the body.

First the active substance is released from the tablet; this is **liberation**. Then it is taken up into the blood, for example in the intestine; this is **absorption**. With the blood it spreads through the body; this is distribution. After that it is changed, mainly in the liver; this is metabolism, and finally it is excreted via the kidneys or intestine; this is excretion.

The **half-life** is the time after which only half of the substance is left in the blood. If someone takes 400 milligrams of a substance with a half-life of 6 hours, 200 milligrams are left after 6 hours, 100 after 12 hours and 50 after 18 hours. If you take a medicine regularly, a balance is reached after about 4 to 5 half-lives, the **steady state**. Then as much is taken in per unit of time as is broken down.

**Bioavailability** tells you what proportion of an active substance actually reaches the bloodstream. With an injection into a vein it is 100 per cent. With a tablet it is often less; for example, with 40 per cent bioavailability only 80 of 200 milligrams reach the blood. One reason is the **first-pass effect**: the blood from the intestine flows through the liver first, which already breaks down part of it.

In the liver, enzymes of the **cytochrome P450** family break down very many medicines. Grapefruit juice blocks the enzyme CYP3A4 in the intestine, which is why the amount of some substances in the blood can rise dangerously. Children and older people also often break down medicines differently from middle-aged adults. That is why you should always take medicines as instructed by your doctor or the **package leaflet**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The substance in a medicine that has the actual effect.
The time until only half of a substance is left in the body.
The proportion of an active substance that really reaches the blood.
A protein in the body that speeds up chemical changes.
The information sheet in the box of a medicine.

gewusst: Even one glass of grapefruit juice can greatly change the effect of some medicines.
Some medicines are stuck onto the skin as patches so that they avoid the liver on the first passage.
The idea that the dose decides between healing and poisoning goes back to the Swiss doctor Paracelsus.

teile.einleitung: A pseudoscience is a teaching that seems scientific but is not. It often uses technical terms, numbers and experts but does not stand up to the strict rules of science. If you know the typical features, you can judge claims better.
wichtigste: A pseudoscience seems scientific but is not.
A typical feature is that its claims cannot be checked.
In cherry picking, only the data that fits is picked out.
Anecdotal evidence means taking individual personal stories as proof.
In the 19th century phrenology wanted to read a person's character from the shape of their skull.
Alchemy tried to turn base metals into gold.
There is no evidence for the belief that Mozart's music makes babies permanently more intelligent.

abschnitte.text: The Greek word “pseudo” means “false” or “sham”. So a **pseudoscience** only gives the appearance of a science. It uses technical terms, tables or titles so that its statements seem believable. But its claims are not carefully checked, or they do not stand up to checking. Real science, on the other hand, is constantly looking for mistakes in its own assumptions.

An important feature is that its claims cannot be checked. The philosopher **Karl Popper** said that it must in principle be possible to disprove a scientific statement. Pseudosciences often use **cherry picking**, picking out only the data that fits. They often rely on **anecdotal evidence**, that is, individual personal stories instead of careful studies. In addition, they hardly change their teaching, even when new findings speak against it.

**Alchemy** tried to turn base metals such as lead into gold. It never worked, but in the process the alchemists discovered many substances and pieces of laboratory equipment from which chemistry later developed. The doctor Paracelsus, who was born in Einsiedeln, also studied alchemy. In the 19th century **phrenology** was popular; it wanted to read character from the shape of the skull. Today we know that this does not work.

**Homeopathy** dilutes starting substances so much that from the dilution C12 onwards, chemically speaking, not a single molecule is left. Large review studies found no effect beyond the placebo effect. **Astrology** claims that the position of the stars at birth determines your character, which could not be confirmed in tests. Another well-known false belief is that Mozart's music makes babies permanently more intelligent. There is no evidence for this.

Always ask: where does the information come from, and who has checked it? Be careful with promises that sound too good to be true. Watch out for whether someone wants to make money with a claim. Serious results are published in scientific journals after **peer review** and repeated by other researchers. Asking critical questions is not rude; it is thinking scientifically.

begriffe.erklaerung: Greek for “false” or “sham”.
A statement can in principle be disproved by an experiment.
Choosing only the data that fits your own opinion.
Individual personal stories that are meant to serve as proof.

gewusst: Even the famous physicist Isaac Newton secretly studied alchemy for many years.
The so-called Mozart effect goes back to a 1993 study that only looked at a short effect in students, not in babies.
In the past you could have your head felt by phrenologists to find out your supposed talents.

teile.einleitung: Earthworms are worms that live in the soil and are enormously important for gardens, meadows and fields. They eat dead plant parts and turn them into fertile soil. Although they have neither eyes nor lungs, they are perfectly adapted to life underground.
wichtigste: Earthworms eat dead leaves and other plant remains.
They loosen the soil and make it fertile.
An earthworm breathes through its skin, which must therefore stay moist.
It has no eyes but senses light with its skin.
Its body consists of many rings, the segments.
The common earthworm can grow to about 30 centimetres long.
An earthworm cut in two does not become two worms.

abschnitte.text: The earthworm's body consists of many **rings**, which are called segments. On each ring there are tiny **bristles**, with which it holds on in its burrow and pushes itself forward. It moves by making parts of its body alternately long and thin and then short and thick. The common earthworm grows to about 30 centimetres long. Instead of a single heart it has five pairs of heart-like vessels that pump the blood.

An earthworm has no eyes, but its skin senses light. That is why it avoids the Sun, which would dry it out. It breathes through its **skin**, which it keeps moist with slime. If the skin dries out, it can no longer breathe. In heavy rain many earthworms come to the surface; exactly why is not yet fully understood.

Earthworms eat dead leaves, plant remains and soil. At **night** they pull leaves into their burrow so that they can eat them there once they have rotted a little. What they pass out are small crumbs of soil full of nutrients, **worm casts**. These are an excellent fertiliser for plants. In a compost heap, too, worms help to turn waste into soil.

With their tunnels earthworms loosen the soil and let air and water in. In this way plant roots can grow better, and rainwater drains away faster. They also mix the upper and lower layers of soil. In 1881 the naturalist Charles Darwin wrote a whole book about the work of earthworms. That is why farmers and gardeners are pleased to have lots of worms in the soil.

Many animals eat earthworms, for example **blackbirds**, hedgehogs, moles and badgers. The blackbird often pulls them skilfully out of the lawn. If an earthworm is cut in two, it does not become two worms. Sometimes the front part with the head can go on living and grow a short new back end. This regrowing is called **regeneration**.

Several dozen kinds of earthworm live in Switzerland, in meadows, woods, gardens and fields. There are especially many in damp meadows that have not been ploughed. Heavy machines that compact the soil, and some pesticides, harm the worms. If you leave leaves lying in the garden, you give them food. The German name “Regenwurm” probably comes from “reger Wurm”, meaning a lively, active worm.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the many rings that make up the earthworm's body.
Small, hard hairs with which the worm holds on.
Dark, fertile soil made of decomposed plant remains.
The regrowing of lost body parts.
A heap of plant waste that turns into soil.

gewusst: Over a hundred earthworms can live in one square metre of healthy meadow.
Earthworms have no bones; their body is supported by the pressure of the fluid inside.
The giant earthworm in Australia can grow over a metre long.

teile.einleitung: Protein folding is the process in which a long chain of amino acids folds up into a very particular three-dimensional shape. Only with this shape can a protein do its job in the body, just as a key only fits a lock with the right pattern. How proteins manage this so quickly and precisely was for a long time one of the great puzzles of biology.
wichtigste: Proteins are long chains of amino acids that fold into a fixed shape.
Christian Anfinsen showed that the amino acid sequence determines the three-dimensional structure.
The alpha helix and beta sheet are common secondary structures, described by Linus Pauling in 1951.
Chaperones help other proteins in the cell to fold correctly.
Water-repelling side chains gather inside the protein.
Misfolded proteins can cause diseases; prions consist only of such proteins.
The AI program AlphaFold predicts protein structures with high accuracy.

abschnitte.text: A **protein** is made in the cell as a long chain of building blocks, the **amino acids**. There are 20 different amino acids, and their order is set down in the genetic material. Shortly after it is made, the chain folds up into a precisely shaped tangle. This shape decides whether a protein carries oxygen, digests food or fights off germs.

The order of the amino acids is called the **primary structure**. From it, local patterns such as the screw-shaped alpha helix and the folded beta sheet form; this is the secondary structure. The whole three-dimensional shape of one chain is called the tertiary structure. If proteins consist of several chains, like the red blood pigment haemoglobin with four chains, this is called the **quaternary structure**.

Proteins fold in the watery surroundings of the cell. Parts of the chain that avoid water gather inside, just as oil droplets come together in water. In addition, **hydrogen bonds** and disulphide bridges between two cysteines keep the shape stable. Helper proteins, the **chaperones**, stop chains from tangling or sticking together wrongly.

In 1951 the chemist **Linus Pauling** described the alpha helix and the beta sheet. With experiments on the enzyme ribonuclease, Christian Anfinsen showed that an unfolded protein finds its way back into the right shape by itself. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1972. The researcher Cyrus Levinthal worked out that if a protein tried out all shapes at random, it would need longer than the age of the universe; this is **Levinthal's paradox**.

Determining the shape of a protein in the laboratory is a lot of work and can take years. The AI program **AlphaFold** from the company Google DeepMind predicts the shape from the amino acid sequence, often almost as accurately as an experiment. There are now predictions for hundreds of millions of proteins. In 2024 Demis Hassabis and John Jumper, together with David Baker, received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this.

Wrongly folded proteins can clump together and damage cells. Such deposits play a role in diseases such as Alzheimer's. **Prions** are misfolded proteins that force other proteins into the wrong shape too; they cause, for example, the cattle disease BSE. You can also see changes in proteins in everyday life: when you boil an egg, the proteins lose their shape, and the egg white becomes firm and white.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building block from which proteins are put together.
A helper protein that helps other proteins to fold.
A screw-shaped, coiled section of a protein chain.
A misfolded protein that can be infectious.
When a protein loses its shape, for example through heat.

gewusst: Many proteins fold into their correct shape in fractions of a second.
The word chaperone comes from French and used to mean a person who accompanied young ladies.
You cannot make a boiled egg raw again, because the proteins do not fold back.

teile.einleitung: René Descartes was a French philosopher, mathematician and natural scientist of the 17th century. He is famous for the sentence “I think, therefore I am”. He is regarded as one of the founders of modern philosophy, and every schoolchild uses his invention: the coordinate system.
wichtigste: The famous sentence “I think, therefore I am” comes from René Descartes.
The Cartesian coordinate system is named after him.
In 1637 his “Discourse on the Method” was published.
His search for certain knowledge began with doubting everything as a matter of principle.
He divided reality into two areas: mind and body.
He lived in the Netherlands for about twenty years.
He died in Stockholm in 1650.
Using x, y and z for unknowns in algebra goes back to him.

abschnitte.text: René Descartes was born in 1596 in La Haye in France; in his honour the town is now called **Descartes**. He attended a Jesuit school and studied law. After that he travelled through Europe as a soldier. For about twenty years he lived in the **Netherlands**, where he could work and publish in peace.

Descartes wanted to find knowledge that is absolutely certain. So he first **doubted** everything, even whether the world around him really existed. But there was one thing he could not doubt: that he himself was doubting and thinking at that moment. From this followed his famous sentence “I think, therefore I am”, in Latin “**Cogito, ergo sum**”.

In 1637 his “**Discourse on the Method**” was published, in which he explains his approach to thinking. It had three appendices, including one on geometry. In 1641 the “Meditations on First Philosophy” followed. Descartes divided reality into two areas: the thinking **mind** and the extended body.

Descartes linked geometry and algebra together. With the **Cartesian coordinate system** you can describe points with numbers and draw formulas as lines. The habit of using x, y and z for unknowns also goes back to him. In physics he studied light, refraction and how rainbows form.

In 1649 Queen **Christina of Sweden** invited Descartes to Stockholm to teach her philosophy. The lessons took place very early in the morning, in the cold Swedish winter. Descartes fell ill with pneumonia and died in **Stockholm** in February 1650. His remains were later moved to Paris.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study that thinks about basic questions, for example what knowledge or reality is.
A grid of two axes with which you give the position of points as numbers.
The teaching that reality consists of two basic areas; for Descartes, mind and body.
Deliberately doubting everything in order to find out what is completely certain.

gewusst: Descartes liked to stay in bed for a long time and is said to have done a lot of thinking there.
A legend says that he got the idea for the coordinate system while watching a fly on the ceiling of his room.
His birthplace in France was later renamed “Descartes”.

teile.einleitung: Auroras are coloured lights in the night sky that look like waving curtains. They arise when particles from the Sun hit the Earth's atmosphere. They are seen most often near the poles, but during strong solar storms they can sometimes even be seen in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Auroras are caused by electrically charged particles from the Sun.
They glow at a height of about 100 kilometres and higher.
The most common colour is green.
In the Northern Hemisphere it is called the northern lights, in Latin aurora borealis.
In the Southern Hemisphere people speak of the southern lights.
Auroras are often seen in countries such as Norway.
In May 2024 auroras could also be seen in Switzerland because of a strong solar storm.

abschnitte.text: An **aurora** is a glow high up in the atmosphere. It appears as bands, arcs, rays or waving curtains that often move quickly. It can only be seen in the dark night sky, because the light is much weaker than daylight. In the Northern Hemisphere it is called the **aurora borealis**, in the Southern Hemisphere the **aurora australis**.

The Sun constantly flings electrically charged particles into space, the **solar wind**. The Earth's magnetic field deflects these particles, but near the poles they can get into the atmosphere. There they collide with oxygen and nitrogen particles and make them glow. This works rather like a fluorescent tube.

Auroras most often glow **green**; this light comes from oxygen at a height of about 100 to 200 kilometres. Even higher up, oxygen can glow red. Nitrogen produces bluish and violet shades, especially at the lower edge. For comparison: aeroplanes fly only about 10 kilometres high.

Auroras occur mainly in a ring-shaped belt around the magnetic poles, the **auroral oval**. Good places are northern Norway, Iceland, Finland, Sweden, Canada and Alaska. The best time is the long, dark nights between autumn and spring. In the Southern Hemisphere the southern lights can be seen, for example, in Antarctica, Tasmania or New Zealand.

During a strong **solar storm** the auroral oval gets bigger and reaches far to the south. In May 2024 there was the strongest geomagnetic storm for over 20 years. At that time many people in Switzerland could see red and violet auroras in the sky. The Sun is especially active about every 11 years, and then such events are more frequent.

Other planets with a magnetic field and an atmosphere also have auroras, for example **Jupiter** and Saturn. These auroras have been photographed with the Hubble Space Telescope, among others. Strong solar storms can disrupt satellites, radio links and power grids on Earth. That is why experts constantly watch the Sun so that they can warn of such storms.

begriffe.erklaerung: A stream of charged particles that the Sun sends into space.
The Earth's invisible field of force, which also lines up compass needles.
An especially strong burst of particles and energy from the Sun.
The Latin word for dawn, the name of a Roman goddess.

gewusst: With a mobile phone camera auroras often look more colourful than with the naked eye.
Auroras in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres can appear at the same time and then often look similar.
The particles of the solar wind usually take one to three days to travel from the Sun to the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Photosynthesis is the process in which plants make their own food with the help of sunlight. From water and carbon dioxide they make sugar and give off oxygen. Without photosynthesis there would be hardly any life on Earth, and no people either.
wichtigste: In photosynthesis plants make their food using sunlight.
For this they take in carbon dioxide from the air.
Besides light and air they need water.
The plant makes sugar in the process.
Photosynthesis takes place mainly in the green leaves.
In the dark night, photosynthesis is not possible because there is no light.
On water plants in bright light you can see small gas bubbles of oxygen.

abschnitte.text: The word **photosynthesis** means “putting together with light”. Plants, algae and some bacteria can make their own food.
