For this they need **light**, **water** and **carbon dioxide** from the air. From these they build sugar, which gives them energy and building material. As a waste product, oxygen is formed, which we need to breathe.

Photosynthesis takes place mainly in the **green leaves**. In their cells there are tiny green bodies, the **chloroplasts**. They contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**, which captures the light. Carbon dioxide enters the leaf through tiny openings on its underside, the stomata. The water comes via the roots and the stem up into the leaves.

The chlorophyll takes in the energy of the light. With this energy the plant splits water, and **oxygen** is released. At the same time it builds the sugar **glucose** from carbon dioxide. Put simply, the formula is: six particles of carbon dioxide and six particles of water produce one particle of glucose and six particles of oxygen. From the sugar the plant also makes starch and cellulose, which wood is made of, for example.

If you put a water plant such as **waterweed** in a glass of water in bright light, small gas bubbles soon rise. This is the oxygen from photosynthesis. If you put the glass in the shade, there are fewer bubbles. In the dark, photosynthesis stops completely. At night plants only breathe, like us, and use up a little oxygen.

In 1771 the Englishman Joseph Priestley found that a plant can “improve” used-up air in a closed glass again. In 1779 the Dutch doctor **Jan Ingenhousz** showed that plants need light for this and that only the green parts can do it. Later researchers found out that carbon dioxide is taken in and sugar is formed in the process. The exact chemical steps were only worked out in the 20th century. Scientists are still researching them today.

Almost all food on Earth ultimately comes from photosynthesis. Animals eat plants, and other animals eat these animals. The **oxygen** in the air was also formed over billions of years through photosynthesis. Today about half of it comes from tiny algae in the sea. In addition, plants take carbon dioxide out of the air, which is why forests and oceans are important for the climate.

begriffe.erklaerung: The green pigment in plants that captures light.
A tiny green body in plant cells in which photosynthesis takes place.
A gas in the air that plants take in for photosynthesis.
Tiny openings in leaves through which gases get in and out.
A simple sugar that the plant makes in photosynthesis.

gewusst: Leaves are green because chlorophyll does not use green light but reflects it.
A large part of the oxygen we breathe comes from tiny algae in the sea.
In autumn the chlorophyll is broken down, so the yellow and red pigments in the leaves become visible.

teile.einleitung: A peer review is the checking of a scientific study by independent experts before it is published. It is like quality control for research. Even so, a peer review cannot guarantee that a result is definitely correct.
wichtigste: A peer review is the checking of a study by independent experts.
The English word “peer” means a person of equal rank.
In double-blind peer review the reviewers and the researchers do not know each other's names.
A preprint is a study that is published before it has been reviewed.
A peer review cannot guarantee that a result is definitely correct.
When other researchers repeat an experiment to check it, this is called replication.
Predatory publishers publish almost anything for money without real review.

abschnitte.text: When researchers have found out something new, they write an article for a **scientific journal**. Well-known examples are “Nature” and “Science”. Before the article appears, independent experts check whether the study was done carefully. This process is called **peer review**, after the English word peer for a person of equal rank.

The reviewers look at whether the research question is clear and the **methods** are suitable. They check whether enough data was collected and whether the conclusions really follow from the results. In the **double-blind** process neither the reviewers nor the researchers know the others' names. The reviewers often ask for improvements, and the article is revised several times.

Sometimes researchers publish their study on the internet before it has been reviewed, as a **preprint**. This is quick, and others can see and discuss the results early. Preprints became very important during the Covid-19 pandemic, for example. But you have to know that they have not yet been checked and may later turn out to be wrong.

Reviewers usually only see the text and not all the raw data, so they do not always spot mistakes or fraud. A well-known example is a 1998 study in the journal “The Lancet” that claimed a false link between the MMR vaccine and autism. It was officially **retracted** in 2010 after it had turned out to be flawed and dishonest. This is why **replication** is so important: only when others repeat an experiment and find the same thing is a result considered well established.

There are publishers who publish almost anything for money, without real review. They are called **predatory publishers**. Their journals often look respectable but contain a lot of poor or false work. So if you read a study, you should check where it was published and whether other experts confirm it.

begriffe.erklaerung: An expert who checks and assesses a piece of work.
A study that is published before it has been reviewed.
Repeating an experiment to check the result.
A publisher that publishes almost anything for money without real checking.
When a journal officially declares a published article invalid.

gewusst: There are websites that collect retracted studies so that nobody is fooled by them any more.
Researchers have deliberately sent nonsense test articles to predatory publishers, and they were accepted anyway.
Even famous journals such as “Nature” sometimes have to retract articles.

teile.einleitung: The pH value shows how acidic or alkaline a liquid is. It is usually given on a scale from 0 to 14, where 7 is neutral. Whether lemon juice, soapy water or blood, everything has a pH value.
wichtigste: The pH value measures how acidic or alkaline a liquid is.
The scale usually goes from 0 to 14.
Pure water has a pH value of 7 and is neutral.
Values below 7 are acidic, values above 7 alkaline.
Each step on the scale means a difference ten times bigger.
The pH value is measured with indicator paper or a pH meter.
The Danish chemist Søren Sørensen introduced the pH value in 1909.

abschnitte.text: Whether a liquid is acidic depends on tiny charged particles, the **hydrogen ions**. The more of them are dissolved, the more acidic it is and the smaller the pH value. The small p stands for power, the capital H for hydrogen. The opposite of acidic is called **alkaline** or basic.

The middle of the scale is 7; that is neutral, like pure water at 25 degrees. From 7 down to 0 it becomes more and more acidic, from 7 up to 14 more and more alkaline. The scale is **logarithmic**: a juice with pH 3 is ten times more acidic than one with pH 4 and a hundred times more acidic than one with pH 5. Very strong acids and alkalis can even be below 0 or above 14.

Stomach acid, with a pH value of about 1 to 2, is very acidic and helps with digestion. Lemon juice has about pH 2, cola about 2.5 and coffee about 5. Our **blood** is very precisely at about 7.4. Seawater is slightly alkaline, soapy water even more so, and drain cleaner reaches values of up to 14.

The easiest way is with **indicator paper**, which changes colour depending on the pH value, from red for acidic to blue or violet for alkaline. An electronic pH meter measures more precisely. Red cabbage juice is also a natural indicator: with vinegar it turns red, with washing soda green. You can easily try this experiment in the kitchen.

The term pH value was introduced in 1909 by **Søren Sørensen**. He worked in the laboratory of the Carlsberg brewery in Copenhagen and studied how acids affect brewing beer. He was looking for a simple number instead of very small decimal numbers. His idea quickly caught on throughout science.

Many plants only grow at a suitable **soil pH**; blueberries, for example, like acidic soil. Hydrangeas flower blue in acidic soil and pink in chalky soil. In swimming pools the pH value is checked constantly so that eyes and skin are not irritated. Because the oceans absorb carbon dioxide, their pH value is slowly falling, which harms corals and shellfish.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that lowers the pH value in water below 7, for example vinegar.
A substance that raises the pH value above 7, for example soap or bicarbonate of soda.
A substance that shows by its colour how acidic or alkaline something is.
Neither acidic nor alkaline, with a pH value of 7.

gewusst: Our skin is slightly acidic, with a pH value of about 5.5, and in this way protects itself against germs.
Even a small change in the blood's pH value of a few tenths can be life-threatening.
Rain is slightly acidic even without air pollution, because carbon dioxide dissolves in it.

teile.einleitung: A preprint is a scientific paper that is published on the internet before other experts have checked it. In this way researchers can share their results with the whole world very quickly. At the same time, preprints have to be read with particular care.
wichtigste: A preprint is a research article before it has been reviewed by experts.
The most important advantage: results become available quickly.
The server arXiv was founded in 1991 and is especially important in physics and mathematics.
bioRxiv specialises in biology, medRxiv in medicine.
Preprints often get a DOI so that they can be cited permanently.
At the start of the Covid-19 pandemic the number of preprints rose sharply.
The media should point out that preprints have not been reviewed.

abschnitte.text: The word **preprint** means roughly “printed in advance”. Normally a scientific paper is checked by independent experts before it is published in a scientific journal. This check is called **peer review** and can take months. With a preprint the researchers put their work freely on the internet beforehand. Anyone can then read it, comment on it and build on it.

The oldest large preprint server is **arXiv**, founded in 1991 by the physicist Paul Ginsparg. It is used mainly in physics, mathematics and computer science and today contains over two million papers. For biology there is **bioRxiv**, for medicine and health sciences **medRxiv**. At CERN in Geneva, too, an open storage place for research results called Zenodo is run. So that preprints can be cited permanently, they often get a **DOI**, a kind of fixed internet address.

The most important advantage is speed: results become available quickly. Researchers can show that they were the first to have an idea. Colleagues can spot mistakes early and give feedback. In addition, preprints are usually free to read, while many scientific journals cost money. This especially helps researchers in poorer countries.

At the start of the **Covid-19 pandemic** in 2020 the number of preprints rose sharply. Doctors and authorities needed new knowledge about the virus very quickly. That is why many important findings were first published as preprints. At the same time, some flawed studies also spread before they had been checked. This showed how important a critical eye is.

A preprint has not yet been **reviewed** by independent experts. So the media should always point this out when they report on a preprint. If the paper later appears in a scientific journal, the preprint is usually linked to the published version. Often individual results or wordings change in the process. So if you read preprints, you should check whether there is already a reviewed version.

begriffe.erklaerung: The checking of a research paper by other experts before it is published.
A magazine in which researchers publish their results.
A fixed identification number with which you can always find a document on the internet again.
A computer that stores data and makes it available over the internet.

gewusst: The Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman published his proof of the famous Poincaré conjecture only as a preprint on arXiv.
The name bioRxiv is pronounced like “bio-archive”, because the X stands for the Greek letter chi.
The name medRxiv is pronounced like “med-archive”.

teile.einleitung: Prokaryotes are tiny living things whose cell has no real nucleus. They include bacteria and archaea. They are the oldest living things on Earth and are found almost everywhere today, from the soil and the sea to our gut.
wichtigste: Prokaryotes lack a nucleus with a nuclear envelope.
The word “prokaryote” literally means roughly “before the nucleus”.
Prokaryotes include bacteria and archaea.
Their DNA lies free in the cytoplasm.
Small extra rings of DNA are called plasmids.
Most bacteria are only a few micrometres in size.
Cyanobacteria carry out photosynthesis and are also called blue-green algae.

abschnitte.text: **Prokaryotes** are single-celled organisms without a real nucleus. The name comes from Greek and means roughly “before the nucleus”. All other living things, that is plants, animals, fungi and humans, are **eukaryotes** and have a nucleus with a nuclear envelope. Prokaryotes include two large groups: bacteria and **archaea**. The archaea were only recognised as a separate group in 1977 by the American Carl Woese.

Most bacteria are only a few micrometres in size, that is, a thousand times smaller than a millimetre. Their DNA lies as a ring-shaped molecule free in the **cytoplasm**, the inside of the cell. In addition, many bacteria have small rings of DNA, the **plasmids**. On the outside a cell wall protects them, and below it is the cell membrane. Many bacteria move with **flagella**, long threads that turn like a propeller.

Prokaryotes multiply when one cell divides into two daughter cells. This **binary fission** often happens very quickly. Under ideal conditions the gut bacterium Escherichia coli can divide about every 20 minutes. In this way a single cell can become millions within a few hours. Fortunately, in nature there are usually not enough nutrients, so growth is slowed down.

Prokaryotes live almost everywhere: in the soil, in the water, in the air and on our skin. Some archaea survive in boiling hot springs, in very salty water or in permanent ice. **Cyanobacteria**, also called blue-green algae, carry out photosynthesis. Over two billion years ago they filled the Earth's atmosphere with oxygen for the first time. The oldest traces of life on Earth probably come from such prokaryotes.

Trillions of bacteria live in our gut and help with **digestion**. Bacteria are also needed to make yoghurt, cheese and sauerkraut. In Swiss cheeses such as Emmental, bacteria even make the typical holes. But some bacteria also cause diseases, against which **antibiotics** help. In sewage works bacteria clean our waste water.

begriffe.erklaerung: A separate space in the cell in which eukaryotes keep their genetic information.
The liquid material inside a cell.
A small extra ring of DNA in bacteria.
A long thread with which some cells move along.
A thousandth of a millimetre.

gewusst: In the 17th century the Dutchman Antoni van Leeuwenhoek was one of the first to see bacteria, with a microscope he had built himself.
In a human body there are about as many bacterial cells as the body's own cells.
The power stations of our cells, the mitochondria, probably come from bacteria that moved into other cells a very long time ago.

teile.einleitung: Recessiveness is a term from the study of heredity. A recessive characteristic is one that is hidden by another, dominant characteristic. It only shows if a living thing has the recessive gene variant twice.
wichtigste: An allele that is hidden by another allele is called recessive.
A recessive characteristic only shows if two recessive alleles are present.
Someone who carries a recessive disease allele but is healthy themselves is called a carrier.
When Aa is crossed with Aa, 25 per cent of the offspring have the combination aa.
When Aa is crossed with aa, 50 per cent of the offspring show the recessive characteristic.
A recessive characteristic can skip a generation.
Cystic fibrosis and haemophilia are inherited recessively.

abschnitte.text: Almost all genes are present twice in our cells; one version comes from the father and one from the mother. The different versions of a gene are called **alleles**. If an allele is **dominant**, it wins through, and the other, **recessive** allele is hidden. Dominant alleles are written with capital letters such as A, and recessive ones with small letters such as a.

These rules were discovered by the monk **Gregor Mendel**, who crossed thousands of pea plants in Brno around 1860. He found that some characteristics disappeared in one generation and reappeared in the next. For example, when he crossed violet-flowered peas with white-flowered ones, at first they all flowered violet. In the following generation white reappeared, in about a quarter of the plants.

With a cross diagram you can calculate probabilities. When Aa is crossed with Aa, the combinations AA, Aa, aA and aa arise, so a quarter, or 25 per cent, have the combination aa. With Aa and aa it is 50 per cent. Someone who has **Aa** does not show the recessive characteristic but can pass the allele on. That is why a recessive characteristic can skip a generation.

Some diseases are inherited recessively. One example is **cystic fibrosis**, in which thick mucus mainly affects the lungs and digestion. People with only one disease allele are healthy; they are called **carriers**. Haemophilia, in which the blood clots poorly, is on the X chromosome, which is why it affects almost only boys and men.

In animals, **albinism**, for example, is recessive, that is, the lack of pigment in skin, fur and eyes. White mice or rabbits with red eyes have two recessive alleles. The coat colour of many dog breeds also follows such rules. In humans, however, most characteristics, such as eye colour, are more complicated, because many genes work together.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of genetic information that affects a particular characteristic.
One of several possible versions of a gene.
An allele that wins through over another one.
Someone who carries a recessive allele but does not show the characteristic.
The visible appearance of a living thing.

gewusst: Gregor Mendel's work was hardly noticed during his lifetime and was only rediscovered around 1900.
In the 19th century haemophilia occurred in several European royal families and was therefore also called the “royal disease”.
A person can carry a recessive allele all their life without ever noticing it.

teile.einleitung: “Post hoc ergo propter hoc” is a Latin expression for a common error in thinking. It means “after this, therefore because of this”. It refers to the false conclusion that something must be the cause of an event just because it happened before it.
wichtigste: The Latin phrase means “after this, therefore because of this”.
The fallacy wrongly assumes a link between cause and effect.
Just because the cockerel crows before sunrise does not mean it makes the Sun rise.
Lucky socks before a win are a typical example of this error in thinking.
Colds usually get better by themselves, so an improvement after a home remedy proves nothing.
Similar is “cum hoc ergo propter hoc”, which concludes a cause from things happening at the same time.
In medicine, randomised controlled trials give the best protection against it.

abschnitte.text: “Post hoc ergo propter hoc” is a **fallacy**, that is, an error in thinking in an argument. Translated literally it means “after this, therefore because of this”. You believe that A is the cause of B just because A happened before B. But an order in time does not prove a **link between cause and effect**. Often it is just chance, or something quite different is behind it.

A cockerel crows every morning shortly before the Sun rises. Even so, the cockerel does not make the Sun rise, even if it looks that way. A footballer wears his “lucky socks” and then wins three matches. He probably won because of training and team spirit instead. Many kinds of **superstition** arise from exactly this kind of conclusion.

Someone takes a home remedy for a cold and is well again a week later. This does not prove that it worked, because colds usually get better by themselves anyway. In addition, people often go to the doctor when they feel at their worst. After that things almost always get better, whatever you do. Experts call this **regression to the mean**.

A close relative is “**cum hoc ergo propter hoc**”, meaning “with this, therefore because of this”. Here you conclude a cause from things happening at the same time rather than one after the other. A well-known example: in summer more ice cream is eaten and there are more swimming accidents. But the ice cream does not cause accidents; both depend on the warm weather. This is called a **correlation** without a direct cause.

In medicine, **randomised controlled trials** give the best protection against this fallacy. Participants are divided by chance into groups that receive different treatments. In everyday life a **comparison group** helps too. If accidents fall after a speed camera is put up, you should check whether they have also fallen elsewhere. Only then can you say whether the camera was really the cause.

begriffe.erklaerung: An argument that sounds logical but is wrong.
That which brings about or triggers something else.
Two things occur together without one necessarily causing the other.
A comparison group in an experiment that is not treated.

gewusst: The Greek philosopher Aristotle described such false conclusions about causes over 2,000 years ago.
In 1948 the researcher B. F. Skinner showed that even pigeons develop a kind of superstition when food happens to come after certain movements.
Many athletes have rituals before a competition that arose from an earlier chance success.

teile.einleitung: The Planck constant is one of the most important natural constants in physics and is abbreviated with the letter h. It shows that in the world of the smallest particles, energy only comes in tiny portions. Quantum physics began with this discovery.
wichtigste: Max Planck introduced the constant in 1900.
He needed it to explain the radiation of black bodies.
Since 2019 h has had the exact value 6.62607015 × 10^-34 joule seconds.
Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined using the Planck constant.
The energy of a particle of light equals h times its frequency.
The reduced Planck constant ħ is h divided by 2π.
The von Klitzing constant and the Josephson constant also contain h.

abschnitte.text: The German physicist **Max Planck** lived from 1858 to 1947. In 1900 he studied the radiation of **black bodies**, that is, objects that swallow all light and glow themselves when heated. The known formulas did not match the measurements. Planck found a formula that fitted when he assumed that energy is only given off in small packets. For this work he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1918.

The size of an energy packet depends on the frequency: E = h times f. You can imagine this like money that only exists in whole centimes (Rappen), never in halves. In 1905 Albert Einstein used it to explain that light, too, is made of particles, the **photons**. A photon with a frequency of 5 × 10^14 hertz has about 3.3 × 10^-19 joules of energy. That is so little that we do not notice the individual portions in everyday life.

The Planck constant has the unit **joule second**. Its value is unimaginably small: 33 zeros follow the decimal point before the first digit comes. Since 2019 the value 6.62607015 × 10^-34 J s has been fixed exactly and is no longer measured. Physicists often also use the **reduced Planck constant** ħ, pronounced “h-bar”. It is h divided by 2π and simplifies many formulas.

In the past the kilogram was defined by a metal cylinder near Paris, the **international prototype of the kilogram**. Because such an object can change very slightly over time, a better solution was sought. Since 20 May 2019 the kilogram has been defined using the Planck constant. With a special balance, the **Kibble balance**, a mass can be determined very precisely in this way. The Federal Institute of Metrology METAS in Bern has also worked on such a balance.

h also plays a role in electrical engineering. The **von Klitzing constant** h/e² corresponds to an electrical resistance of about 25,813 ohms. It is named after the German physicist Klaus von Klitzing, who received the Nobel Prize for it in 1985. The **Josephson constant** 2e/h forms the basis of modern voltage standards. With them, measuring laboratories all over the world can define the volt and the ohm in exactly the same way.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quantity in physics that has the same value everywhere and always.
A particle of light, that is, the smallest portion of light.
How often an oscillation happens per second, measured in hertz.
The part of physics that describes the world of the smallest particles.

gewusst: At first Max Planck himself thought his energy portions were just a mathematical trick.
Since 2019, as well as the kilogram, all SI base units have been defined by fixed natural constants.
A research society in Germany, the Max Planck Society, is named after him.

tegppdk.t: Prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps

teile.einleitung: The prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps are the remains of villages that stood on lake shores and in moors about 7,000 to 2,500 years ago. Since 2011, 111 of these sites have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and most of them are in Switzerland. Because wood, seeds and cloth survived in the damp ground, they tell us in particular detail about life in the Stone Age and the Bronze Age.
wichtigste: Pile dwellings are settlements of the Neolithic and Bronze Age on lakes and moors around the Alps.
About 1,000 pile-dwelling sites are known around the Alps.
Since 2011, 111 selected sites in six countries have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Today experts often speak of wetland settlements.
The Horgen culture and the Pfyn culture are named after Swiss sites.
Because lake levels rose and fell, the villages were often abandoned or moved.
Many sites are left undisturbed as an archive for future research methods.

abschnitte.text: Pile dwellings were houses made of wood, clay and reeds that stood on posts. They were on lake shores, by rivers and in moors. Today experts often call them **wetland settlements**, because we know that many houses stood on the shore and not in open water. The settlements date from the period from about 5000 to 500 BC.

About 1,000 sites are known around the Alps. Of these, 111 are part of the **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, spread across Switzerland, Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Slovenia. With 56 sites, Switzerland has the largest share, for example on Lake Zurich, Lake Biel, Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Constance. In Germany the **Federsee moor** in Upper Swabia is especially well known.

In the very dry winter of 1853/54 the water level of Lake Zurich fell sharply. Near Obermeilen wooden posts and many finds came to light. The Zurich scholar **Ferdinand Keller** described them and created the idea of villages on platforms above the water. After that a real enthusiasm for pile dwellings began throughout Switzerland.

The people grew cereals, kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs and went fishing and hunting. In the **occupation layer**, a layer of settlement waste, remains of bread, apples, nets, cloth and tools have survived. Because wood does not rot under water, **dendrochronology** can often use the tree rings to tell to the exact year when a tree was felled. Two Neolithic cultures are named after sites on Lake Zurich and in Thurgau: the **Horgen culture** and the Pfyn culture.

In the 19th century the pile dwellers were seen as the ancestors of the young Switzerland. They were shown in pictures, school books and festival parades and were meant to strengthen the sense of community in the new federal state. However, many of these pictures were fantasy. Today's research paints a more accurate and more varied picture.

The sites are threatened by erosion of the shore, building work and waves from boats. Many are deliberately not excavated but covered and protected, so that later generations can study them with better methods. Pile-dwelling finds can be seen, for example, at the **Laténium** in Hauterive on Lake Neuchâtel and at the Swiss National Museum in Zurich. On Lake Constance the Pfahlbaumuseum Unteruhldingen shows reconstructed houses.

begriffe.erklaerung: A house that stands on wooden posts driven into the ground.
A settlement on lake shores or in moors whose remains are preserved in the wet ground.
A layer of ground made of waste and remains from a settlement.
Dating wood using its tree rings.
The period when people settled down and began farming.

gewusst: In the moors of Ljubljana in Slovenia one of the oldest wooden wheels in the world was found; it is over 5,000 years old.
Because wood hardly rots under water, some posts have survived after thousands of years.
Switzerland has more than half of all the pile-dwelling World Heritage sites.

teile.einleitung: Plateosaurus was a large, plant-eating dinosaur that lived about 210 million years ago. In Switzerland it is especially famous because many of its skeletons were found in the village of Frick in the canton of Aargau. This makes Frick one of the most important dinosaur sites in Europe.
wichtigste: Plateosaurus lived in the late Triassic about 210 million years ago.
It ate plants and grew up to about 10 metres long.
According to what we know today, it walked on two legs.
Many skeletons were found in a clay pit in Frick in the canton of Aargau.
In 2015 a large skeleton about 8 metres long was dug up in Frick.
It is an early relative of the huge long-necked dinosaurs.
There are also finds in Germany, for example near Trossingen.

abschnitte.text: Plateosaurus had a long neck, a small head and a long, strong tail. Fully grown animals reached up to about 10 metres long. Its front legs were shorter than its back legs and had hands with claws, especially on the thumb. According to what we know today, it walked on **two legs** and held its tail in the air as a counterweight. In the past it was often shown on all fours, but studies of the bones have disproved this.

Plateosaurus was a **plant-eater**. Its teeth were leaf-shaped and had fine serrations with which it could cut off plants. With its long neck it could also reach high branches. The landscape at that time was warm and rather dry, with ferns, horsetails and conifers. There were no flowers or grass yet at that time.

Plateosaurus lived in the **Triassic**, the first age of the dinosaurs. The bones from Frick are about 210 million years old. At that time all the continents still belonged to the supercontinent **Pangaea**. Plateosaurus is an early relative of later giants such as Brachiosaurus and Diplodocus. The first finds were scientifically described in Germany as early as 1837.

In Frick in the canton of Aargau, numerous Plateosaurus skeletons were discovered in the **clay pit** of a brickworks. Experts think that some animals got stuck in the muddy ground and died. As a result many bones were well preserved. In 2015 a large skeleton about 8 metres long was dug up there. At the **Sauriermuseum Frick** visitors can marvel at original bones and a skeleton.

Because there are so many finds, Plateosaurus is one of the best-studied dinosaurs of all. Using its bones, researchers have been able to investigate, for example, how fast dinosaurs grew. This showed that animals of the same age could be very different in size. Apart from Frick, there are large sites in Germany, for example near **Trossingen** and Halberstadt. Bones have also been found in Greenland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A geological period about 252 to 201 million years ago in which the first dinosaurs lived.
The petrified remains of a living thing from earlier times.
A place where clay for bricks is dug.
A researcher who studies extinct living things using fossils.

gewusst: The name Plateosaurus means roughly “flat lizard”.
Because so many dinosaur bones were found in Frick, the place is often called the “dinosaur village”.
At the time of Plateosaurus, the area of today's Switzerland lay in a flat, warm landscape near the sea.

teile.einleitung: The polymerase chain reaction, PCR for short, is a method for copying tiny sections of DNA millions of times. In this way even the smallest traces of genetic material become visible and can be studied. Many people got to know PCR through the coronavirus tests from 2020.
wichtigste: PCR stands for polymerase chain reaction.
It is used to copy sections of DNA many times.
It was invented by the American Kary Mullis in 1983.
For this he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993.
The method works by repeated heating and cooling in a machine called a thermal cycler.
With each cycle the amount of the DNA being looked for doubles.
PCR is used in medicine, crime investigation and research.

abschnitte.text: **DNA** is the genetic material of all living things and many viruses. Often there are only tiny amounts of it, for example in a hair or a swab from the nose. With PCR a chosen section is copied so many times that there is enough material for a test. You can think of it like a photocopier that only copies one particular page of a thick book.

One cycle has three steps. First the sample is heated to about 95 degrees so that the two strands of the DNA separate. Then it is cooled, and short starting pieces, the **primers**, attach to the place being looked for. Finally, at about 72 degrees, an enzyme, the **DNA polymerase**, builds new matching strands. A **thermal cycler** repeats these steps automatically about 30 to 40 times.

Because the amount doubles with each cycle, it grows incredibly fast. After 10 cycles, a single piece of DNA becomes about 1,000 copies. After 30 cycles there are already about a billion. This takes only about one to two hours.

Normal enzymes would be destroyed when heated to 95 degrees. The solution was found in the bacterium **Thermus aquaticus**, which lives in hot springs in Yellowstone National Park in the USA. Its polymerase, Taq polymerase, easily withstands the heat. Only with it could PCR run fully automatically.

Kary Mullis worked for a biotechnology company in California. In his own words, the idea for PCR came to him in 1983 during a night-time car journey. Just a few years later laboratories all over the world were using his method. In 1993 he received the **Nobel Prize** in Chemistry.

In medicine PCR is used to detect germs, such as the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 or flu viruses. The police use it to create a **genetic fingerprint** from traces of blood or skin. PCR can also be used to settle questions of fatherhood or to recognise inherited diseases. Researchers have even used it to study genetic material from the bones of Neanderthals.

begriffe.erklaerung: The molecule in which genetic information is stored.
An enzyme that puts together new DNA strands.
A short piece of DNA that shows the polymerase where to start copying.
A machine that automatically heats and cools samples again and again.
A DNA pattern that makes almost every person clearly identifiable.

gewusst: Kary Mullis was also a keen surfer.
PCR is so sensitive that even a single flake of skin from a laboratory worker can spoil a test.
Because PCR finds the genetic material of viruses, it can detect an infection even before the first signs of illness.

teile.einleitung: A prion is a wrongly folded protein that can be infectious. Prions are unusual germs, because they have no genetic material of their own like viruses or bacteria. They cause rare but fatal diseases of the brain, such as mad cow disease, BSE.
wichtigste: A prion is a wrongly folded, infectious protein.
Stanley Prusiner received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1997 for discovering prions.
In the diseased form there are many more beta sheets.
Prion diseases make brain tissue full of holes like a sponge.
In the 1990s BSE led to a major food crisis in Europe.
In sheep the prion disease scrapie has existed for centuries.
The best-known human prion disease is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

abschnitte.text: A **prion** is a protein that is folded into the wrong shape. The normal prion protein is found in humans and animals mainly in nerve cells and is harmless. In the diseased form there are many more **beta sheets**, a particular way the protein chain is folded. The wrongly folded prion can make healthy proteins fold wrongly too. This creates a chain reaction, rather like dominoes falling over.

For a long time people believed that every infectious disease was caused by a germ with genetic material. In the 1980s the American researcher **Stanley Prusiner** put forward the idea that a protein on its own can be infectious. He also coined the name prion, from “proteinaceous infectious particle”. At first many experts doubted his idea. In 1997 he received the **Nobel Prize** in Medicine for it.

In sheep and goats the prion disease **scrapie** has existed for centuries. The animals scratch themselves a lot and become unsteady on their legs. In the 1980s and 1990s **BSE**, also called mad cow disease, spread among cattle. The disease spread through meat and bone meal in the feed, which was made from the remains of slaughtered animals. In Switzerland too there were several hundred cases of BSE, and feeding meat and bone meal was banned.

The best-known human prion disease is **Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease**. It is very rare and usually occurs in older people without any recognisable cause. A new form was linked in 1996 in Great Britain with eating beef contaminated with BSE. In all prion diseases nerve cells die, and the brain becomes full of holes like a **sponge**. That is why they are also called spongiform encephalopathies.

Prions are unusually resistant to heat and chemicals. A normal **autoclave programme**, which hospitals use to sterilise instruments with hot steam, is not reliably enough. That is why there are especially strict cleaning rules for operations on the brain. Cooking or frying does not destroy prions in meat either. That is why controlling animal feed was so important for stopping BSE.

begriffe.erklaerung: An important building material in all living things.
The three-dimensional shape that a protein chain takes.
Mad cow disease, a prion disease in cattle.
Like a sponge, with many small holes.
A machine that sterilises objects with hot steam under pressure.

gewusst: Prions have neither DNA nor RNA and are therefore the only known germs without genetic material of their own.
Deer and elk in North America have a prion disease called chronic wasting disease.
In Papua New Guinea there used to be the prion disease kuru, which was passed on through a special funeral ritual.

teile.einleitung: The periodic table is a table in which all the chemical elements are arranged. It shows at a glance how the elements are built and which ones are similar to each other. Almost every chemistry classroom in the world has a periodic table on the wall.
wichtigste: The chemical elements are arranged in the periodic table.
The elements are ordered by their atomic number, that is, by the number of protons in the nucleus.
Today 118 elements are known.
The horizontal rows are called periods, the vertical columns groups.
Elements in the same group have similar properties.
The Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev presented the first periodic table in 1869.

abschnitte.text: A **chemical element** is a basic substance that cannot be broken down any further chemically, such as gold, oxygen or iron. Every element has a symbol of one or two letters, for example Fe for iron or Au for gold. In the periodic table each element has its own box with its symbol, name and atomic number. The first element is hydrogen with the number 1; the last so far is oganesson with the number 118.

The elements are sorted by their **atomic number**, that is, by the number of protons in the atomic nucleus. There are 7 horizontal **periods** and 18 vertical **groups**. On the left are mainly metals, on the right the non-metals. With each new period, another shell of electrons is added.

Elements in a group behave similarly, like brothers and sisters. On the far left are the alkali metals such as sodium, which react violently with water. On the far right are the **noble gases** such as helium and neon, which react with almost nothing. Next to them are the halogens such as chlorine, which are very reactive.

In 1869 the Russian chemist **Dmitri Mendeleev** arranged the 63 elements known at the time in a table. At almost the same time the German Lothar Meyer had a similar idea. Mendeleev deliberately left gaps and predicted that elements not yet known belonged there. Later gallium, scandium and germanium were indeed discovered, and they fitted exactly into his gaps.

About 90 elements occur in nature. The rest were made artificially in laboratories and particle accelerators. The heaviest of them often decay within fractions of a second. Some elements are named after researchers, such as einsteinium or mendelevium, others after places, such as europium or darmstadtium.

With the periodic table you can predict how a substance will behave without trying it out. Chemists use it to develop new materials, medicines or batteries. That is why pupils all over the world learn with it. In 2019 the United Nations celebrated the **International Year of the Periodic Table**, 150 years after Mendeleev.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic substance made of only one kind of atom.
The number of protons in the atomic nucleus; it decides the place in the periodic table.
A horizontal row in the periodic table.
A vertical column of elements that behave similarly.
Gases such as helium or neon that hardly react with other substances.

gewusst: Mendeleev is said to have developed the idea for ordering the elements using cards, as in a card game.
The element helium was first discovered in the light of the Sun and only later found on Earth.
Only two elements are liquid at room temperature: mercury and bromine.

teile.einleitung: The trial of Galileo Galilei was a famous trial held by the Roman Inquisition in 1633. The Italian scholar was convicted because he had spread the teaching that the Earth goes round the Sun. To this day the case is seen as a symbol of the conflict between new science and the authority of the Church.
wichtigste: Galileo Galilei was convicted in Rome in 1633.
The trial was conducted by the Roman Inquisition.
It was triggered by his book “Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems” of 1632.
At the time of the trial Pope Urban VIII was in office.
Galileo had to renounce his teaching publicly.
He was under house arrest until the end of his life.
In 1992 Pope John Paul II admitted that the Church had wronged Galileo.

abschnitte.text: **Galileo Galilei** lived from 1564 to 1642 and was a mathematician, physicist and astronomer in Italy. From 1609 he observed the sky with a telescope he had built himself. He discovered the four large moons of Jupiter, the phases of Venus and craters on the Moon. These observations supported the **heliocentric view of the world** of Nicolaus Copernicus, in which the Sun is at the centre.

At that time most scholars believed in the **geocentric view of the world**, in which the Earth stands still and everything goes round it. Some passages in the Bible were understood as if they confirmed this view. In 1616 the Church declared the teaching of Copernicus incompatible with the faith, and Galileo was warned not to support it. He was allowed to discuss it at most as a mathematical assumption.

In 1632 Galileo published the “**Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems**” in Florence. In it three people discuss the old and the new view of the world. The character **Simplicio**, who defends the old view, often seems simple-minded. Pope Urban VIII, who had admired Galileo in the past, felt attacked by the book.

Galileo had to travel to Rome and was questioned by the **Inquisition**, a Church authority that pursued departures from the faith. In June 1633 he was convicted and had to **renounce** his teaching in the church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva. His book was banned. After that he lived under **house arrest** in his country house at Arcetri near Florence until his death in 1642.

After his conviction Galileo is said to have muttered “And yet it moves”. But this sentence only appears more than a hundred years later and is probably a legend. Under house arrest Galileo wrote another important work about motion and the strength of materials. It was printed in 1638 in Leiden in the Netherlands, because it was not allowed to be published in Italy.

Over time the heliocentric view of the world won through, thanks also to Johannes Kepler and Isaac Newton. The Catholic Church removed Galileo's Dialogue from the list of banned books in 1835. In 1992, after an investigation, Pope **John Paul II** admitted that the Church had wronged Galileo. Today the case is often mentioned when the freedom of research is discussed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A Church authority that investigated and punished departures from the faith.
A view of the world in which the Sun is at the centre.
A view of the world in which the Earth is at the centre.
To declare publicly that you are giving up an opinion.
A punishment in which you are not allowed to leave your house.

gewusst: Galileo was not tortured, but he was threatened with torture during questioning.
The space probe Galileo, which explored Jupiter, was named after him.
In the last years of his life Galileo went blind.

teile.einleitung: Pavlov's dog is one of the most famous experiments in science. With it, the Russian researcher Ivan Pavlov discovered that animals learn to react to a signal as if something important were about to happen. This kind of learning is called classical conditioning.
wichtigste: Ivan Pavlov was a researcher from Russia.
In 1904 he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his research on digestion.
In his experiments in Saint Petersburg he measured the flow of saliva in dogs.
In stories the food is usually paired with the sound of a bell.
Pavlov called the learned reaction a conditioned reflex.
The sound has to come shortly before the food so that the dog learns the connection best.
Someone who reacts “like Pavlov's dog” reacts automatically to a learned signal.

abschnitte.text: Ivan Petrovich Pavlov lived from 1849 to 1936 in **Russia**. He was a doctor and physiologist, that is, a researcher who studies how the body works. In **Saint Petersburg** he spent years studying digestion, for example how the stomach and salivary glands work. For this, in 1904 he became the first Russian to receive a **Nobel Prize**. During this work he made a discovery that made him even more famous.

Pavlov noticed that his dogs produced saliva even before they were given food. They already reacted when the assistant with the food entered the room. Pavlov looked into this more closely and always sounded a particular signal before feeding. In stories this is usually a **bell**, but in the laboratory he also used buzzers, metronomes and other stimuli. After a few repetitions the saliva started to flow at the sound alone, without any food.

That a dog produces saliva when it sees food is innate. This is an **unconditioned reflex**. At first the sound means nothing at all to the dog; it is a neutral stimulus. But if it always sounds shortly before the food, the dog links the two in its brain. The sound becomes a signal, and the flow of saliva in response is called a **conditioned reflex**.

If the sound is played many times without any food coming, the reaction becomes weaker and finally disappears. This is called **extinction**. The order also matters: if the sound only comes after the food, the dog hardly learns the connection. Pavlov's discovery became the basis of **classical conditioning**. Later, researchers such as John B. Watson in the USA built a whole branch of psychology on it, behaviourism.

People learn like this too. If you immediately think of your break-time snack when the school bell rings, you are showing a similar link. Pets often run to the kitchen when they hear the sound of the food tin. Advertising also links music and beautiful images with products. The expression **“like Pavlov's dog”** describes someone who reacts automatically to a learned signal.

begriffe.erklaerung: An automatic reaction of the body that you do not think about.
An innate reaction, for example producing saliva at the sight of food.
A learned reaction to a signal, for example producing saliva at the sound of a bell.
Learning by linking two stimuli that often occur together.
The science of how the bodies of living things work.

gewusst: Whether Pavlov really used a bell is disputed; he worked mainly with buzzers and metronomes.
Pavlov was the first Russian to receive a Nobel Prize.
Pavlov did not get his Nobel Prize for the dog learning experiments but for his research on digestion.

teile.einleitung: The barn swallow is a small, elegant migratory bird with long tail streamers and a reddish-brown throat. It likes to build its nests in stables and catches insects in flight. In autumn it flies all the way to Africa and returns in spring.
wichtigste: The barn swallow has a reddish-brown throat.
In flight you recognise it by the long streamers on its tail.
It usually builds its nest inside stables.
It eats insects that it catches in flight.
It spends the winter in Africa.
Before a thunderstorm swallows often fly low, because the insects fly low too.
An old saying goes: one swallow does not make a summer.

abschnitte.text: The **barn swallow** is about as long as a hand, if you count the tail streamers, and weighs about 20 grams. Its back has a metallic blue-black sheen, and its belly is light. Typical features are the reddish-brown throat and forehead and the long **tail streamers**. In males these streamers are usually longer than in females.

The barn swallow eats almost only **insects**, which it catches in flight, for example midges and flies. It often flies close over meadows, water or cattle pastures. Before a thunderstorm swallows often fly low, because in damp air the insects fly low. It even drinks in flight by skimming just above the water.

The barn swallow usually builds its nest inside stables, barns or garages. It is an open cup made of little balls of mud and stalks, which it sticks to beams or walls. The female usually lays four to five eggs, and there are often two broods a year. The young are fed with insects by both parents.

The barn swallow is a **migratory bird** and spends the winter in Africa south of the Sahara. In autumn swallows often gather on power lines before they set off. The journey is several thousand kilometres long and leads across the Mediterranean and the desert. In spring, usually in April, many swallows return to the same farm.

In Switzerland the barn swallow breeds mainly on farms with livestock. Because there are fewer open stables and fewer insects, it has become rarer in some areas. You can help it by leaving stable doors or windows open and allowing muddy puddles for nest-building. It can be confused with the **house martin**, which has a white rump and builds its closed nests on the outside of house walls.

An old saying goes: one swallow does not make a summer. It means that a single good sign does not yet prove that everything will turn out well. In the past swallows in the stable were seen as bringing luck to the house and the animals. That is why many farmers were happy to let them live with them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that flies to warmer areas in autumn and returns in spring.
The long, narrow outer tail feathers of the barn swallow.
The eggs or young that bird parents raise together.
The back part of a bird's back, above the tail.

gewusst: Barn swallows can catch their insect prey in flight without ever landing.
For one nest a swallow has to carry hundreds of little balls of mud.
Many barn swallows return to exactly the same stable every year.

teile.einleitung: A test tube is a thin glass tube with a round bottom that is used in laboratories and in chemistry lessons. In it you can mix, heat and watch small amounts of substances. It is one of the best-known pieces of equipment in science.
wichtigste: A test tube is a thin tube that is round at the bottom.
It is used mainly for experiments with small amounts.
It is made of special glass that can withstand heat.
Test tubes are placed in a test tube rack.
When heating, you hold the glass with a test tube holder.
When heating, the opening must never point at people.
For heating, a test tube is filled to at most about a third.

abschnitte.text: A **test tube** is a narrow tube made of glass, open at the top and rounded at the bottom. The German name “Reagenzglas” comes from **reagent**, a substance that triggers or detects a chemical reaction. Through the clear glass you can easily see when a colour changes, gas rises or a solid forms. There are test tubes in different sizes; most fit easily into one hand.

Ordinary glass can shatter if it gets hot or cold quickly. That is why test tubes are often made of **borosilicate glass**, which copes well with changes in temperature. This glass is also used for ovenproof baking dishes. There are also tubes made of plastic, for example for blood samples in doctors' surgeries.

So that test tubes do not fall over, they are put in a **test tube rack**. For heating, they are held with a test tube holder made of wood or metal, because the glass gets very hot. With a **stopper** made of rubber or cork you close the tube before shaking it. For cleaning there are special brushes that reach down to the round bottom.

In the laboratory you always wear **safety goggles**. When heating, you fill the tube to at most a third and hold it at a slight angle over the flame. The opening never points at yourself or other people, because hot liquid can suddenly spurt out. If a test tube breaks, you tell the teacher straight away and do not clear up the pieces with your bare hands.

In chemistry lessons a test tube is used to show, for example, how substances dissolve or how indicators change colour. In medicine, blood and urine samples are examined in similar tubes. Biologists also grow small amounts of bacteria in them. The expression “**in vitro**”, Latin for “in glass”, refers to experiments that take place in the laboratory outside a living thing.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that triggers a chemical reaction or detects another substance.
An especially heat-resistant glass for laboratory equipment.
A holder with which you can safely grip a hot test tube.
Latin for “in glass”, an experiment in the laboratory.

gewusst: Test tubes have a round bottom so that they spread heat more evenly and are easier to clean.
You cannot simply stand a test tube on the table, which is why you need the rack.
The picture of a test tube is often used as a symbol for science and research.

teile.einleitung: A mushroom inspection is a place where experts check wild mushrooms that people have gathered. They tell you which mushrooms are edible and which are poisonous. In Switzerland many municipalities have an official mushroom inspection, and it can save lives.
wichtigste: If you are unsure while picking, you take your mushrooms to the mushroom inspection.
A person who officially checks mushrooms is called a mushroom inspector.
Mushrooms are taken to the inspection whole and with their stem, ideally in a basket.
You never eat a mushroom that you do not know for sure.
The death cap causes most fatal mushroom poisonings.
In case of poisoning in Switzerland you dial the emergency number 145.
Edible wild mushrooms are always cooked thoroughly.

abschnitte.text: At the **mushroom inspection**, trained experts look closely at every single mushroom from your basket. They sort poisonous, inedible and edible mushrooms apart. They keep the poisonous ones back so that nobody eats them by mistake. In many Swiss municipalities this inspection is free during the mushroom season.

A **mushroom inspector** has done special training with an exam. In Switzerland the official inspectors are united in **VAPKO**, the association of official mushroom inspection bodies of Switzerland. They know hundreds of kinds of mushroom and pay attention to fine features such as gills, bulb, ring and smell. Many of them work for the municipality as experts alongside their job.

Mushrooms belong in an airy **basket** and not in a plastic bag, because in it they quickly go soft and spoil. You take the whole mushroom with its stem and bulb out of the ground, because important identifying features are found right at the bottom. You do not mix unknown mushrooms with known ones, because otherwise small poisonous pieces could end up among the good mushrooms. It is best to gather only as many mushrooms as you can really eat.

The **death cap** is the most dangerous poisonous mushroom in Europe. Its poison destroys the liver, and the first symptoms often only appear many hours after eating. It can be confused with edible mushrooms such as the field mushroom. So the most important rule is: if you do not know something for sure, you do not eat it.

abschnitte.titel: What to do in an emergency?
abschnitte.text: If you suspect mushroom poisoning, call the number **145** straight away; that is Tox Info Suisse. Experts there help round the clock. In serious cases you dial 144 for the ambulance. It helps to keep leftovers of the mushrooms or the meal so that the mushroom can be identified.

Mushrooms are not plants but living things of their own with an underground network, the **mycelium**. What we gather is only the fruiting body. In many cantons there are rules, for example maximum amounts per day or days when picking mushrooms is not allowed. In this way the forest stays healthy and there will be mushrooms again next year.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place where experts check gathered mushrooms.
The visible part of the mushroom with cap and stem.
A fine network of fungal threads in the soil; the actual fungus.
Thin plates on the underside of the cap of many mushrooms.
The association of official mushroom inspectors in Switzerland.

gewusst: Even a single death cap can be fatal for an adult.
Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.
Even edible mushrooms can give you stomach ache if raw or spoiled, so they are cooked thoroughly.

teile.einleitung: Before a new medicine is given to a person for the first time, it has to be tested in the laboratory for a long time. This phase is called preclinical research. Here experts study whether an active substance works at all and whether it might be toxic.
wichtigste: Preclinical research takes place before an active substance is tested on people for the first time.
Above all, its effect and toxicity are studied in cell cultures and animal experiments.
“In vitro” means a study in a test tube or in cell cultures.
The Ames test uses bacteria to check whether a substance can damage genetic material.
The thalidomide disaster around 1961 led to much stricter testing rules.
The 3R principle stands for replace, reduce and refine.
Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) sets out how safety studies must be carried out.

abschnitte.text: **Preclinical research** is the stage of medicine development before studies on people. Researchers test whether a new substance works against a disease. But above all they want to know whether it is harmful or **toxic**. They also study how the body takes in the substance, distributes it and gets rid of it again. Only if these results are good may an active substance be tested on people in clinical trials.

abschnitte.titel: In the test tube and on the computer
abschnitte.text: Many tests are carried out **in vitro**, that is, in a test tube or in cell cultures. A well-known example is the **Ames test**, which uses bacteria to check whether a substance can damage genetic material. Computer models, called “in silico”, are also becoming more and more important. A new technique is the **organ-on-a-chip**, a microsystem with human cells that imitates the functions of an organ. In this way, for example, a small artificial lung or liver can be tested.

Some questions can so far only be answered on living animals, usually mice or rats. Such experiments are called “in vivo”. So that animals suffer as little as possible, the **3R principle** applies: replace, reduce, refine. This means replacing animal experiments where possible, reducing their number and improving the conditions for the animals. The principle was described in 1959 by the British researchers William Russell and Rex Burch.

At the end of the 1950s the sedative **Contergan**, with the active substance thalidomide, was sold. It caused severe malformations of the arms and legs in thousands of children. Around 1961 it was taken off the market. This disaster showed how dangerous too little testing can be. After it, many countries introduced much stricter rules for medicines.

In Switzerland animal experiments must be approved by the cantonal authorities, and a commission examines every application. Preclinical safety studies must be planned, carried out and documented according to **Good Laboratory Practice (GLP)**. Later, the authority **Swissmedic** decides whether a medicine is approved. In February 2022 Swiss voters voted on an initiative to ban experiments on animals and humans. They rejected it very clearly, with almost 80 per cent voting no.

begriffe.erklaerung: The substance in a medicine that has the effect.
Latin for “in glass”, that is, experiments in a test tube or in cell cultures.
Latin for “in the living”, that is, experiments on living organisms.
The science of poisons and their effects.
Testing a medicine on people according to strict rules.

gewusst: Of many thousands of substances studied in the laboratory, often only one ends up as an approved medicine.
Developing a new medicine usually takes more than ten years.
The Ames test is named after the American biochemist Bruce Ames.

teile.einleitung: Peer review is a checking process in science: before a study appears in a scientific journal, it is assessed by experts from the same field. They look for mistakes and give advice on how to improve it. Research funding, for example from the Swiss National Science Foundation, is also awarded through peer review.
wichtigste: Peer review is assessment by experts from the same field.
In single-blind peer review the reviewers are anonymous.
In double-blind peer review the reviewers and the authors do not know each other.
In the end the editor of the journal decides.
“Major revision” means that a larger revision and a new review are needed.
In open peer review the reviews and sometimes the names are made public.
The Swiss National Science Foundation assesses research applications with peer review.

abschnitte.text: The English word **peer** means “someone of equal rank”; here it means experts from the same field. In **peer review** such experts read a new study carefully before it is published. They check whether the methods are right, whether the results can be followed and whether the conclusions fit. This is meant to stop faulty work from being published.

Researchers send their article to a scientific journal. The **editor** usually chooses two or three reviewers. They write a **review** with a recommendation: accept, minor changes, “major revision” for a larger rewrite with a new review, or reject. In the end the editors decide whether the article is published.

In the **single-blind** process the authors do not know the names of the reviewers. In the **double-blind** process the reviewers also do not know who wrote the article. This is meant to avoid prejudice, for example towards famous or unknown researchers. In **open peer review** the reviews and sometimes also the names are made public.

In 1665 the Royal Society in London published the “Philosophical Transactions”, one of the first **scientific journals** in the world. Even early on, contributions were read by members before printing. But regular review by outsiders only became standard at most journals in the 20th century. Today peer review is usual in almost all sciences.

Peer review improves a lot of work, but it also has weaknesses. Reviewers usually work unpaid, have little time and do not reliably spot **fraud**. The **Swiss National Science Foundation** (SNSF) uses peer review to decide which research applications receive money. For this it asks experts in Switzerland and abroad for reviews.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person of equal rank; here an expert from the same field.
A written assessment by an expert.
A magazine in which researchers publish their results.
The person who decides on the content of a journal.

gewusst: The Royal Society's “Philosophical Transactions” has been published since 1665 and is one of the oldest journals in the world.
Reviewers for scientific journals usually work without pay.
Some articles go through several rounds of peer review before they are published.

teile.einleitung: A polymer is a huge molecule made up of many identical or similar small building blocks. You can imagine it like a long string of beads. All plastics are polymers, but so are wood, silk and our DNA.
wichtigste: A polymer is a large molecule made of many identical or similar basic building blocks.
The individual building blocks are called monomers.
The word comes from Greek and means “many parts”.
There are natural polymers such as starch, cellulose and proteins.
Plastics such as PET or polyethylene are artificial polymers.
The chemist Hermann Staudinger, who did research at ETH Zurich for a long time, proved that such giant molecules exist.
Many plastics break down only very slowly in nature.

abschnitte.text: A **monomer** is a small molecule, a single bead, so to speak. If thousands of them are linked together, a polymer forms, a long chain. This process is called **polymerisation**. Some chains are straight, others branched or linked to each other like a net.

Nature makes many polymers. **Cellulose** makes wood and plant fibres firm, and starch is found in potatoes and bread. Proteins in muscles and hair are chains of amino acids. Silk, wool, natural rubber and DNA are also natural polymers.

For about 100 years people have been making polymers in factories, mostly from crude oil. Polyethylene is the most produced plastic in the world and is found in plastic bags and films. Drinks bottles are made from **PET**, tights and ropes from nylon. Polystyrene is known as the light, white foam in packaging.

**Thermoplastics** become soft when heated and can be reshaped, like PET. Thermosets stay hard and cannot be melted again after they have set, for example in plug sockets. Elastomers are stretchy and spring back into shape, like rubber bands or bicycle tyres. Which kind forms depends on how the chains are linked to each other.

For a long time researchers did not believe that such huge molecules could exist. **Hermann Staudinger** put forward this idea from 1920, at that time as a professor at ETH Zurich. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1953 and is regarded as the father of polymer chemistry. As early as 1908 the Swiss Jacques Edwin Brandenberger had invented the transparent film called cellophane.

In nature many plastics only break down into smaller and smaller pieces after hundreds of years. This **microplastic** is found today in seas, lakes and even in the snow of the Alps. In Switzerland PET bottles are collected, and a large part of them is made into new bottles again. Researchers are also developing plastics from plants that break down more easily.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small molecule that serves as a building block for a polymer.
The chemical reaction in which many monomers are joined into a chain.
A polymer that is usually made artificially.
Tiny plastic particles smaller than five millimetres.

gewusst: A single polymer chain can consist of more than a hundred thousand building blocks.
If you unrolled the DNA from a single human cell, it would be about two metres long.
Chewing gum consists largely of an artificial polymer.

teile.einleitung: Regression analysis is a statistical method for studying how one quantity depends on one or more other quantities. The best known is linear regression, in which a straight line is placed as well as possible through a cloud of points. With this line you can describe relationships and predict values.
wichtigste: Regression analysis describes how a target variable depends on explanatory variables.
In linear regression the line of best fit is usually found with the method of least squares.
The residual is the difference between the observed and the predicted value.
The coefficient of determination R² shows how well the line explains the data.
The term “regression” was coined by Francis Galton in the 19th century.
A relationship does not automatically mean that one quantity causes the other.
For target variables with only two possible values, logistic regression is used.

abschnitte.text: Imagine you record the temperature and the number of ice creams sold on many days in a chart. This produces a **cloud of points** that rises towards the top right. Regression analysis places a line through it that best describes the relationship. The quantity you want to explain is called the **target variable**, and the explaining quantities are called explanatory variables.

A straight line has the form y = a times x plus b. If the equation is, for example, y = 2x + 3, it predicts the value 13 for x = 5. The best line is usually found with the **method of least squares**: you make the sum of the squared distances of the points from the line as small as possible. The distance of a point from the line is called the **residual**; if the observed value is 20 and the prediction 17, the residual is 3.

abschnitte.titel: How well does the line fit?
abschnitte.text: The **coefficient of determination** R² lies between 0 and 1 and tells you what proportion of the variation is explained by the line. In simple linear regression R² is the square of the correlation coefficient r. So with r = 0.8, R² is 0.64, and the line explains 64 per cent of the variation. The closer R² is to 1, the more closely the points lie along the line.

On hot days more ice creams are sold and there are more swimming accidents. Even so, ice creams do not cause accidents; the **temperature** affects both. That is why further explanatory variables are included in a multiple regression to take out such confounding factors. It is also risky to use the line far beyond the observed data, because the relationship may no longer hold there.

Adrien-Marie Legendre published the method of least squares in 1805, and Carl Friedrich Gauss also worked with it. In the 19th century the Englishman **Francis Galton** studied the height of parents and their adult children. He noticed that children of very tall parents were on average a little less tall and moved towards the middle. He called this effect regression, meaning “going back”, and so the whole method got its name.

Regressions are used in almost all sciences, for example in medicine, economics, climate research and sport. With **logistic regression** you can estimate, for example, how likely someone is to fall ill or to stay healthy. Companies use it to estimate how the price affects sales. Many machine learning methods are also built on regression.

begriffe.erklaerung: The line that best describes the relationship in a cloud of points.
The distance between the observed value and the prediction.
A number between 0 and 1 that shows how well a model fits.
A measure of how strongly two quantities rise or fall together.
A prediction outside the range of the measured data.

gewusst: Regression to the mean explains why an exceptionally good match is often followed by a more average one.
With spreadsheet programs you can calculate a regression line in a few clicks.
Francis Galton was a cousin of Charles Darwin.

teile.einleitung: A trophy cup is a winner's cup that you can win in competitions. Originally it was a splendid drinking vessel for celebrations. Today trophies stand in display cabinets in clubs and schools and remind people of great victories.
wichtigste: A trophy cup is a winner's cup for winners.
Originally a cup like this was used for drinking.
A classic trophy cup often has two handles.
The name of the winner and the year are often engraved on trophies.
A challenge trophy is passed on to the new winner every year.
To defend a trophy means to win it again.
You stand a trophy up; you wear a medal.

abschnitte.text: A **trophy cup** is a cup or goblet, usually on a foot, that is awarded as a prize for winning. Classic trophies often have **two handles**. They are made of metal such as silver or brass, sometimes gilded, and today often also of plastic or glass. The German word “Pokal” comes from the Italian “boccale”, which means cup or jug. Unlike a medal, which you hang round your neck, you stand a trophy up.

abschnitte.titel: From drinking vessel to winner's prize
abschnitte.text: In the past a cup like this was a valuable **drinking vessel**. At feasts of nobles, guilds and towns, guests drank wine from it. Particularly elaborate cups of gold and silver were made by goldsmiths and were real treasures. Later such cups were awarded as gifts of honour. In this way the cup developed into the prize for winners in sport.

A **challenge trophy** does not belong to one team for ever. It is passed on to the new winner every year. The name of the winner and the year are often **engraved** on the trophy or its base. Over the years this creates a list of all the winners. Anyone who wins the trophy again has successfully **defended** it.

The best-known trophy in football is the golden **World Cup trophy**, which the best national teams in the world play for. In ice hockey there is the Stanley Cup, which has existed since 1892 and is one of the oldest sports trophies. The Champions League trophy has such big handles that it is nicknamed “big ears”. In Switzerland football clubs compete every year for the Swiss Cup. Many winners today receive a replica, while the original stays with the association.

It is not only professionals who win trophies. Schools, gymnastics clubs, chess clubs or shooting clubs also award trophies at tournaments. They often display their trophies in a **display cabinet** so that everyone can see their successes. At Swiss wrestling festivals, by the way, there are often live prizes such as a young bull as well as wreaths. For many children their first small trophy is a very special memory.

begriffe.erklaerung: A grip on the side of a vessel by which you can hold it.
Writing or decoration scratched into metal or glass.
A trophy that goes to the new winner every year.
A glass cupboard in which valuable things are displayed.

gewusst: Every year the names of the players of the winning team are added to the Stanley Cup in ice hockey, which is why it kept getting bigger.
The first football World Cup trophy, the Jules Rimet Trophy, was stolen in Brazil in 1983 and never found again.
Some trophies are so heavy that athletes can only lift them up with difficulty.

teile.einleitung: Petrichor is the name for the special smell that arises when rain falls on dry ground. Almost everyone knows this earthy, fresh scent after a summer shower. Behind it are tiny bacteria, plant oils and a bit of physics.
wichtigste: Petrichor is the name of the smell when rain falls on dry ground.
The earthy scent substance geosmin is made by tiny bacteria in the soil.
Oils from plants also contribute to the smell of rain.
Rain smells especially strong after a long dry spell.
People can smell even tiny amounts of geosmin.
Raindrops splash up tiny bubbles that carry the scent into the air.
Before a thunderstorm you sometimes smell fresh, sharp ozone.

abschnitte.text: The word **petrichor** was invented in 1964 by the Australian researchers Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas. It is made up of two Greek words. “Petra” means stone, and “ichor” was the blood of the gods in Greek legend. So the name means roughly “blood of the stones”. The two researchers studied where the typical smell of rain comes from.

An important part of the smell is the substance **geosmin**. It is made by tiny soil bacteria, above all the so-called streptomycetes. Translated, geosmin means “earth smell”. It is also the reason why freshly dug garden soil smells so typical. In addition, during dry periods **plant oils** collect on stones and in the soil, and these are also released when it rains.

abschnitte.titel: How does the scent get into the air?
abschnitte.text: In 2015 researchers in the USA filmed the process with high-speed cameras. When a drop falls on dry, loose ground, it traps small air bubbles. These rise and burst at the surface. In doing so, tiny droplets, called **aerosols**, are flung into the air. They carry the scent substances to our nose, similar to the bubbles in a glass of sparkling mineral water.

The human nose is extremely sensitive to **geosmin**. Even tiny amounts, much less than one drop in a swimming pool, are enough for us to smell it. After a long **dry spell** a particularly large amount of scent substances has built up, which is why the first rain then smells strongest. Light rain produces more bubbles than a heavy downpour. You also notice geosmin in drinking water immediately as an earthy aftertaste.

Sometimes it smells fresh and a little sharp even before a thunderstorm. That is **ozone**, a gas made of three oxygen atoms. It forms, among other things, through lightning, which splits oxygen in the air. Strong downdraughts from the storm cloud can carry the ozone down to the ground. So ozone does not smell of earth, but rather like chlorine.

Geosmin is found not only in the soil but also in some foods. **Beetroot**, called “Randen” in Switzerland and “Rote Bete” in Germany, tastes so earthy because of geosmin. Some freshwater fish such as carp can also taste of it. For the bacteria, geosmin is probably a lure. Researchers found out that tiny soil animals, springtails, are attracted by it and spread the bacteria's spores as they do so.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smell that arises when rain falls on dry ground.
An earthy-smelling substance made by soil bacteria.
Tiny droplets or particles that float in the air.
A gas made of three oxygen atoms with a fresh, sharp smell.

gewusst: When tap water sometimes tastes slightly musty or earthy, geosmin is often behind it too.
In India a perfume is even made from soil that smells of rain.
Beetroot tastes earthy because it contains the same scent substance as wet soil.

teile.einleitung: Pompeii was a Roman town on the Bay of Naples in Italy. In AD 79 a huge eruption of the volcano Vesuvius buried the town under a thick layer of ash and pumice. Because it was so well preserved, today it shows us everyday life in the Roman Empire like no other town.
wichtigste: Pompeii was buried in AD 79 in the eruption of Vesuvius.
The neighbouring town of Herculaneum was also buried at that time.
