Most of the people who stayed died in scorching avalanches of gas and ash.
Pliny the Younger described the eruption as an eyewitness in letters to Tacitus.
Systematic excavations began in 1748.
The famous casts of the victims were made by pouring plaster into hollows in the ash.
An inscription found in 2018 suggests that the eruption happened in the autumn rather than the summer.

abschnitte.text: Pompeii lay in the region of **Campania** south-east of Naples, at the foot of Vesuvius. The town probably had over 10,000 inhabitants. There was a forum as a marketplace, temples, theatres, public baths and an amphitheatre for gladiator fights. Traders sold bread, wine and hot food in bakeries and snack bars. As early as AD 62 a strong earthquake had damaged many buildings.

In AD 79 **Vesuvius** erupted. First pumice and ash rained down on the town for hours, and many roofs collapsed. Then **pyroclastic flows** of hot gas and ash raced down the mountain and killed the people who had stayed. As well as Pompeii, the neighbouring town of **Herculaneum** was also buried. For a long time 24 August was thought to be the date, but a charcoal inscription discovered in 2018 suggests that the eruption happened in the autumn instead.

The young Roman **Pliny the Younger** watched the eruption from a distance. Later he described it in two letters to the historian Tacitus. He told of a huge cloud that looked like a pine tree. His uncle, **Pliny the Elder**, was a fleet commander and wanted to rescue people but died in the attempt. That is why experts still call such eruptions “Plinian” today.

After the eruption Pompeii was forgotten for many centuries. In 1748 systematic **excavations** began. In the 19th century the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli had a brilliant idea. The bodies of the victims had left hollows in the hardened ash, into which he poured liquid **plaster**. This produced casts that show the position of the people at the moment of their death.

Pompeii has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 1997 and is visited by millions of people every year. You can walk through paved streets with stepping stones and cart tracks. On many house walls there are painted **election notices** and graffiti that tell us what people were thinking. At the entrance to one house, a floor mosaic with a dog and the words “Cave canem”, meaning “Beware of the dog”, gives a warning. The whole town has still not been excavated, and there are new discoveries all the time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mountain from which hot, molten rock and ash from inside the Earth come out.
A very hot cloud of gas, ash and rock that races down a volcano.
The science that studies the past through excavations.
A light, holey volcanic rock that can even float on water.

gewusst: In a bakery in Pompeii, charred loaves almost 2,000 years old were found.
Vesuvius is still active today and is considered one of the most dangerous volcanoes in the world, because very many people live near it.
Herculaneum was buried under a much thicker layer, so even wooden beams and furniture survived there.

teile.einleitung: Protein synthesis is the process in which cells make proteins according to the building plan in the DNA. Proteins are the most important tools and building materials of life. Every second, countless such production processes take place in your body.
wichtigste: Protein synthesis has two main steps, transcription and translation.
In translation, amino acids are linked together at the ribosomes.
The peptide bond forms between the carboxyl group and the amino group of two amino acids.
The chain grows from the N-terminus to the C-terminus.
During elongation, mainly GTP is used as the energy carrier.
In bacteria transcription and translation take place at the same time, because they have no nucleus.
After translation, proteins are often changed chemically.

abschnitte.text: The building plans for proteins are stored in the **DNA**. First a gene is copied into a messenger RNA, the **mRNA**; this is **transcription**. In plants, animals and humans this happens in the nucleus, after which the mRNA moves into the cytoplasm. In the second step, **translation**, the mRNA is translated into a chain of amino acids. You can compare it to a cookery book: the DNA is the book, the mRNA a copy of the recipe, and the protein is the finished dish.

mRNA is made of four building blocks, the bases A, U, G and C. Every three bases form a **codon**, which stands for a particular amino acid. This gives 64 possible codons for the 20 standard amino acids. The codon AUG is usually the **start signal**, and three other codons mean stop. The first part of this code was cracked by Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei in 1961.

Translation takes place at the **ribosomes**, the cell's small protein factories. Small transport molecules, the **tRNA**, each bring the matching amino acid to the ribosome. There the amino acids are linked by a **peptide bond** between the carboxyl group and the amino group. The chain grows from the N-terminus to the C-terminus. For this lengthening, elongation, mainly GTP is used as the energy carrier.

Proteins for the cell membrane or for export from the cell are made at ribosomes on the **rough endoplasmic reticulum**. A **signal peptide** at the start of the growing chain directs the ribosome there. In bacteria everything happens faster, because they have no nucleus. There transcription and translation happen at the same time, and the mRNA is already being translated while it is still being made. After translation many proteins are changed chemically; this is called **post-translational modification**.

Without protein synthesis there would be no life, because proteins do almost all the work in the cell. They build muscles, carry oxygen in the blood and fight off germs as antibodies. Many **antibiotics** work by blocking the ribosomes of bacteria but not those of humans. In biotechnology, bacteria or yeasts are made to produce proteins such as **insulin**. mRNA vaccines also use the protein synthesis of the body's cells.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance made of a chain of amino acids.
The basic building block of proteins.
A tiny cell machine that puts proteins together.
Messenger RNA, a copy of a gene that serves as building instructions.
Three bases in a row that stand for an amino acid.

gewusst: A ribosome in a bacterium can join about 15 to 20 amino acids together per second.
The hormone insulin consists of only 51 amino acids, while the muscle protein titin has over 30,000.
The genetic code is the same in almost all living things, from bacteria to humans.

teile.einleitung: A caterpillar is the larva of a butterfly or moth. Before it turns into an adult, it eats almost non-stop and grows very quickly. There are caterpillars of every colour, smooth or hairy, camouflaged or with striking patterns.
wichtigste: A caterpillar is the larva of a butterfly or moth.
A caterpillar spends most of the day eating.
When its skin becomes too tight, it moults.
At the front, on its thorax, a caterpillar has six legs.
Many caterpillars are green so that they are camouflaged on leaves.
You should not touch hairy caterpillars, because the hairs can irritate the skin.
The caterpillar of the silk moth spins a cocoon of silk.
In the end the caterpillar pupates and turns into a butterfly or moth.

abschnitte.text: A caterpillar has a soft, long body with a hard head and strong **mouthparts** for chewing. At the front, on its thorax, there are six real legs. Further back it also has fleshy **prolegs** with small hooks, with which it holds on to leaves. On its head there are silk glands, from which it can make silk threads.

After hatching, the caterpillar often first eats its **eggshell**. After that it eats leaves almost without stopping. Many caterpillars specialise in particular plants; the caterpillar of the peacock butterfly, for example, eats nettles. The caterpillars of the **large white** like to eat cabbage and are therefore not popular in vegetable gardens.

A caterpillar's skin does not grow with it. When it becomes too tight, the caterpillar slips out of its old skin; this is called **moulting**. A caterpillar usually moults four or five times. When it is fully grown, it turns into a pupa, from which the adult butterfly or moth later emerges.

Caterpillars are popular food for birds, so they have many tricks. Green caterpillars are well **camouflaged** on leaves, and others look like a twig or bird droppings. Some have bright warning colours because they are poisonous or taste bad. Hairy caterpillars such as those of the oak processionary moth have stinging hairs that can cause itching and rashes in people.

The caterpillar of the **silk moth** eats mulberry leaves and spins itself into a cocoon made of a single, very long silk thread. Silk has been made from these threads for thousands of years, first in China. Switzerland also used to have an important silk industry, especially in Zurich and Basel. In nature caterpillars are important food for birds, which feed them to their young.

begriffe.erklaerung: The young form of an animal, which looks different from the adult.
Shedding the old skin when it has become too tight.
The resting stage in which the caterpillar is rebuilt into a butterfly or moth.
The complete change from caterpillar via pupa to butterfly or moth.
A protective covering of silk threads around the pupa.

gewusst: During their life as caterpillars, some caterpillars become a thousand times heavier than they were when they hatched.
A silk thread from a single cocoon can be several hundred metres long.
When in danger, the caterpillar of the swallowtail can push out an orange fork behind its head that smells unpleasant.

teile.einleitung: The replication crisis refers to the discovery that many published research results cannot be confirmed when the studies are repeated. Psychology and medicine are especially affected. The crisis has led researchers today to do many things differently and more openly.
wichtigste: In a 2015 project, only about a third of 100 psychology studies again showed a significant result.
According to a 2012 report, only 6 out of 53 landmark cancer studies could be confirmed.
In 2005 John Ioannidis published the article “Why Most Published Research Findings Are False”.
In 2011 experiments by Daryl Bem sparked a debate about research methods.
In preregistration, hypotheses and analysis are set down before the data is collected.
“HARKing” means making up hypotheses only after knowing the results.
In 2017, 72 researchers proposed lowering the significance threshold for new discoveries to 0.005.

abschnitte.text: A **replication** is the repetition of a study to check whether the result is right. From about 2010 researchers found that many well-known results no longer appeared when the studies were repeated. This affected mainly psychology, but also medicine, biology and economics. So people spoke of a crisis of trust in research.

As early as 2005 the article “Why Most Published Research Findings Are False” by **John Ioannidis** appeared. In 2012 researchers at a pharmaceutical company reported that only 6 out of 53 landmark cancer studies could be confirmed. In 2015 a large team repeated 100 psychology studies in the **Reproducibility Project**. Only about a third again showed a significant result.

In 2011 the psychologist **Daryl Bem** published experiments that supposedly showed that people can sense the future. The studies had been carried out correctly according to the usual rules of the time. That is exactly what made many experts suspicious. If the usual methods could “prove” something so unlikely, something had to be wrong with the methods.

One reason is that scientific journals prefer to print spectacular results rather than studies that found nothing. Some researchers tried out different analyses until a result became **significant** by chance; this is called p-hacking. In **HARKing** you only make up the hypothesis once you already know the results. In addition, many studies had been carried out with too few participants.

In **preregistration** researchers set down their hypotheses and analysis before they collect data. With a “registered report” the study is even reviewed before the data is collected, and the journal promises to publish it whatever the result. More and more researchers put their data openly on the internet. In 2017, 72 researchers also proposed lowering the threshold for new discoveries from 0.05 to 0.005.

begriffe.erklaerung: Repeating a study to check its result.
A result that probably did not come about just by chance.
A guess that you want to test with a study.
Setting down the plan of a study before collecting data.
Analysing data in different ways until a desired result comes out by chance.

gewusst: Today the replication crisis is seen as an example of how science can check and improve itself.
Studies that found nothing often used to disappear into a drawer; this is called the file drawer problem.
About 270 researchers from all over the world worked on the 2015 Reproducibility Project.
